articles.title: Cardano’s 2027 budget proposal would let funding stewards seek grants too
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Three institutions could shape Cardano funding assessments and seek grants under a proposed framework requiring disclosure and safeguards.
- DReps would retain withdrawal approval, and Open Contributions would let applicants seek funding directly without a steward.
- The proposed 2027 trial leaves direct funding allocations and common conflict procedures unspecified before a tentative November 10 concept submission.
Cardano’s proposed 2027 budget process would let three institutions help design how funding requests are assessed while remaining eligible to seek money from the same spending domains.
The proposed Cardano Ecosystem Budget Process, or CEBP, published by Intersect on Oct. 28, would assign stewardship roles to Intersect, PRAGMA and the Cardano Foundation across six areas of spending. Delegated representatives, or DReps, would retain approval of the stewards, budget distribution and every treasury withdrawal. The institutions’ influence would come earlier, through the plans and assessment processes that help shape those votes.
For independent applicants, the balance depends on how conflicts are handled and how much funding remains available through Open Contributions, a proposed route that would let anyone approach DReps without a steward. The published framework leaves that route’s allocation and common procedures for assessing steward-related funding unspecified.
In its Oct. 30 update, Intersect said feedback remained open ahead of a tentative Nov. 10 submission of the overall concept. The process would run as a trial in 2027 only if DReps approve.
How Cardano budget stewards would shape funding choices
Each proposed steward would help develop its domain’s strategy, recommend a dollar-denominated budget cap in coordination with other stewards, and define how applications are collected and assessed. It could submit proposals itself or support others in bringing them to an on-chain vote.
Delivery oversight would also depend on the structure chosen for each proposal. The framework allows different arrangements, from teams retaining their own administration to more coordinated delivery contracts.
| Proposed steward | Spending domains | 
|---|---|
| Intersect | Core Development and Maintenance; Applied Research; Governance Coordination | 
| PRAGMA | Developer Support | 
| Cardano Foundation | Marketing, Analysis & Events; Adoption & Ecosystem Growth | 
| No steward | Open Contributions, allowing direct applications to DReps | 
These responsibilities could influence which needs are prioritized, how competing requests are compared and what information reaches voters. DReps would still decide whether the resulting proposals receive funding.
Intersect presents the approach as a response to overloaded DReps facing numerous, hard-to-compare requests with insufficient expert guidance. Common presentation standards and domain expertise could make those decisions easier. The same assessment role makes the treatment of an institution’s own funding proposals consequential.
The proposal expressly allows a steward to receive funding from its domain, provided that funding is transparently declared and accompanied by safeguards. An award would still require DRep approval.
The published framework promises a common public code of conduct in the planned information action, a proposal seeking DRep support for the concept. Common recusal, independent assessment and appeals procedures for funding proposals involving stewards remain unspecified in the published text.
There are existing, narrower provisions. Intersect’s Growth & Marketing Committee working terms, which remain subject to ratification and adjustment, require potential conflicts to be disclosed to committee leadership. They specifically address reviews involving members’ working relationships and allow sanctions for code violations.
The Budget Committee grievance process covers conflicts and concerns about process fairness, with escalation through Intersect’s leadership to its board. The procedure applies specifically to that committee’s activities and stakeholder interactions.
Existing payment oversight applies after funding approval. The existing 2026 budget FAQ says the five-member independent Oversight Committee checks administrative disbursements, with funding selection outside its remit.
The direct route and decisions still ahead
Open Contributions would be the seventh domain, with no steward. Any proposer could go straight to DReps. The Net Change Limit, or NCL, sets the overall treasury withdrawal limit. The framework says the information action setting it would suggest moving a rejected stewarded domain’s proposed budget into that open route.
Those provisions preserve alternatives to the institutional process. Their practical importance will depend partly on the numbers: domain caps and any guaranteed share for Open Contributions remain unspecified. The framework anticipates an allowance to be developed alongside the other budgets.
In DRepTalk consultation feedback, the participant posting as SIPO proposed giving Open Contributions its own explicit share of the overall withdrawal limit. SIPO also sought disclosure of stewards’ roles and relationships with applicants. Those suggestions remain part of the consultation.
DReps’ own commitments would matter too. Intersect says direct on-chain enforcement of the framework is unavailable. It would rely on supporting DReps making a social commitment to follow the process in the relevant domains, including withholding support from withdrawals outside the agreed process.
That could make the agreed application rules influential without introducing a technical barrier to submission. DReps would remain able to reject a domain plan or move to another model, while independent applicants would still need to persuade them to approve funding.
The tentative Nov. 10 action would seek support for the concept and task stewards with preparing detailed domain plans. DReps’ commitment to the framework for 2027 would be sought through the later domain actions.
Intersect envisages a second round in December 2026 or January 2027 covering domain arrangements and the 2027 NCL. The framework sets a goal of at least 51% DRep support for the concept and at least 60% DRep support for each domain’s stewardship mandate. It describes 51% DRep support for the NCL. Those statements concern the proposed information-action process and social commitments. Individual treasury withdrawals would continue to require their own approvals.
The published versions also leave an action-count discrepancy. Six stewarded domains plus an NCL action imply seven; the blog describes eight. Intersect’s forum copy says seven before referring to an eighth. Neither version consistently explains the total.
Existing contracts are separate from those future choices. On Oct. 17, Intersect reported 25 vendor smart contracts worth 204,639,279 ADA from the 2026 budget cycle.
For applicants, the proposed next round would set out how much money each route could offer and how assessment would work when a steward also seeks funding. DReps would retain the final funding decision; the code of conduct and the size of Open Contributions will help determine how much choice applicants have before that vote.

articles.title: Tracked Binance wallets record $2.5 billion in outflows as withdrawals reopen after hack
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Tracked Binance wallets recorded $2,510 million in net crypto outflows on Nov. 1 as withdrawal access resumed after the $6.3 billion hack.
- Bitcoin and USDT accounted for nearly $2 billion in tracked net outflows.
- Binance warned of possible congestion and moved withdrawals to newly generated wallets, complicating any customer-exit estimate.
Binance's tracked cryptocurrency wallets recorded $2,510 million in net outflows on Nov. 1 after the exchange resumed withdrawals following its $6.3 billion security breach.
According to DeFiLlama data, the outflows included approximately $1,083 million in USDT, $912 million in Bitcoin, $385 million in USDC and $131 million in wrapped Ethereum.
These outflows coincided with Binance's phased reopening of withdrawal services after the Oct. 29 attack, which the FBI attributed to North Korea's TraderTraitor hacking operation.
Binance restores withdrawals as executives warn of possible congestion
In a Nov. 1 announcement, Binance said it was gradually restoring withdrawal access across 15 blockchain networks after completing additional security reviews.
The exchange initially reopened withdrawals for Bitcoin, Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain, XRP and Base, then confirmed support for Dogecoin and Optimism.
Other supported networks in the first phase include Solana, Tron, Arbitrum, Avalanche, Polygon, Zcash and Sui, with individual assets becoming available as security checks are completed.
Binance co-founder Yi He said withdrawal processing was proceeding without significant disruption, although increased demand could temporarily affect transaction processing. She wrote on X:
“Things are currently running fairly smoothly. If there are many withdrawal requests, congestion cannot be ruled out, after which it will smooth out again.”
He also urged customers to verify withdrawal addresses and ensure their devices and operating environments were secure before transferring funds.
Meanwhile, Binance has updated its proof-of-reserves wallet address list to include newly generated wallets, which it said would process all subsequent withdrawals.
The infrastructure changes followed the multibillion-dollar breach that forced Binance to temporarily suspend withdrawals while investigators examined its compromised hot-wallet systems.
Binance has maintained that customer funds remain protected and that the company will absorb the financial losses from the attack.
The exchange said it replenished about 95% of the affected assets through corporate resources and market purchases, up from 90% in its previous update.
It also reported that balances in Bitcoin, Ethereum, USDT, USDC, BNB, Solana, XRP, USD1, RLUSD and Zcash were fully backed, while the remaining unreplenished assets consisted primarily of less-liquid tokens.
However, replacing stolen assets does not mean the original funds have been recovered from the attackers. Binance continues working with law enforcement and industry partners to trace and potentially recover those assets.
The extent to which the observed on-chain outflows reflect customers moving assets elsewhere remains uncertain, particularly as Binance transitions withdrawals to newly generated wallets.
The exchange has pledged to publish a detailed post-incident investigation report, while its updated proof-of-reserves disclosures are expected to provide further information about the assets backing customer balances.

articles.title: Crypto scammers used SEC's website to lure investors into alleged $130 million fraud
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Two crypto firms allegedly exploited the SEC's own filing system to promote a $130 million scheme promising 60% monthly returns.
- More than 223,000 blockchain addresses sent funds to the scheme as fabricated trading profits and false regulatory claims fueled investor confidence.
- The SEC has removed the misleading filings and sued both firms, but recovering the more than $100 million in alleged investor losses remains unresolved.
The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has removed regulatory filings allegedly used to legitimize a $130 million crypto investment fraud.
In an Oct. 29 announcement, the regulator said BG Wealth Sharing and DSJ Exchange submitted false disclosures to its public databases and subsequently presented those records to prospective investors as evidence of government authorization.
The scheme allegedly raised more than $130 million from tens of thousands of investors across the United States and abroad, resulting in losses exceeding $100 million.
According to the SEC, the companies operated between at least October 2025 and June 2026, promoting a cryptocurrency investment program that promised monthly returns of at least 60% and claimed investors could double their money within 40 days without risk.
BG Wealth portrayed itself as the world's largest hedge fund and an SEC-licensed investment adviser, while DSJ Exchange claimed to run a secure cryptocurrency trading platform that executed profitable trades.
However, investigators alleged that the promised trading activity was fictitious and the companies diverted most investor deposits rather than investing them as advertised.
How the firms exploited the SEC's own filing system
The alleged fraud relied heavily on the credibility of the SEC's public disclosure infrastructure, which allows investors to research financial businesses and securities offerings.
According to the SEC's civil complaint, BG Wealth submitted a Form ADV claiming exempt reporting adviser status, while DSJ Exchange filed a Form D announcing a purported $100 million securities offering.
The filings became publicly accessible through the SEC's Investment Adviser Public Disclosure system and EDGAR database, allowing the promoters to direct prospective investors to government-hosted records as supposed proof of legitimacy.
The companies allegedly reinforced those claims with fabricated registration certificates bearing the SEC's official seal and identifiers associated with their filings.
Neither company was registered with or licensed by the SEC, and submitting those forms did not constitute regulatory approval.
The deception extended beyond regulatory credentials.
BG Wealth claimed its proprietary trading technology generated signals with 99.6% accuracy, while DSJ Exchange displayed fictitious trades, profits, and growing account balances.
Investigators found that the defendants received more than $130 million from over 223,000 blockchain addresses between March and early June 2026.
The SEC alleges that no more than $25 million was returned to addresses likely belonging to investors through Ponzi-like payments, while the remaining funds were largely misappropriated.
The operation also employed social media campaigns, encrypted messaging platforms, weekly video conferences, and recruitment incentives to attract new participants.
When investors tried to withdraw their funds, the companies allegedly imposed fees of up to 20% and delayed withdrawals before eventually blocking access altogether.
The defendants subsequently demanded additional tax payments and encouraged investors to move their assets to another platform, HQI Exchange, without restoring withdrawal access.
The SEC has now removed BG Wealth's Form ADV and DSJ Exchange's Form D from its public websites.
The regulator also filed a civil lawsuit in the Northern District of California seeking permanent injunctions, financial penalties and the repayment of allegedly unlawful gains with interest.
It additionally asked the court to prohibit BG Wealth from submitting future Form ADV filings as an exempt reporting adviser.

articles.title: Cursor urges credential resets after malicious Claude Code marketplace update
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Cursor identified malicious Claude Code extension versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for macOS and Windows in its marketplace.
- Uninstalling may leave persistence behind, while successful remote access depended on SSH configuration and host permissions.
- Cursor recommends host cleanup and rotating accessible credentials and sessions from a trusted system; crypto theft is not established.
Code editor Cursor is urging developers who installed malicious Claude Code extension packages from its marketplace to clean affected machines and rotate accessible credentials and sessions from a trusted system. Removing the extension alone may leave persistent components running, the company warns.
The affected packages are Anthropic.claude-code versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for macOS and Windows. Cursor’s security notice places their availability between about 2:27 a.m. and 1:35 p.m. PT on Oct. 29, 2026. Cursor says Anthropic did not develop the malicious versions and reports no evidence that other versions or the official distribution were affected.
Cursor clarified the affected versions and indicators on Oct. 30. Security researcher Phorion updated its malware analysis on Oct. 31 to include both versions, having initially identified only 2.1.313.
Why uninstalling may leave access behind
According to Phorion, the payload attempts to add an attacker-controlled SSH key, enable the machine’s SSH remote-login service and establish a reverse tunnel. With SSH running, the planted key could let an attacker log in through that tunnel. Persistence mechanisms include a macOS LaunchAgent and, on Windows, an attempted scheduled task with a Startup-folder fallback.
Phorion says the injected code executes when Node loads the extension module, before its normal activation callback. No further interaction with the extension is required at that point.
Successful remote access also depended on the host. Phorion found that a permission-check bug causes the macOS code to skip enabling Remote Login when run as a standard user. If SSH was already enabled, or enabled later, the planted key could still permit access while the tunnel was operational.
Cursor says it worked with the hosting provider to take the attacker server offline. It also removed the packages, rotated its keys and rebuilt and reopened the marketplace. Those steps do not remove components already left on an affected machine.
The initial beacon reported host information and up to 40 matching environment-variable names, rather than their secret values, according to Phorion. Cursor cautions that this limited collection does not rule out later credential access through the backdoor.
For crypto developers, Cursor’s advice would extend to development or financial-service credentials accessible to the affected local user account, if present. Neither advisory establishes cryptocurrency theft or crypto-specific targeting.
Cursor recommends checking endpoint, network and extension-installation records, isolating hosts showing payload execution or backdoor installation, and removing unauthorized SSH keys, persistence mechanisms and running tunnels. Its notice provides platform-specific remediation scripts and advises assessing whether the host should be rebuilt.
Cursor also recommends rotating credentials and sessions accessible from affected hosts using a trusted system.

articles.title: Bitcoin redemption freeze puts $136 million Aave market under scrutiny
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Threshold's unexpected Bitcoin redemption shutdown prompted Aave and Gauntlet to restrict exposure to the tokenized BTC asset.
- Approximately $136 million in tBTC sits on Aave, with holders facing potential liquidity risks if the bridge suspension persists.
- Despite assurances that no funds were lost, Threshold has yet to explain the security issue or confirm when Bitcoin redemptions will resume.
Aave has restricted new deposits and borrowing against $136 million in tokenized Bitcoin after Threshold Network suspended tBTC minting and redemptions.
The Oct. 31 intervention followed Threshold's decision to halt operations on its Bitcoin bridge while conducting undisclosed security maintenance, prompting decentralized lending protocols to limit their exposure to the asset.
In an Oct. 31 security update, Threshold said the token remained fully backed, with approximately 4,320 BTC held in bridge wallets against 4,185 tBTC in circulation.
“tBTC remains fully backed, and no funds have been lost,” the project stated, adding that investigators had found no unauthorized token minting.
The reserves exceed the circulating supply by about 135 BTC, reassuring holders about the assets backing the token even as they temporarily lose access to direct Bitcoin redemptions.
Threshold maintained that the situation was contained and that bridge functionality would return after remediation. However, it has not disclosed the specific security issue that prompted the suspension or provided a reopening date.
Existing tBTC remains transferable across Ethereum and layer-2 networks, although new Bitcoin deposits, token minting and redemption requests are suspended. Pending transactions will be completed when operations resume.
Aave and Gauntlet move to contain Bitcoin lending exposure
The suspension prompted Aave risk service provider LlamaRisk to recommend an immediate freeze of tBTC on the protocol's Ethereum V3 Core market.
According to an Oct. 31 governance notice, Aave's guardian multisig executed the restriction at 10:01 UTC, preventing users from depositing additional tBTC or using the token to increase borrowing power.
At the time, approximately 1,760 tBTC worth $136.6 million was supplied to the market, representing roughly 42% of the token's circulating supply.
The concentration highlights the significance of Aave's decision, especially because tBTC lets Bitcoin holders deploy their assets as collateral for loans across decentralized finance.
The restriction applies only to Aave's Ethereum Core tBTC reserve, as the token's markets on Base and Arbitrum had already been frozen during earlier asset deprecation rounds.
Existing users can continue repaying loans and withdrawing eligible collateral, while liquidations remain active under existing risk parameters.
LlamaRisk said it would continue monitoring collateral positions and secondary-market liquidity before recommending that Aave restore normal operations.
Other DeFi risk managers have also moved to reduce exposure.
In an Oct. 31 statement, Gauntlet disclosed that its Ethereum Morpho USDC Core vault had approximately 704,000 USDC supplied to a lending market backed by tBTC collateral.
The firm placed the market on its emergency exclusion list and withdrew approximately 65,000 USDC in available liquidity, leaving around 640,000 USDC supplied.
Gauntlet warned that the redemption suspension could affect tBTC's secondary-market liquidity and the ability of lenders to exit positions during liquidations.
The concern arises because tBTC holders who want native Bitcoin must rely on secondary-market buyers while Threshold's redemption mechanism remains suspended.
Any significant deterioration in liquidity or a discount to Bitcoin could make collateral liquidations more difficult, particularly for lending markets with substantial exposure to the token.
Threshold has urged users not to send Bitcoin to previously generated deposit addresses or repeat pending transactions. It pledged to provide another security update within 24 hours of its Oct. 31 announcement, or sooner if circumstances change.

articles.title: Binance Sees $5.8B in Net Outflows After Record Hack
articles.text:
Binance net outflows surge to $5.8B as withdrawals resume after record hack
The exchange says withdrawals surged after some services resumed but have since slowed, with the outflows representing a fraction of its roughly $171 billion in customer assets.
Binance has recorded $5.8 billion in net outflows over the past 24 hours as customers withdraw funds following the exchange’s record $6.3 billion hack, according to data from DefiLlama.
Binance said it began restoring withdrawals at 6:00 UTC on Sunday. By 3:30 UTC, it had processed $4.6 billion in withdrawals against $1 billion in deposits, resulting in net outflows of $3.6 billion.
Separate data from DefiLlama showed $5.8 billion in net outflows over the preceding 24 hours, as funds continued leaving the exchange after its initial update.
Binance said withdrawals initially surged but have since slowed and are stabilizing. The exchange noted that the outflows represented a small portion of the approximately $171 billion in assets it holds. Cointelegraph reached out to Binance for comment but did not receive an immediate response.
The flows offered an early test of customer confidence following the $6.3 billion hack against Binance, the largest crypto theft on record.
Related: Binance says phase one of withdrawals opens after $6.3B hack
Binance’s latest update at 12:36 UTC shows it enabled withdrawals for tokens across 15 networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain and XRP Ledger, adding that it will continue to restore additional assets and networks in phases.
Early data shared by Binance shows that the largest share of withdrawals were in USDt (USDT), followed by USDC (USDC) and Bitcoin (BTC).
On Saturday, Binance said it had replaced 90% of the assets lost in the $6.3 billion hack using funds from its corporate treasury, its Secure Asset Fund for Users and its futures insurance fund.
Magazine: $3.64B flees Binance on reopen, THORChain co-founder opposes coin freeze: Hodler’s Digest

articles.title: $3.6B Flees Binance On Reopen, THORChain Founder Opposes Coin Freeze: Hodler’s Digest
articles.text:
Billions flee Binance on reopen, THORChain founder opposes coin freeze: Hodler’s Digest
Binance has reopened withdrawals following the world’s biggest ever hack, and THORChain co-founder argues it should not halt the protocol to comply with FBI demands.
Binance reopens withdrawals
Binance has reopened withdrawals for 15 blockchain networks, after $6.3 billion was stolen by North Korean hackers from its hot wallets late last week.
Binance said today it had processed around $4.65 billion in withdrawals after reopening and received $1 billion in deposits. Founder Changpeng Zhao said that in the first 12 hours there had only been a 2.1% net outflow and that “98% choose to stay!”
DeFi Llama’s Binance wallet tracker shows $5.8 billion in outflows over 24 hours, however its figures may include internal transfers or movements into new hot wallets.
About 95% of the stolen crypto has already been replenished, using a mixture of Binance’s corporate reserves, insurance and 50% of the funds in the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU).
The biggest hack in history happened on Thursday, when North Korea’s TraderTraitor group gained access to delegated wallet permissions via a compromised laptop. Blockaid CEO Ido Ben-Natan told Cointelegraph that attackers could have stolen the funds without using EIP-7702 (account abstraction), but it may have helped them bypass safeguards and drain assets in one sweep.
Binance co-CEO Richard Teng rejected the idea the hack could be attributed to a single compromised laptop.
“To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer’s permissions, and this was not a single ‘one-click’ action,” he said. “Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual.”
FBI and Secret Service swoop in to help save billions
Zhao thanked the Secret Service today for “acting within minutes to help track and freeze stolen funds... your speed, expertise and dedication helped contain the damage.”
Elliptic estimated that about $2.84 billion of the stolen assets, mostly USDC and USDT, had been frozen on chain leaving the hackers with $3.33 billion. The attacker raced against time to beat the unprecedented stablecoin blocks by borrowing about $44.6 million of ETH against stablecoins on Aave.
The FBI attributed blame for the attack to the TraderTraitor hackers, which is associated with North Korea’s Lazarus Group and were also blamed for multibillion hacks of Bybit and Bitget. President Donald Trump indicated “we’ll talk to North Korea about it.” The FBI also released a list of addresses connected to the hack and pointedly singled out THORnode operators, RPC node operators, instant exchanges, DeFi services, blockchain analytics firms and other digital asset service providers to block transactions with or derived from addresses.
Source: CZ
THORChain founder rejects freeze request
The North Korean hackers have used THORChain to permissionlessly swap cryptocurrencies following previous attacks, and the price of the protocol’s native token RUNE jumped 13% in expectation of all those fees. 
Unfortunately for TraderTraitor, nine chains on THORChain, including Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tron on THORChain, are currently halted after automated systems paused the protocol for unrelated reasons shortly after the hack occurred.
Source: Vadim
According to THORChain developer Chad Barraford on the Unchained podcast, only around 50 or so individuals operate the 100 THORChain nodes. If the node operators refuse to halt the protocol or block addresses, as seems likely based on past incidents and public statements, they could face prosecution given the scale of the thefts and the involvement of the FBI and Secret Service.
THORChain founder JP Thor (who claims he is no longer involved) argued strongly that THORNode operators should not cooperate and should remain true to the ideals of decentralization and permissionlessness. “IMO if THORNodes decided to take the protocol offline next week then the experiment is over,” he said. 
“The last bastion of unencumbered and neutral settlement is over. There will simply be no other venue and the protocol would have failed.” 
If one third plus one of THORnode operators vote in favor they can halt activity. Nodes can also leave the network if they do not wish to process the funds. THORChain can operate with as few as four nodes processing transactions.
Lookonchain reports the attackers have also been using cross chain platform Relay to swap about half of $95.9 million of stolen SOL into Bitcoin.
Source: JP Thor
Ramifications of the hack
Crypto related stocks including Coinbase, Circle and Strategy sold off sharply following the hack, and crypto markets took a dive. But Strive CEO Matt Cole commented on Friday that Bitcoin had held up better than expected.
“I do have conviction that over any reasonable time frame, this does not change the investment thesis on Bitcoin,” Cole said. Bitcoin bottomed out around $76.5K and had recovered to 77,745 at the time of writing.  
In the wake of the attack, Nasdaq-listed firm Next Technology Holding announced its board has approved selling off its 5833 Bitcoin Treasury worth around $450 million. 
The attackers have reportedly amassed at least 18,000 Bitcoin and 430,000 Ether from the theft and subsequent swaps, although some tallies of the funds in the addresses identified by the FBI put the tally much higher at 551,612 ETH and 18,270 BTC. There are concerns that if those currencies are sold off quickly, that it would put downward pressure on BTC and ETH prices.
Meanwhile, Senator Cynthia Lummis and The Digital Chamber both used the hack to again push for crypto legislation to help prevent and mitigate the effects of future attacks. 
Tampered Trezor linked to CryptoBilis reseller
Trezor has urged customers who bought its hardware wallets from former authorized reseller CryptoBilis since March to move their funds after a report of a suspected implant in a Safe 5 device.
Trezor said Friday that a customer in Indonesia reported an unauthorized circuit board inside a Trezor Safe 5 bought on Tokopedia in August. Trezor said it had not yet examined the device and had received no reports of related losses.
The warning follows reports of crypto losses involving Ledger wallets sold through CryptoBilis that surfaced on Oct. 9. Ledger confirmed an unauthorized hardware implant in one device.
Winners and Losers
At the end of the week, Bitcoin (BTC) is down 3% to trade at $77,745, Ethereum (ETH) is down 3.5% to trade at $2,260 and XRP (XRP) is down 3.9% to $1.02. The total market cap is at $2.21 trillion according to CoinMarketCap.
Among the biggest 100 cryptocurrencies, the top three altcoin winners of the week are Hyperliquid (HYPE) with a 13.7% gain, Midnight (NIGHT) on 12.6%, and Pepe (PEPE) on 12.6%.
The top three altcoin losers of the week are Curve DAO (CRV) which was down 18.6%, VeChain (VET) down 15.9% and Worldcoin down 13.8%.
Prediction of the Week
Binance hack could accelerate shift to DEXs: Standard Chartered
Standard Chartered’s Geoffrey Kendrick said one big winner from the hack was likely to be decentralized exchanges and reaffirmed his conviction in Uniswap and the UNI token.
“The decentralized exchange [Uniswap] has never had any exploits, and the hack of the largest centralized exchange, in Binance, should see the ratio of DEX to CEX trading continue to increase.”
The ratio is currently around 23.5%. Kendrick said he retains his $100 price target for Uniswap (UNI) for 2030. He said the Binance hack is “another reason why that forecast may end up being too low.”
Top FUD of the Week
CFTC chair warns of AI Agents dangers
CFTC chair Mike Selig says autonomous AI agents could challenge financial rules built around human traders, and regulators need to adapt. Selig said Super Intelligence (SI) could give smaller traders and businesses access to risk-management that was once reserved for larger institutions.
“SI can help process the vast amount of information significantly faster than human brain power and with greater accuracy,” he said.
But greater autonomy also comes with new risks. Agents could react unexpectedly to market conditions, while those using similar models could generate correlated trading behavior. The speed of autonomous transactions could also complicate market surveillance and risk management, he said.
Blockchain investigator Chainalysis hit by cybersecurity incident
Blockchain analytics company Chainalysis said it was targeted in a cybersecurity incident, similar to those suffered recently by other platforms.
“Based on the investigation to date, we have found no evidence of unauthorized access to investigation content, authentication credentials, or session tokens,” it said in a blog post on Friday. Some non-sensitive customer data was exposed, including user IDs, names and email addresses.
Chainalysis said it was using large language models to review its security and added the incident was not related to the recent crypto theft at Binance.
Texas brothers sentenced to 15 years in prison for armed crypto robbery
Raymond Christian Garcia and Isiah Angelo Garcia, both of Waller, Texas, were sentenced to 180 months and 186 months in prison, respectively, for their armed robbery of cryptocurrency and kidnapping of a family in Grant, Minnesota.
The brothers were sentenced on Thursday before US District Judge Donovan W. Frank, according to a Friday news release. They had pleaded guilty in June.
On Sept. 19, 2025, the brothers, who had traveled from Texas to Minnesota, kidnapped Victim 1 and his family in their home at gunpoint, court documents said. They zip‑tied the family at gunpoint and held them for more than nine hours, demanding access to Victim 1’s cryptocurrency accounts.
Top Magazine Features of the Week
Bitcoin turns 18: Has the original rebel grown up?
In typical Bitcoin style, the number one cryptocurrency turns 18 amid AI-driven security threats, quantum fears and the biggest exchange hack in crypto history.
Binance hackers raced to move billions before it could be frozen
Attackers raced to convert stolen stablecoins into crypto that issuers could not freeze as industry players like Tether and Circle moved to immobilize billions of dollars in assets.
Will gold’s ‘infinite mint bug’ make Bitcoin more valuable?
A US fusion startup says it has turned mercury into gold. Could a potential increase in the gold supply strengthen Bitcoin’s claim to be a better form of digital gold?

articles.title: OneKey founder warns BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF could be a North Korean target
articles.text:
Quick Take
- OneKey's founder warns that BlackRock's $62 billion Bitcoin ETF could be a North Korean target following the $6 billion Binance hack.
- IBIT’s roughly 815,000 BTC in the Oct. 29 holdings file represented about 3.9% of Bitcoin’s maximum supply.
- Coinbase said it adjusted cold storage systems as a precaution; the Bybit hack showed how a compromised signing interface could defeat offline key storage.
North Korean hackers could target BlackRock's $62 billion Bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF), crypto wallet maker OneKey founder Yishi Wang warned.
“I suspect IBIT is already on North Korea's shortlist,” Wang said, following the $6 billion Binance hack that US authorities attributed to North Korea's TraderTraitor operation.
The warning puts fresh attention on Coinbase, which serves as the primary Bitcoin custodian for BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT), the world's largest spot Bitcoin ETF. CryptoSlate’s April 8 snapshot put funds naming Coinbase in a custody role at more than 80% of US Bitcoin ETF assets.
Coinbase has already made precautionary changes to its offline storage infrastructure following the Binance breach. In an Oct. 29 statement, Chief Security Officer Jeff Lunglhofer said the exchange was blocking transfers to compromised Binance wallets and had adjusted its cold storage systems out of an abundance of caution.
The company maintained that its infrastructure remained secure.
Why BlackRock's Bitcoin ETF could face significant risks
Wang's concern stems from the techniques North Korean attackers have used in previous cryptocurrency thefts, particularly the February 2025 Bybit hack, which resulted in approximately $1.5 billion in losses.
During that operation, hackers compromised a Safe{Wallet} developer's computer through malicious software disguised as legitimate development tooling.
According to a forensic investigation by Sygnia, the attackers manipulated the transaction interface used by Bybit's authorized signers, deceiving them into approving a malicious transfer from a cold wallet.
The attackers did not need to extract the private keys to execute the theft because they had compromised the process through which legitimate transactions were approved.
Similar concerns have emerged following the Binance breach.
Blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs found that the attackers executed coordinated transfers across 10 blockchains, including transactions involving pre-signed authorizations on Ethereum.
TRM assessed that the attack likely involved compromised hot-wallet signing infrastructure.
Binance initially identified a compromised employee laptop as a possible entry point before disclosing additional breach points. The exchange maintained that investigators had found no evidence of leaked private keys.
These incidents have raised questions about the security of institutional custody arrangements, where offline storage can still depend on vulnerable software, hardware, and transaction approval systems.
According to BlackRock's fund data, IBIT held approximately $62 billion in net assets as of Oct. 30. Its Oct. 29 holdings file listed roughly 815,000 BTC.
That represents nearly 4% of Bitcoin's maximum supply, making the fund a particularly consequential concentration of cryptocurrency under institutional custody.
Although BlackRock has appointed Anchorage Digital as an additional custodian, its June 30 quarterly filing said the fund has no current plans to transfer Bitcoin away from Coinbase.
Wang argued that this concentration creates significant exposure because a compromise affecting critical custody infrastructure could threaten assets held on behalf of investors.
However, there is no evidence that IBIT or Coinbase's custody systems have been compromised, and Wang's warning does not establish that North Korean hackers are actively targeting the fund.
The potential financial consequences nevertheless extend to the insurance and liability protections covering the assets.
BlackRock's annual filing shows that Coinbase maintains commercial crime insurance shared among its customers, rather than coverage reserved exclusively for IBIT.
The custody agreement also generally limits Coinbase's liability to $100 million per cold storage address, subject to contractual exceptions and other provisions.
Unlike stablecoins, which issuers can freeze at the token level, Bitcoin has no equivalent centralized mechanism for restricting stolen assets.
That leaves IBIT shareholders potentially exposed to losses that may not be fully recovered through blockchain tracing, insurance claims, or compensation from its custodian.

articles.title: Japan’s central bank will sell ETFs 2.6 times faster and could still take 43 years to exit
articles.text:
Quick Take
- The BOJ will increase annual ETF sales 2.6-fold from January 2027.
- Its estimated exit falls from 112 years to 43, without a fixed deadline.
- Bitcoin could be affected if yen-funded investors face pressure to sell.
Japan's central bank has decided to sell its stock funds about 2.6 times faster than usual, reducing the estimated time needed to dispose of them from 112 years to 43.
If you're wondering why such a supercharged exit still stretches across more than four decades, it's because the Bank of Japan is trying to undo years and years of purchases without disrupting the market it helped support.
Those numbers come from the BOJ's own calculation, which divides its end-September holdings by annual sales. They show just how long a monetary-policy experiment can outlast the decision to end it.
On Oct. 30, the bank held its overnight interest-rate target around 1.25% while approving faster ETF disposals from January 2027. The rate decision governs the current cost of money, and the sales program deals with assets accumulated under an earlier effort to make investors more willing to take risks.
Private buyers now have to accept more of that equity exposure, at prices the BOJ is prepared to accept.
How the Bank of Japan ended up owning stock funds
The BOJ brought equity funds into its monetary easing program in 2010, when the bank wanted to encourage investment in an economy struggling with weak demand and deflation.
By buying exchange-traded funds, which hold baskets of company shares, the bank could gain broad stock market exposure rather than pick individual companies to invest in.
At the time, its stated objective was to reduce the extra return investors demanded for holding risky assets. When a central bank adds demand for equities, it can support their prices and encourage investors to accept lower prospective returns for owning them.
That was a way to ease financial conditions when short-term interest rates were already near zero.
Even at the outset, the bank acknowledged the consequences of moving into these assets. In a November 2010 explanation of the program, then-Governor Masaaki Shirakawa discussed potential losses and the effects of the central bank's deeper involvement in allocating resources across companies and industries.
That kind of ownership brought responsibilities that would continue beyond the purchases themselves.
The bank ended new ETF purchases in March 2024, but stopping purchases left the existing investments on its balance sheet. Unlike an individual bond, an ordinary equity ETF has no maturity date when the issuer repays principal, so the BOJ couldn't just stop reinvesting and wait for the portfolio to expire.
To exit this trade, the bank needs to transact with actual buyers, who assume the risk of future gains and losses.
ETF units can pass between investors without selling every underlying share immediately, but the central bank still needs demand for the investment it wants to relinquish. It would be much easier to announce an end to support than to find acceptable prices for the accumulated holdings.
That explains the restraint in its disposal rules, which require seeking “appropriate prices” and want to avoid both losses and disruptions to the market in Japan as far as possible.
Selling faster transfers risk sooner but asks buyers to absorb more each year. Selling slowly leaves the bank exposed to equities longer. ETF sales began in January 2026 and have now accelerated, while retaining the option to adjust or suspend disposals when market conditions warrant it.
Selling faster without selling in a hurry
The new pace is about ¥860 billion annually at book value, up from ¥330 billion. Book value is the accounting amount assigned to the holdings being removed, rather than the cash the BOJ expects to receive. However, the difference between these values can be huge.
Using the relationship between market prices and book values in ETFs it sold during January through September, the bank estimates that the new pace corresponds to about ¥2.46 trillion at market value.
The market value equivalent can also move as prices move, while the book value pace defines how much of the recorded portfolio is being sold.
| Measure | Existing pace | From January 2027 | 
|---|---|---|
| Annual ETF sales, book value | About ¥330 billion | About ¥860 billion | 
| Sales as a share of market trading value | About 0.05% | About 0.1% | 
| Implied time to dispose of end-September holdings | About 112 years | About 43 years | 
Source: Bank of Japan, Oct. 30, 2026. Disposal horizons assume a constant book-value sales pace; they are arithmetic estimates, not completion forecasts.
The bank estimates that its revised sales will represent roughly one-thousandth of market trading value, based on activity in the Tokyo Stock Exchange's Prime Market during January through September.
BOJ arithmetic estimates using end-September 2026 holdings divided by a constant annual book-value sales pace. Approximately 112 years at ¥330 billion annually and 43 years at ¥860 billion. The revised pace begins January 2027; these are not completion forecasts.
Chart: Bank of Japan estimates of approximately 112 and 43 years at the respective annual sales paces. Constant-pace arithmetic, not completion forecasts.
That's why an increase of roughly 161% in annual book-value sales can coexist with a cautious exit. Spreading transactions over time gives buyers opportunities to adjust their portfolios and allows the BOJ to reassess execution if conditions deteriorate.
Officials say sales since January have gone smoothly, with no major effect on the market. The decision to accelerate also accounts for higher overall trading activity.
The 43-year estimate doesn't establish that Japan's market needs four decades to absorb the portfolio, or that the BOJ couldn't finish dumping its bonds sooner under another policy.
The bank is accepting prolonged equity ownership in exchange for limiting the volume it puts before buyers now, and future officials will inherit both the remaining assets and the discretion to sell them.
Bitcoin's exposure runs through the borrowing
A direct route runs from Japanese monetary policy to Bitcoin, since the yen carry trade has been a favorite strategy for financing large Bitcoin buys for years.
Traders who borrow yen and buy unhedged dollar-denominated investments (Bitcoin or others) owe yen debt against an asset priced in a foreign currency. That makes the exchange rate capable of eroding the trade even if the asset's dollar price remains stable.
If the yen strengthens, converting the asset back produces fewer yen to repay the loan. Higher borrowing costs can further reduce the return, and lenders may require more collateral under the financing terms.
Investors who need cash can sell other holdings, including Bitcoin, which allows trouble in one part of a portfolio to affect assets with no direct connection to the original trade.
Unfortunately, we can't know for sure whether this is happening now or at what scale. The BOJ's ETF program and private investors' financing are different, even if they can be affected by the same market currents.
Japan's inflation outlook and yen funding are conditionally connected, but this still requires evidence of actual borrowing stress.
The latest foreign investment numbers make the need for precision concrete. During Oct. 18-24, investors covered by the Ministry of Finance's weekly report recorded ¥92.6 billion of net disposals of foreign long-term debt, but bought ¥430.8 billion of foreign securities overall.
Purchases in other categories more than offset the debt reduction, so the numbers don't describe a general withdrawal of Japanese money from foreign markets, nor does that debt category identify US Treasury sales or prove that proceeds were converted into yen.
The report covers designated major investors, and disposals include redemptions, so it measures securities transactions rather than investors' funding needs.
Establishing a forced selling episode would require financing stress connected to position reductions. Declining futures open interest could help document deleveraging, but would not identify the currency borrowed.
For now, the Bank of Japan's four-decade calculation captures the consequences of prolonged intervention: ending a purchase program can leave a central bank managing its investments for much longer than it spent building them.
Private investors will gradually take over that exposure, while the bank can slow its exit when conditions worsen.
Bitcoin becomes vulnerable when investors elsewhere need to sell assets to meet obligations, and the decisive difference is whether those investors can afford the patience Japan has built into its own program.

articles.title: Crypto Today: FBI Blames North Korea for Binance hack
articles.text:
Here’s what happened in crypto today
Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.
Today in crypto: The FBI said that North Korea was responsible for the theft of about $6.3 billion in digital assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance. Soon after the $6.3 billion hack of Binance, some political and administration figures began offering their opinions with a US election approaching on Nov. 3 and voting already having begun in many locations. Coinbase led a selloff in crypto-linked stocks following Binance’s record-breaking $6.3 billion hack.
FBI blames North Korea for record $6.3B Binance hack
The FBI said that the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of about $6.3 billion in digital assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance on Thursday.
The FBI said on Saturday in a news release that it refers to this specific North Korean malicious cyber activity as “TraderTraitor,” which it has most recently observed converting stolen assets mostly into Ether (ETH).
It expects these assets to be further converted, using DeFi and instant swap services, as the hackers move to more advanced laundering stages.
The FBI urged private sector entities including THORNode operators, RPC node operators, instant exchanges, DeFi services, blockchain analytics firms and other digital asset service providers to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets. A full list of addresses is provided on the news release.
Binance hack sparks pre-election political clashes
Soon after the $6.3 billion hack of Binance, the biggest in crypto history, some political and administration figures began offering their opinions with a US election approaching on Nov. 3 and voting already having begun in many locations.
President Donald Trump was asked at a news conference on Friday about the hack of Binance. “We don’t know. We’re looking at that, the hack with Binance. They’re saying they’re going to get it back, they’re saying they’re guaranteeing it,” he replied.
The crypto exchange said in a post on X late Friday that it would cover any losses. “We want to be clear about our commitment: Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users.” It added that about $3 billion of the stolen funds had already been frozen in various locations. On Saturday, Binance said it had already covered 90% of the impacted amount of the hacked loss.
It was not clear whether there was any immediate political advantage to be gained from the hack, which was widely attributed to a North Korean group, but Republican and Democratic sides began staking out positions almost immediately.
Coinbase leads crypto stock selloff following $6.3 billion Binance hack
Shares of publicly traded cryptocurrency companies fell sharply Friday, with Coinbase dropping more than 13% a day after reporting a decline in third-quarter revenue, as the industry dealt with Binance’s $6.3 billion hack.
Other crypto-linked stocks also declined, with stablecoin issuer Circle Internet Group (CRCL) falling more than 9% and Bitcoin treasury company Strategy (MSTR) dropping about 8%, according to Yahoo Finance data at the time of writing.
The selloff also hit Bitcoin mining and data center operator IREN (IREN), whose shares fell more than 10%, and blockchain-based financial services company Figure Technology Solutions (FIGR), which dropped about 9%.
The declines followed Thursday’s disclosure of the Binance breach. The exchange confirmed Friday that hackers stole about $6.3 billion in the largest cryptocurrency theft on record.

articles.title: Ethereum validators pocket $30 million windfall as Binance hackers lose $119 million in rushed trades
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Binance hackers lost approximately $119 million in rushed crypto trades, creating a massive windfall for Ethereum validators and arbitrage bots.
- Trading firms captured roughly $60 million in profits as competition drove Ethereum block-builder tips more than 2,200-fold higher.
- Not every bot profited, with some losing hundreds of thousands of dollars as fierce competition drove transaction costs above trading gains.
Ethereum validators captured the bulk of nearly $30 million in payments generated during the trading frenzy surrounding Binance's $6.3 billion hack.
According to an Oct. 30 investigation by Bitquery, the attackers lost approximately $119 million by exchanging stolen cryptocurrency at unfavorable prices while racing to move funds beyond the reach of stablecoin issuers.
The hurried transactions created extraordinary arbitrage opportunities, allowing trading firms and automated bots to retain approximately $60 million in profits after costs.
Another $29.5 million flowed to Ethereum block builders and validators as traders competed to exploit price differences created by the attackers' massive transactions.
Ethereum validators capture windfall from arbitrage frenzy
Bitquery found that Ethereum block builders received 10,251 ETH in tips between 20:30 UTC on Oct. 29 and 01:00 UTC on Oct. 30, compared with just 4.6 ETH during the equivalent period the previous night.
The more than 2,200-fold increase followed aggressive cryptocurrency swaps by the hackers, who were converting stolen stablecoins and other assets into ETH and TRX before their holdings could be frozen.
On Ethereum alone, the attackers paid approximately $71.5 million above prevailing market prices to acquire ETH.
The buying pressure pushed prices in Uniswap's main WETH/USDT liquidity pool as much as 38% above the broader market, creating opportunities for arbitrage bots to purchase ETH elsewhere and sell it into the inflated pool.
However, capturing those profits required priority access to Ethereum's limited blockspace, triggering an intense bidding war among automated traders.
The competition unfolded through Ethereum's maximal extractable value (MEV) market, where traders pay specialized block builders to prioritize transactions and capture profitable trading opportunities.
Those builders subsequently bid for validators to propose their blocks, passing much of the revenue to the network participants responsible for finalizing transactions.
Bitquery's payment tracing showed that validators received approximately 11,217 ETH during the four-and-a-half-hour period, while builders retained about 564 ETH after distributing the payments, largely through Titan's relay.
Validators operating through staking services such as Lido can also distribute execution rewards to participating stakers, extending the windfall to investors securing the Ethereum network.
The frenzy also overwhelmed some trading strategies. Bitquery recorded 10,235 failed Ethereum transactions during the period, compared with approximately 3,500 the previous night, as bots paid gas fees while competing for the same opportunities.
The profit opportunities extended to other assets and blockchains.
On Tron, the hackers exchanged approximately 234 million USDT for TRX, paying $22.4 million above market prices. Traders exploiting the resulting discrepancies generated another $12.4 million before fees.
The attackers also sacrificed approximately $24.8 million by selling stolen tokens, including UNI, PEPE and ENA, below market prices.
Some arbitrage firms captured substantial gains from the discounted tokens, although the intense competition proved costly for others.
Bitquery identified a wallet associated with the prominent MEV bot jaredfromsubway that captured $2.87 million in trading discounts but paid $2.95 million in fees, leaving it with a loss of roughly $110,000.
Another unnamed bot paid $3.51 million to capture $3.24 million in trading opportunities, recording a loss of approximately $820,000.

articles.title: DeepSeek developing AI requiring less human input
articles.text:
DeepSeek developing AI agent requiring less human input: Report
The proposal comes amid intense competition among AI developers, including US companies Anthropic and OpenAI, the SCMP said.
Chinese artificial intelligence company DeepSeek has revealed a design to increase the autonomy of AI coding assistants so they can perform multiple tasks with less human intervention.
The aim is to reduce human input in coordinating and monitoring multiple AI agents, according to a paper published by the company’s DeepSeek Harness team and reported by Singapore’s South China Morning Post on Sunday.
Managing multiple agents demands human attention, the team said, noting that “single-task limits depend on model capabilities, while multitask limits depend on human attention.”
The DeepSeek paper said a person can oversee only three to five active AI agent sessions simultaneously. Its proposed system would distribute tasks among agents and coordinate their work, leaving humans free to review results and make decisions.
The proposal comes amid intense competition among AI developers, including US companies Anthropic and OpenAI, according to the SCMP.
Cointelegraph reported last October that Chinese artificial intelligence models were outperforming US counterparts in cryptocurrency trading, according to data from blockchain analytics platform CoinGlass.
AI chatbot DeepSeek led a crypto trading experiment, being the only AI model to generate a positive unrealized return of 9.1%. The results surprised crypto traders, given that DeepSeek was developed at a fraction of the cost of its US rivals.
Magazine: New DeepSeek ban in US, Swiss-Asia crypto ties deepen: Asia Express

articles.title: Zero-token withdrawals let a hacker drain 97 million CORE from Bitcoin staking platform b14g
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Bitcoin staking platform b14g lost 97 million CORE, valued by Bitquery at $1.47 million, after an attacker exploited zero-value withdrawal requests.
- The attacker emptied 91 staking positions in one transaction, exploiting contract logic that had reportedly existed for 17 months.
- As of Oct. 31, about 68 million CORE remained unmoved in three wallets, while b14g said exchange partners had frozen about 9 million CORE.
Bitcoin staking platform b14g suffered a $1.47 million exploit on Oct. 31, losing approximately 97 million CORE tokens.
The attacker drained 91 staking positions in a single transaction by submitting withdrawal requests for zero CORE, according to an investigation by blockchain analytics firm Bitquery.
The staking platform confirmed the unauthorized withdrawals and said it had paused the affected contracts while coordinating with the Core team, security partners, and exchanges to recover the funds.
However, b14g clarified that the breach was limited to CORE deposits. Bitcoin staked through the protocol remains time-locked on the BTC blockchain and was not affected.
How hackers exploited b14g's withdrawal mechanism
Bitquery's investigation revealed that the attacker exploited a weakness in the interaction between b14g's withdrawal mechanism and Core's staking contracts.
Under normal circumstances, b14g allows Bitcoin holders to pair their BTC with CORE deposits to earn enhanced staking rewards. The protocol manages these arrangements through staking positions that hold CORE and delegate it to validators.
However, Core's staking contract contains an unusual provision that interprets a withdrawal request for zero tokens as an instruction to withdraw the entire staked balance.
The attacker exploited this behavior by submitting 99 zero-value withdrawal requests against staking positions it had not funded.
Rather than rejecting the unauthorized requests, b14g's contract accepted them and passed the instructions to Core's staking system, which released approximately 97 million tokens.
Bitquery said the exploit occurred at 09:29 UTC, with the stolen tokens transferred to an attacker-controlled wallet.
The investigation found no evidence that the attacker needed a compromised administrator key or a newly deployed malicious contract. Instead, the underlying contract logic had reportedly been in place for approximately 17 months.
However, Bitquery cautioned that it had not reviewed b14g's underlying source code and could not identify the precise programming error that allowed the unauthorized withdrawals.
Meanwhile, blockchain records showed that b14g did not pause the affected contracts until 10:35 UTC, approximately 66 minutes after the initial attack.
During that interval, the attacker transferred 23 million CORE from the original wallet through several newly created addresses.
The timeline does not establish when b14g discovered the breach, although the platform said it paused the contracts immediately after identifying the incident.
Further tracing revealed that some stolen funds moved through intermediary addresses connected to exchange infrastructure associated with Bybit, Gate.io, and MEXC.
Bitquery also identified a service that supplied the attacker's initial transaction fees, then received about 11 million CORE from the stolen funds and forwarded them to an MEXC deposit address.
However, the analytics firm cautioned that some intermediary wallets also handled other customers' assets, making it difficult to attribute every subsequent transfer directly to the attacker.
By the evening of Oct. 31, approximately 68 million CORE, representing 70% of the stolen tokens, had remained unmoved in three wallets.
Separately, b14g reported that exchange partners had frozen approximately 9 million CORE linked to the attacker.
In its response, Core DAO maintained that the underlying blockchain had not been compromised, stressing that its consensus mechanism, validators, and staking contracts continued operating normally throughout the incident.
It also said CORE staked directly with validators or through other protocols remained unaffected.
b14g has pledged to publish a detailed post-mortem explaining the technical cause of the exploit, the extent of user losses, and the next steps for affected depositors. The platform has not yet disclosed a compensation plan.

articles.title: Binance says withdrawals begin
articles.text:
Binance says phase one of withdrawals opens after $6.3B hack
The crypto exchange said it has begun phased withdrawals after the record hack the FBI has blamed on North Korea.
Binance said it has reopened its Bitcoin network in phase one of resuming withdrawals after a major hack of about $6.3 billion in funds.
The crypto exchange had suspended user withdrawals after the attack on Thursday, which the FBI blamed on North Korean operatives.
“First batch network now opened in phase one of withdrawals is $BTC bitcoin network,” Binance said on X.
In an earlier X announcement on Sunday, Binance had said it would roll out withdrawal services in phases, which will be progressively available. Updates will be available on its official X channel, it added.
“We are taking a phased approach by prioritizing tokens based on the past week data of user demand, so that each network and asset pair can be restored carefully, with stability and security checks completed before access is reopened,” Binance said.
Users should check the withdrawal page for their selected asset and network, or visit the Binance network status page to confirm availability, the company said.
During the phased rollout, it is expected that there will be some congestion, longer processing times and even temporary delays, Binance said, so if a withdrawal is not successful, users should try again after a short while.
Cointelegraph reported on Saturday that Binance said it had replenished 90% of the assets stolen in the hack, up from 80% a day earlier, and remained on track to resume withdrawals Sunday.
Magazine: Binance hackers raced to move billions before it could be frozen

articles.title: Bitcoin ETF Investors Head for the Exits After Record Binance Hack - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs shed $643.2 million on Friday, their biggest outflow of October, in the first session after Thursday’s $6.4 billion Binance hack.
- Ethereum ETFs extended a five-day outflow streak to about $431 million, and Solana ETFs lost about $72 million over the week.
- Bitcoin fell about 4% Friday before steadying near $77,520 Saturday, while Myriad traders turned bearish on Ethereum and Solana.
The first real test of how ETF investors would react to the largest crypto hack in history came back red.
U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs shed $643.2 million on Friday, according to Decrypt’s ETF tracker, their biggest single-day outflow of October. It was the funds’ first full session since attackers began draining roughly $6.4 billion from Binance at 4:05 p.m. ET Thursday, after U.S. markets had closed. Thursday’s $17.2 million in inflows predated the theft.
The selling erased a four-day, $441 million inflow run, leaving the funds down about $202 million for the week and roughly $516 million for October. Cumulative net inflows since launch slipped to $57.4 billion, with total net assets at $103.2 billion.
Ethereum and Solana ETFs fared worse relative to their size. Ethereum funds lost $155.7 million on Friday, extending a five-day outflow streak to about $431 million and pushing October losses to roughly $1.61 billion. Solana ETFs shed $10.8 million, their fifth straight day of outflows, totaling about $72 million for the week. They logged net inflows on just two days all month.
Spot crypto ETFs hold the underlying asset, such as Bitcoin or Ethereum, and trade on stock exchanges like ordinary shares, giving investors exposure through a regular brokerage account.
Bitcoin funds have drawn $57.4 billion in net inflows since debuting in January 2024, and Ethereum funds have taken in $12.2 billion since launching that July. Because issuers report flows daily and much of the money comes from institutions and financial advisers, the figures have become a closely watched gauge of investor sentiment.
Crypto markets initially appeared to take the Binance hack largely in stride, considering the scale of the theft. Bitcoin fell about 4% to roughly $76,400 on Friday, and more than $1.3 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated. It’s a sharp drop, but a far smaller one than the nearly 11% plunge after a failed attack on Binance in 2018.
Binance has pledged to cover all losses with company funds and an emergency reserve, while Tether and Circle froze more than $2.3 billion in stolen stablecoins. Some Wall Street firms even urged clients to buy crypto-linked stocks on the potential weakness in markets.
By Saturday, Bitcoin had steadied at about $77,520, up 0.5% over 24 hours but down 3.3% on the week. Ethereum traded near $2,251, down 3.9% for the week, and Solana near $96, down 4.5%. Total crypto market cap held at about $2.7 trillion.
Macro headwinds remain in play. The Federal Reserve held rates at 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday, but two officials voted for a hike, and traders had priced odds above 70% for an increase in December.
Traders on Myriad, a prediction market developed by Decrypt’s parent company Dastan, have turned bearish on Ethereum and Solana. They now give Ethereum a 51.3% chance of falling to $1,500 before reaching $3,000, flipping a market that favored the upside at 61.3% a week ago. Solana’s odds of sinking to $40 before hitting $160 rose to 53.7%.

articles.title: FBI blames North Korea for $6 billion Binance hack, urges THORChain to block stolen funds
articles.text:
Quick Take
- The FBI blamed North Korea for the $6 billion Binance hack and urged THORChain and other DeFi operators to block stolen funds.
- Hackers are exploiting DeFi lending protocols to evade stablecoin freezes and move stolen assets through fresh wallets.
- An unrelated technical glitch temporarily halted THORChain swaps for all users, including the Binance attackers.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has blamed North Korea's TraderTraitor operation for stealing more than $6 billion from Binance.
In an Oct. 31 security alert, the agency attributed the Oct. 29 attack to North Korean cyber actors, providing official US government confirmation of the perpetrators behind one of history's largest cryptocurrency thefts.
The FBI said investigators working alongside the US Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation had observed the attackers converting stolen assets primarily into Ethereum.
It warned that the hackers were expected to move those holdings through decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols and instant swap services to obscure their origins.
To disrupt those efforts, the agency published hundreds of cryptocurrency addresses associated with the theft and urged THORNode operators, RPC node operators, DeFi platforms, instant exchanges and other service providers to block transactions involving the identified wallets.
THORChain faces fresh scrutiny as hackers exploit DeFi platforms
The FBI's intervention comes as blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis has identified sophisticated laundering operations already underway across decentralized platforms.
According to Chainalysis, the hackers have been using DeFi lending protocols on Tron to circumvent stablecoin freezes, which have already restricted approximately $3 billion in stolen assets.
The technique involves converting TRX into stablecoins, depositing those assets into lending protocols, and receiving deposit receipt tokens that stablecoin issuers cannot directly freeze.
The attackers then transfer the receipt tokens to fresh wallets, redeem them for stablecoins, and bridge the funds into assets such as ETH.
Chainalysis traced approximately $500,000 through this process, demonstrating how the attackers could exploit DeFi liquidity while minimizing their exposure to asset freezes.
Meanwhile, Chainalysis reported that an unrelated technical failure on THORChain inadvertently disrupted another laundering route used by the Binance attackers.
An Ethereum blockchain reorganization caused THORChain to mistakenly issue a double refund on a 10 ETH deposit, triggering an emergency pause that prevented users, including the North Korean hackers, from conducting swaps across most of its bridges.
The disruption was temporary and indiscriminate rather than a deliberate attempt to block stolen funds.
THORChain has previously faced criticism for facilitating transactions involving stolen cryptocurrency.
In September, the protocol rejected calls to block funds linked to Bitget's $388 million hack, arguing that its permissionless architecture prevented selective transaction censorship.
The controversy coincided with a surge in THORChain's activity. The protocol earned about 63% of its $3 million September income during the five-day hack-linked trading surge.
The protocol maintained that emergency network shutdowns, including one following its own $11 million exploit in May, were fundamentally different from blacklisting individual addresses.
Responding to the FBI's latest appeal, THORChain co-founder Chad Barraford said node operators held no information beyond what was publicly available in real time.
“No subpoenas required, a best case scenario for investigations,” he wrote.

articles.title: FBI blames North Korea for Binance hack
articles.text:
FBI blames North Korea for record $6.3B Binance hack
US agency seeks private-sector help to block further money-laundering of stolen digital assets.
The FBI said that the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of about $6.3 billion in digital assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance on Thursday.
The FBI said on Saturday in a news release that it refers to this specific North Korean malicious cyber activity as “TraderTraitor,” which it has most recently observed converting stolen assets mostly into Ether (ETH).
It expects these assets to be further converted, using DeFi and instant swap services, as the hackers move to more advanced laundering stages.
The FBI urged private sector entities including THORNode operators, RPC node operators, instant exchanges, DeFi services, blockchain analytics firms and other digital asset service providers to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets. A full list of addresses is provided on the news release.
Cointelegraph reported earlier this year that North Korea-linked hackers stole about 60% of the value lost to crypto hacks in 2025, with proceeds used to help fund the regime’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs, highlighting a growing reliance on digital assets to generate hard currency.
North Korean defense spending supplemented
Related: Crypto losses from North Korea hackers in 2025 rose 51% YoY: Report
Those findings came from a CertiK report that attributed more than $2 billion of an estimated $3.4 billion in 2025 crypto security losses to groups tied North Korea, across 79 of 656 incidents documented that year.
While North Korea does not publish credible budget data, according to independent research organization MilitarySpend, mid-range consensus places its actual annual defense spending at as much as $6 billion, using purchasing-power-adjusted GDP estimates, though this figure is uncertain.
MilitarySpend adds that revenue from Russia arms transfers — estimated at as much as $5 billion in munitions exported to Russia from 2022-2025 per South Korean intelligence — supplements domestic weapons programs, as does cryptocurrency theft, which provides additional off-budget financing for WMD development.
As Cointelegraph reported, between 2016 and early 2026, North Korea-linked actors stole an estimated $6.75 billion in cryptocurrency across 263 documented incidents, according to CertiK, citing findings by independent onchain researcher Taylor Monahan.
CertiK’s analysis concluded that North Korea has industrialized crypto theft into a core state revenue mechanism.
