articles.title: Lò phản ứng năng lượng mặt trời biến nước thành hydro
articles.text:
Trong thử nghiệm, lò phản ứng mới tạo ra khoảng 500 gram hydro mỗi ngày, đáp ứng khoảng 1/2 nhu cầu điện của hộ gia đình 4 người.
Các kỹ sư tại Viện Công nghệ Liên bang Lausanne (EPFL) chế tạo và thử nghiệm thành công một lò phản ứng năng lượng mặt trời có thể sản xuất hydro từ ánh sáng mặt trời và nước, New Atlas hôm 17/4 đưa tin. Hệ thống mới không chỉ đạt hiệu quả cao trong việc sản xuất hydro mà còn thu giữ các phụ phẩm gồm oxy và nhiệt để sử dụng. Nghiên cứu mới xuất bản trên tạp chí Nature Energy.
Đĩa parabol đóng vai trò quan trọng trong lò phản ứng năng lượng mặt trời giúp sản xuất hydro. (Ảnh: EPFL)
Hydro đóng vai trò quan trọng trong năng lượng tái tạo. Một trong những cách hiệu quả nhất để sản xuất hydro là tách nước thành các phân tử cấu thành. Việc thực hiện quá trình này bằng năng lượng mặt trời được gọi là quang hợp nhân tạo.
Lò phản ứng của EPFL trông giống đĩa vệ tinh và hoạt động theo nguyên lý tương tự - diện tích bề mặt cong lớn thu nhận càng nhiều ánh sáng càng tốt và tập trung ánh sáng vào thiết bị nhỏ treo lơ lửng ở giữa. Trong trường hợp này, chiếc đĩa thu nhiệt từ mặt trời và tập trung nhiệt khoảng 800 lần vào một lò phản ứng quang điện hóa. Nước được bơm vào lò phản ứng này và tại đây, năng lượng mặt trời giúp phân tách các phân tử nước thành hydro và oxy.
Lò phản ứng giữ lại hai phụ phẩm của quá trình sản xuất hydro thường bị lãng phí là oxy và nhiệt. Oxy có thể dùng trong các bệnh viện hoặc cho công nghiệp, còn nhiệt được truyền qua bộ trao đổi nhiệt, có thể giúp đun nước hoặc sưởi ấm các tòa nhà.
Nhóm nghiên cứu đã thử nghiệm lò phản ứng tại cơ sở của EPFL trong hơn 13 ngày, vào tháng 8/2020, tháng 2 và tháng 3/2021, để hiểu cách thức hoạt động của nó trong những điều kiện thời tiết khác nhau. Hiệu suất chuyển hóa năng lượng mặt trời - hydro đạt mức trung bình trên 20%, tạo ra khoảng 500 gram hydro mỗi ngày. Nhóm nghiên cứu cho biết, với sản lượng này, trong hơn một năm, hệ thống có thể cung cấp năng lượng cho 1,5 xe chạy bằng pin nhiên liệu hydro (với quãng đường di chuyển trung bình) hoặc đáp ứng khoảng 1/2 nhu cầu điện của một hộ gia đình 4 người.
"Với công suất đầu ra hơn 2 kW, chúng tôi đã phá vỡ mức trần 1 kW cho lò phản ứng thí điểm trong khi vẫn duy trì hiệu suất cao kỷ lục ở quy mô này. Mức sản xuất hydro đạt được trong nghiên cứu mới cho thấy bước tiến đáng khích lệ trong việc thương mại hóa công nghệ này", Sophia Haussener, thành viên nhóm nghiên cứu, cho biết.
Nhóm nghiên cứu dự định xây dựng một nhà máy thí điểm công suất vài trăm kW tại một cơ sở sản xuất kim loại. Hydro sẽ được dùng để ủ kim loại, nhiệt dùng để đun nóng nước còn oxy cung cấp cho các bệnh viện gần đó.

articles.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
articles.text:
The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
- Date:
- November 1, 2026
- Source:
- University of Sydney
- Summary:
- Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.
- Share:
Crown-of-thorns starfish (COTS) are among the most feared creatures on coral reefs. Covered in sharp, toxin-filled spines, these predators are notorious for consuming coral and leaving widespread destruction in their wake.
However, new research from the University of Sydney suggests these infamous reef destroyers may also have a surprisingly beneficial side. When their populations remain under control, crown-of-thorns starfish can help maintain healthy coral communities and support greater biodiversity.
Native to Australia's Great Barrier Reef, these coral-eating starfish have caused enormous damage during population explosions. Since the 1960s, the reef has experienced four major outbreaks, occurring roughly every 15 years. Declining numbers of natural predators, including tritons and several species of reef fish, have made the Great Barrier Reef and other marine ecosystems more vulnerable to these destructive events.
Scientists Discover That Coral Often Survives Starfish Attacks
In a study published in Ecology and Evolution, researchers investigated what happens to coral after crown-of-thorns starfish feed on it. The team examined feeding scars and remaining living tissue at the University of Sydney's One Tree Island Research Station, located on the Great Barrier Reef.
The study sites were within protected areas where healthy fish populations help keep starfish numbers under control. Unlike other parts of the reef that experience devastating outbreaks, these locations maintain relatively low populations of crown-of-thorns starfish.
The results revealed an unexpected pattern. A team led by Dr. Shawna Foo found that living coral tissue survived nearly 75 percent of the observed feeding events.
"At One Tree Reef, COTS appear to consume a relatively consistent amount of coral during each meal and move on, rather than demolishing the entire coral colony," said Dr. Foo, a University of Sydney Horizon Fellow in the School of Life and Environmental Sciences. "This meant live coral tissue remnants were frequently left behind."
How Coral-Eating Starfish Can Boost Reef Biodiversity
The discovery suggests that small populations of crown-of-thorns starfish may play an important role in maintaining the balance of coral reef ecosystems.
Some coral species grow quickly and can take over large areas, limiting the space available to slower-growing varieties. By feeding on these dominant species, crown-of-thorns starfish may create opportunities for other corals to survive and establish themselves.
The researchers found that surviving fragments of fast-growing Acroporidae corals did not regenerate over the areas damaged by starfish feeding. In contrast, regrowth occurred primarily among slower-growing Montipora and Porites corals.
"By feeding on fast-growing corals such as Acropora, low-density COTS populations create space for slower-growing coral species to persist, helping to increase coral diversity," Dr. Foo said.
This finding challenges the idea that all coral consumption by crown-of-thorns starfish is harmful. Under the right conditions, their feeding behavior may actually prevent a few dominant coral species from taking over the reef.
Why Eliminating Crown-of-Thorns Starfish Could Be a Mistake
Despite these potential benefits, researchers caution that large outbreaks of crown-of-thorns starfish remain a serious threat. When their numbers increase dramatically, they can destroy extensive areas of coral, leaving reefs struggling to recover.
The key difference is whether starfish populations remain at naturally manageable levels or grow into destructive outbreaks.
"It's important to distinguish between COTS populations performing their natural role as coral predators and outbreaks causing sustained reef decline."
Although the research was conducted mainly in protected areas with healthy fish populations and little risk of major outbreaks, the findings could help scientists and conservation managers improve strategies for controlling crown-of-thorns starfish.
In particular, the results suggest that removing every starfish may not be the best approach once an outbreak has been brought under control.
"The implications of our work can help us decide when and why culling should occur and the ecological endpoint of a cull. Once an outbreak is suppressed, the goal should not necessarily be to eliminate COTS entirely. Culling needs to be complemented by strong marine management to protect COTS predators and keep COTS populations in check."
Research co-author Professor Maria Byrne connected the findings to a well-established ecological concept.
"The results are consistent with the intermediate disturbance hypothesis, an important framework in ecology and conservation."
According to this hypothesis, ecosystems can benefit from occasional, moderate disturbances that prevent any single species from becoming too dominant.
The research suggests that crown-of-thorns starfish may be an example of this natural balancing process. While uncontrolled outbreaks can devastate coral reefs, smaller populations may help maintain the diversity that makes these ecosystems so valuable.

articles.title: Chiếc bồn cầu chuyển phân thành năng lượng và tiền mã hóa
articles.text:
Bồn cầu thân thiện với môi trường BeeVi, phát minh đến từ một trường đại học ở Hàn Quốc, phần nào giúp đời sống sinh viên theo học dễ dàng hơn.
Cho Jae-weon, giảng viên khoa Kỹ thuật môi trường thuộc Viện Khoa học và Công nghệ Quốc gia Ulsan (UNIST), là người sáng tạo ra BeeVi, chiếc bồn cầu có thể biến phân thành khí sinh học và phân bón.
Để tiết kiệm nước, BeeVi sẽ hút phân xuống một bồn chứa đặt ngầm dưới đất. Tại đây, các vi sinh vật sẽ phân hủy chất thải, tạo thành khí mê tan. Khí sau đó được chuyển hóa thành năng lượng cung cấp cho 1 tòa nhà trong trường.
Cho Jae-weon đứng bên cạnh một bể chứa phân ở Ulsan. (Ảnh: Reuters).
Nhờ phát minh này, sinh viên tại tòa nhà được sử dụng điện miễn phí. Bên cạnh đó, mỗi lần sử dụng BeeVi được quy đổi ra một đơn vị tiền mã hóa lưu hành nội bộ mang tên "Ggool", nghĩa là "Mật ong".
Sinh viên có thể dùng Ggool để mua nhiều thứ trong khuôn viên trường như cà phê, mì ramyeon hay thậm chí là sách. Mỗi người sử dụng BeeVi sẽ kiếm được 10 Ggool một ngày.
"Nếu nghĩ rộng ra, phân có giá trị trong việc tạo ra năng lượng và phân bón. Việc tôi làm là đặt giá trị đó vào vòng tuần hoàn", ông Cho cho biết.
500 gram phân, lượng trung bình một người thải ra trong một ngày, có thể sản sinh ra 50 lít khí mê tan. Theo ông Cho, lượng khí này giúp tạo ra khoảng 0,5 kWh điện, đủ cho một chiếc xe hơi điện chạy 1,2 km.
Khi tất cả bồn cầu trong khuôn viên trường đều được thay bằng BeeVi, lượng điện năng sạch thu được là rất lớn.
"Tôi không còn xem phân là một thay dơ bẩn nữa, bây giờ nó là một báu vật đối với tôi. Tôi thậm chí còn nói về phân trong các bữa ăn khi nghĩ về những cuốn sách mình muốn", Heo Hui-jin, cựu sinh viên UNIST cho biết.
Vài năm trước, Cho đã giới thiệu một nghiên cứu miêu tả cách ông sử dụng phân hữu cơ và nhiên liệu được tạo ra bởi phiên bản cũ của BeeVi để trồng và nấu mầm lúa mạch.
Trước BeeVi cũng có một số loại bồn cầu không dùng nước và thân thiện với môi trường được phát triển. Nổi bật nhất có lẽ là Tiger Toilet. Nó trông giống như mọi nhà vệ sinh khác nhưng được vận hành bởi một quần thể giun hổ ở phía dưới.
Tiger Toilet không cần xả nước như thông thường và cũng không kết nối với hệ thống thoát nước. Những con giun được cho vào một thùng chứa đặt bên dưới và chúng sẽ ăn chất thải. Hoạt động của những con vật này sẽ tạo ra hỗn hợp gồm nước, carbon dioxide và một lượng nhỏ phân giun (ít độc và giàu dinh dưỡng hơn phân người).
Sản phẩm phụ còn sót lại của quá trình trên có thể tạo ra loại phân bón tuyệt vời gồm nitơ, phốt pho, carbon và kali, rất tốt cho việc trồng trọt. Ngoài ra, Tiger Toilet cũng không thu hút ruồi muỗi hay các loại côn trùng có hại khác.

articles.title: Drinking tea may help protect your heart, but there’s a surprising catch
articles.text:
Drinking tea may help protect your heart, but there’s a surprising catch
- Date:
- November 1, 2026
- Source:
- Wiley
- Summary:
- A massive study of nearly 486,000 adults found that regularly drinking tea was associated with an 11% lower risk of heart and blood vessel diseases. The lowest risk was linked to drinking roughly six to eight cups per day, with black tea showing more consistent benefits than green tea.
- Share:
Drinking tea regularly may offer important benefits for your heart and blood vessels, according to a massive study involving nearly 500,000 adults. Researchers found that people who consumed tea regularly had a lower risk of developing several vascular diseases compared with those who did not drink tea.
However, the findings also revealed some unexpected differences. The type of tea, how strong it was, and even the temperature at which it was consumed were all associated with vascular health. While certain tea drinking habits were linked to a lower risk of disease, drinking tea at extremely high temperatures appeared to have the opposite association.
The research, published in the Journal of Internal Medicine, provides new insights into how an everyday beverage may be connected to long-term cardiovascular health.
Nearly 500,000 Adults Reveal a Link Between Tea and Vascular Health
The study included 485,934 adults in China who were followed for a median of 9.05 years. During that period, researchers recorded 14,863 cases involving several types of vascular disease.
These conditions included cardiovascular disease, which affects the heart and blood vessels, and cerebrovascular disease, which involves blood vessels that supply the brain. The researchers also examined pulmonary heart disease, a condition in which problems involving the lungs or their blood vessels place strain on the heart, and peripheral artery disease, which occurs when arteries carrying blood to areas such as the legs become narrowed or blocked.
Although these conditions affect different parts of the body, they share an important feature: they interfere with the circulation of blood, which delivers oxygen and nutrients to organs and tissues.
When the researchers compared tea drinking habits with the incidence of these diseases, they found that regular tea consumption was associated with an 11% lower risk of the combined vascular outcomes.
The relationship also appeared to vary with the amount consumed. Among people who drank tea at least weekly, the lowest estimated risk occurred at approximately six to eight cups per day.
This does not necessarily mean that drinking more tea directly prevents disease or that everyone should consume that amount. Because the research was observational, it could identify connections between tea drinking and health outcomes but could not establish that tea itself was responsible for the differences.
Black Tea vs. Green Tea: Does the Type Matter?
One particularly interesting finding involved the type of tea participants consumed.
Black tea showed more consistent associations with a reduced risk of vascular disease than green tea. This suggests that different varieties of tea may not have identical relationships with cardiovascular health.
Both black and green tea come from the same plant, Camellia sinensis, but they undergo different processing methods. Black tea is typically allowed to undergo extensive oxidation, a chemical process that changes the composition of compounds in the leaves, while green tea is processed to limit oxidation.
Tea naturally contains plant compounds known as polyphenols, which have attracted scientific interest because of their antioxidant properties and potential effects on blood vessel function. Antioxidants can help limit certain types of cellular damage caused by reactive molecules.
However, the study does not establish whether these compounds explain the observed differences between black and green tea.
Tea strength also appeared to matter. Participants who drank tea of moderate strength had the lowest associated vascular disease risk, suggesting that stronger tea was not necessarily linked to greater benefits.
Drinking Tea Too Hot May Carry Unexpected Risks
Perhaps the most surprising finding concerned tea temperature.
Although regular tea consumption was generally associated with a reduced risk of vascular disease, drinking tea described as "burning hot" was linked to an increased risk.
The result suggests that the temperature of tea may be an important consideration alongside how much people drink and which variety they prefer.
Very hot beverages can expose tissues in the mouth and digestive tract to high temperatures, but the study did not establish the biological mechanism behind the observed vascular risk. It also did not identify a specific temperature at which tea becomes harmful.
The findings therefore should not be interpreted as proof that drinking extremely hot tea directly causes vascular disease. They do, however, raise questions about whether certain drinking habits could offset some of the favorable associations seen with regular tea consumption.
Tea, Exercise, and Smoking Habits May Work Together
The researchers also examined how tea consumption related to other lifestyle factors, including smoking and physical activity.
Their analysis showed that people who regularly drank tea, were not current smokers, and maintained high levels of physical activity had the lowest vascular disease risk.
"Joint analyses showed that tea consumption, smoking status and physical were collectively associated with vascular risk, with the favorable combination of habitual tea consumption, non-current smoking and high physical activity associated with the lowest risk," the authors wrote.
These results highlight the importance of considering overall lifestyle rather than looking at a single food or beverage in isolation.
Regular physical activity supports cardiovascular health in several ways, including improving circulation, helping regulate blood pressure, and supporting the function of the heart and blood vessels. Avoiding smoking also reduces exposure to substances that can damage blood vessels and increase cardiovascular risk.
Taken together, the findings suggest that tea drinking may be one component of a broader pattern of habits associated with better vascular health.
Although more research is needed to determine whether tea consumption directly influences disease risk, the study offers encouraging evidence that this widely consumed beverage is associated with cardiovascular health. It also highlights an important distinction: when it comes to tea, the amount, variety, strength, and temperature may all be worth considering.

Journal Reference:

Habitual tea consumption is associated with lower cardiovascular disease risk. Journal of Internal Medicine, 2026; DOI: 10.1111/joim.70172

articles.title: Scientists use sound waves to deliver a new attack on deadly brain cancer
articles.text:
Scientists use sound waves to deliver a new attack on deadly brain cancer
- Date:
- November 1, 2026
- Source:
- University of Virginia Health System
- Summary:
- Scientists at the University of Virginia have developed a promising new strategy to fight glioblastoma, one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat forms of brain cancer. Their experimental approach combines focused ultrasound, tiny nanoparticles, and genetic molecules called microRNAs to attack multiple cancer-driving genes simultaneously.
- Share:
Scientists at the University of Virginia Comprehensive Cancer Center have developed a promising experimental strategy for treating glioblastoma, the most common and aggressive malignant brain tumor in adults. The new approach could help overcome some of the biggest obstacles that have limited the effectiveness of existing brain cancer treatments.
The research team, led by UVA's Roger Abounader, MD, PhD, identified tiny genetic molecules known as "microRNAs" that can interfere with several genes responsible for the development and growth of glioblastoma. To deliver these molecules into the brain, the researchers combined specialized nanoparticles, focused ultrasound and microscopic bubbles. Together, these technologies offer a way to temporarily cross the brain's protective barrier, which normally prevents many treatments from reaching brain tumors and other neurological conditions.
"This new approach could help target numerous molecules that promote cancer growth, including those for which no drugs exist, at the same time to achieve better therapies," said Abounader, a professor at UVA's School of Medicine in the Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Cancer Biology, as well as its Comprehensive Cancer Center and Center for RNA Science and Medicine. "We are hoping to translate our findings into future clinical trials for patients with glioblastoma and other brain tumors."
Why Glioblastoma Is So Difficult to Treat
Glioblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in adults and one of the most aggressive forms of cancer. It claims more than 13,000 lives in the United States each year. One reason it is so difficult to treat is that cancer cells spread into surrounding healthy brain tissue, making it nearly impossible for surgeons to remove the entire tumor.
Another major challenge is the brain's natural "blood-brain barrier." This protective system helps shield the brain from harmful substances, including toxins and infectious agents. Unfortunately, it also blocks many drugs that could otherwise be used to attack brain cancer.
Current treatment generally begins with surgery to remove as much of the tumor as possible. Patients then receive radiation therapy and chemotherapy to help control the remaining cancer and extend survival. Despite these efforts, glioblastoma remains exceptionally difficult to manage.
The UVA researchers are pursuing a different strategy. Instead of relying on drugs that target individual cancer-related processes, their approach uses microRNAs, small pieces of genetic material capable of suppressing the activity of multiple problematic genes at the same time.
By disrupting several genes that help glioblastoma grow and survive, the treatment could potentially slow or even stop tumor growth. This ability to target multiple cancer-driving mechanisms is especially important because combining several conventional cancer drugs can produce harmful side effects. In addition, many of the molecules involved in cancer growth cannot currently be targeted by available medications.
Using Ultrasound to Deliver Cancer-Fighting Molecules
Getting these genetic molecules into the brain presents another major challenge. To overcome it, Abounader's team uses focused ultrasound guided by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), allowing researchers to direct sound waves precisely toward the intended area.
The ultrasound works with tiny "microbubbles" to temporarily open the blood-brain barrier. This creates a brief opportunity for nanoparticles carrying the microRNAs to pass through the barrier and enter the brain, where they can act on genes involved in tumor growth.
The researchers tested this approach in laboratory experiments and animal models of glioblastoma. Their findings showed that the microRNA treatment slowed tumor growth and helped the animals survive longer.
Although these results are encouraging, the strategy remains experimental and will require additional research before it can be evaluated in human patients. Abounader believes the findings provide an important early indication that the technology could eventually benefit people with glioblastoma and potentially those with other types of cancer.
"This approach could have broad applications for several brain and other human diseases," Abounader said. "We and many others are intensively working to lighten the burden of cancer, and hopefully also completely cure it, but this requires a continued investment in cancer and medical research."
UVA Expands Focused Ultrasound Cancer Research
UVA Health has been at the forefront of focused ultrasound research since the technology's early development. Over the years, its scientists have built an extensive research program investigating how precisely directed sound waves might be used to treat a wide range of medical conditions.
Recognizing the technology's potential in cancer care, UVA partnered with the Charlottesville-based Focused Ultrasound Foundation to establish the Focused Ultrasound Immuno-Oncology (FUSION) Center. It is the first center in the world devoted specifically to investigating how focused ultrasound can be combined with cancer immunotherapy. Researchers believe this combination could lead to major advances in cancer treatment during the 21st century.
The effort also supports the broader missions of UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center and UVA's Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology, both of which are working to improve care through new medical discoveries.
UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center is among just 57 cancer centers nationwide to receive the National Cancer Institute's prestigious "comprehensive" designation. The recognition reflects its excellence in cancer research and patient care.
The Manning Institute was established to speed the discovery and development of new medicines and potential cures for some of the most difficult diseases. Its work is supported by a statewide clinical trials network designed to make emerging treatments more accessible to patients as they move through research and testing.
Study Findings and Research Support
Abounader and his colleagues published their experimental approach and initial laboratory findings in JCI, the Journal of Clinical Investigation. The study is open access and can be read free of charge.
The research team included Shekhar Saha, Ying Zhang, Myron K. Gibert Jr., Collin Dube, Farina Hanif, Elizabeth Qian Xu Mulcahy, Sylwia Bednarek, Yunan Sun, Pawel Marcinkiewicz, Xiantao Wang, Gijung Kwak, Ahsan H. Polash, Haolin Li, Kadie Hudson, Manikarna Dinda, Tapas Saha, Matthew McCord, Fadila Guessous, Nichola Cruickshanks, Rossymar Rivera Colon, Lily Dell'Olio, Rajitha Anbu, Wenjie Liu, Songy Choi, Benjamin Kefas, Pankaj Kumar, Alexander L. Klibanov, David Schiff, Jung Soo Suk, Justin Hanes, Jamie Mata, Markus Hafner and Abounader. The researchers reported having no financial interest in the work.
Funding came from the National Institutes of Health's National Cancer Institute through grants U01 CA220841 and P30 CA044579, along with the NIH's National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke through grants R01 NS122222 and R21 NS122136. Additional support was provided by a UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center pilot grant, a Schiff Foundation grant, the Ben and Catherine Ivy Foundation, and the Focused Ultrasound Foundation.

articles.title: Giống gà quý hiếm biết bay, chỉ có ở Trung Quốc
articles.text:
Gà lôi tai nâu là giống gà đặc hữu của Trung Quốc, được đưa vào Sách đỏ của Liên minh Bảo tồn Thiên nhiên Quốc tế (IUCN). Loài gà này không chỉ quý hiếm mà còn sở hữu bộ lông rất đẹp và độc đáo.
Gà lôi tai nâu có tên khoa học là (Crossoptilon Mantchuricum).
Giống gà này phân bố chủ yếu ở một số tỉnh miền núi phía Bắc Trung Quốc.
Gà lôi tai nâu thích sống ở những rừng lá kim có độ cao từ 1.100-2.600m so với mực nước biển.
Chúng thường sống thành bầy đàn.
Gà lôi tai nâu trưởng thành có chiều dài từ 96 - 100cm.
Gà lôi tai nâu có bộ lông pha trộn giữa màu nâu sẫm, màu kem và màu đen.
Chân của gà lôi tai nâu có màu đỏ.
Xung quanh viền mắt có màu đỏ và hai bên tai của gà lôi tai nâu có 2 chỏm lông dài màu trắng trông rất đẹp mắt.
Mỗi lứa gà lôi tai nâu thường đẻ từ 5-8 trứng. Trứng sẽ nở sau 28 ngày ấp.
Gà lôi tai nâu thường ăn các loại hạt, rễ, củ, lá cây…
Gà lôi tai nâu bị đe dọa bởi nạn săn bắn. Chúng được đưa vào sách đỏ của Liên minh Bảo tồn Thiên nhiên Quốc tế (IUCN).

articles.title: 'Metroid Prime' needs some 'Resident Evil'-style remakes to rediscover its sci-fi shooter mojo
articles.text:
'Metroid Prime' needs some 'Resident Evil'-style remakes to rediscover its sci-fi shooter mojo
Nintendo's sci-fi shooter franchise is in dire straits, but we've got the solution to Samus's problems.
Metroid Prime 4: Beyond was, unfortunately, not the return many were hoping for when it finally arrived on Nintendo Switch consoles in 2025. After five years in development at Retro Studios, the original makers of the Metroid Prime series, fans were greeted with annoying side characters, a bike for Samus to roam the barren landscape on, and a deeply unsatisfying ending.
It’s a shame, considering how beloved the Metroid Prime series has been since the first title’s 2002 debut for the Nintendo GameCube. Many franchises were jumping from 2D to 3D at the turn of the millennium, and there were plenty of failures — but Metroid wasn’t one of them. The two sequels would enhance how players control Samus with powerful weapons and a multiplayer mode, but the 18-year gap between Metroid Prime 3 and 4 left players expecting something special.
Metroid Prime 4: Beyond’s average reception left fans wondering where the series can go next. It’s admittedly strange that Metroid Prime 2 and 3 have yet to debut on Nintendo Switch, either through the Nintendo Online service or as remasters.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake has just dropped for Switch 2, and seeing Nintendo leverage one of the best games of all time for a modern take has given us an idea: let's give the Metroid Prime trilogy the remake treatment, taking inspiration from Capcom’s efforts with Resident Evil.
To Prime and Beyond
From 2002’s Resident Evil remake to the more recent successes with Resident Evil 2 & 4, Capcom has managed to recreate the feeling and survival horror tropes of the originals while modernizing the gameplay.
Whether it's the constant tension of being stalked by a Terminator-like Mr. X in 2019’s Resident Evil 2, or the palpable paranoia you feel exploring in Resident Evil 4 — the skin might be new, but the bones are undeniably "Resi."
Even recently-announced Resident Evil: Veronica — whilst a remake of 1999’s Code: Veronica — looks set to be a brand new take that evokes the feeling of the original game, but brings it into the modern era.
Prime 4 felt like a game out of time. Sure, it looked the part, but it felt decidedly like a GameCube game. So why not take a leaf out of Capcom's book, apply their "recapturing the vibes" mindset for a Metroid Prime Trilogy Remake, using the Prime 4 engine as its foundation.
2023’s Metroid Prime Remastered showed off the venerable title with better textures and widescreen support, but a remake powered by the fourth game’s engine could showcase the opening and Tallon IV in a whole new light.
Similar to 2002’s Resident Evil Remake with the Spencer Mansion, places would feel familiar but fresh, thanks to updated graphics, better sound, and support for HD Rumble 2 that could help the player become more immersed in the game. And of course, you can change a few things to play off people's expectations.
If Nintendo is feeling brave, the reimagining could even begin at the end of Zero Mission, which is set just before Metroid Prime. Controlling Samus with all her abilities, facing off against Mother Brain in an area not seen in 3D, could be a great introduction to old and new players, as well as giving the opportunity to remake an area from a previous title. Then, players could escape to Samus’ ship, with the ability to pilot it to the Orpheron ship, where Prime begins.
The Return of Metroid Prime Multiplayer
A remake (or remakes) would obviously mean a big step-up in graphics and gameplay across all three games, but it could also herald the long-awaited return of its multiplayer mode from Metroid Prime 2, something that Metroid Prime 4: Beyond bizarrely left out.
Up to four players could take part in one of two modes here - Deathmatch and Bounty Mode, which had players compete against one another by collecting coins to win matches. There were four arenas to choose from, with an additional two to unlock when players got far enough in Prime 2’s single-player mode.
It was a fun time, and its absence in Prime 4: Beyond felt like a big miss, especially with the prospect of playing this mode online with others and using the Switch 2 features like Game Chat.
A remake could fix this injustice, and even expand on the concept by offering new multiplayer modes alongside maps based on locations from across the Prime series. You could even add a co-op mode for the campaign, and a horde mode for co-op fans to enjoy online too.
Give Samus the Itchy Tasty Treatment
As it stands in 2026, the Metroid series feels adrift once more. Metroid Prime 4: Beyond will be lost to the sands of time, a mediocre entry in a series filled with bangers. As the latest Nintendo Direct eagerly showcased Donkey Kong, Zelda, and plenty of third-party releases, Samus was notably absent. Sure, she's just had a game, but it's hard not to be nervous after the drought that Metroid players had to suffer in the 2010s.
Capcom was in a similar lull after 2012’s disappointing Resident Evil 6, a bloated and confusing entry that made players fear the end of the series. But the seventh entry, alongside the Resident Evil 2 Remake in 2019, breathed new life into the franchise, which has proved as tough to kill as any of Umbrella's bioweapons.
Metroid's fate feels equally in the balance right now, and in a world where game studios are closing down and rivals like Microsoft are shrinking their focus to big-hitter franchises, Nintendo could easily let Metroid fall back into obscurity. Refocusing on what makes the series iconic is the key to its success, and modern remakes of the originals might just be what they need to rediscover that Metroid magic.
There are some easy wins out there to keep fans engaged; it’d still be great to see more games appear on the Nintendo Online service, like Metroid Prime 2, and we'd love more 2D entries after the excellent Metroid Dread, but nothing hits like Prime, and Prime isn't hitting right now.
If not, then I fear Samus will be riding her Vi-O-La into the sunset, deep within the barren wasteland of Sol Valley for the foreseeable future.
Daryl is an entertainment writer and author of two books—The Making of Tomb Raider and 50 Years of Boss Fights.
With over a decade of experience, his work has been featured in TechRadar, Tom’s Guide, SUPERJUMP, Pocket Tactics, Radio Times, and more. He also owns Springboard, a copywriting business focused on no AI, and publishes a fortnightly newsletter of the same name.

articles.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
articles.text:
Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
A remarkable 18-million-year-old fossil discovered in Egypt suggests that the evolutionary roots of humans and other modern apes may lie in an unexpected part of Africa.
- Date:
- November 1, 2026
- Source:
- Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center (MUVP)
- Summary:
- A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.
- Share:
An ancient ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging a long-standing theory about where the ancestors of modern apes, including humans, first evolved. The remarkable find suggests that a crucial chapter of our evolutionary history may have unfolded much farther north than scientists previously believed.
The newly identified species, named Masripithecus moghraensis, lived approximately 17 to 18 million years ago during the Early Miocene. Its fossilized remains were recovered from Wadi Moghra in northern Egypt, making it the first definitive fossil ape ever discovered in North Africa.
The discovery, described in a study published March 26, 2026, in Science, comes from an international team at the Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center (Egypt) and the University of Southern California (USA). Their findings suggest that northern Africa and the Middle East may have played a central role in the emergence of the evolutionary lineage that eventually gave rise to all living apes.
A Missing Piece of the Ape Evolutionary Puzzle
For decades, scientists believed that early apes and their close relatives were concentrated primarily in regions farther south in Africa. Fossil sites in North Africa had produced remains of ancient monkeys from the Early Miocene, but researchers had never found definitive evidence of apes from the same period.
That gap helped shape prevailing theories about ape evolution. Although younger ape fossils have been discovered across Africa, Europe, and Asia, their evolutionary relationships and geographic origins remain subjects of scientific debate.
The newly discovered Egyptian fossil may help explain what was missing from this picture.
"We spent five years searching for this kind of fossil because, when we look closely at the early ape family tree, it becomes clear that something is missing -- and North Africa holds that missing piece," said Hesham Sallam, a paleontologist at Mansoura University and senior author of the study.
The discovery is especially important for understanding the origins of crown Hominoidea, the evolutionary group that includes the last common ancestor of all living apes and its descendants. Today, that group encompasses gibbons, orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, and humans.
Scientists suspect that the incomplete geographic distribution of ancient fossils has obscured important details about when and where this group first emerged.
An 18-Million-Year-Old Ape With Unusual Teeth
The fossils were uncovered during expeditions in 2023 and 2024 by researchers from the Sallam Lab at Wadi Moghra, a well-known fossil site in northern Egypt.
The team named the species Masripithecus moghraensis. Its genus name combines Masr (مصر), the Arabic name for Egypt, with píthēkos, the Greek word for ape. The species name honors Wadi Moghra, where the fossils were found.
Although the remains consist only of lower jaw material, they contain an unusual combination of anatomical features that distinguishes the animal from other apes of similar age.
The jaw is exceptionally sturdy, with remarkably large canine and premolar teeth. Its molars also have rounded chewing surfaces covered in pronounced textures. These characteristics offer valuable clues about the foods the animal could eat and how it survived in its environment.
Researchers believe Masripithecus primarily consumed fruit but had teeth powerful enough to process tougher foods when necessary. This dietary flexibility may have been an important survival advantage.
"Together, they suggest that Masripithecus was adapted for versatility. The study interprets its chewing anatomy as evidence of a flexible, mainly fruit-based diet, with the ability to process harder foods such as nuts or seeds when needed. This flexibility would have helped Masripithecus to thrive at a time when climatic changes were leading to more pronounced seasonality in northern Africa and Arabia," said Shorouq Al-Ashqar, a researcher at the Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center and a first author of the study.
As seasonal differences became more pronounced, the availability of certain foods likely changed throughout the year. An ape capable of eating a wider range of foods would have been better equipped to cope with those fluctuations.
A Discovery That Challenges the Ape Family Tree
The importance of Masripithecus extends well beyond its unusual anatomy. When researchers examined where the species belonged on the evolutionary family tree, they uncovered a surprising result.
Their analysis suggests that Masripithecus was more closely related to living apes than any known ape species from the Early Miocene of East Africa.
To investigate these relationships, the team used advanced statistical techniques known as Bayesian methods. These approaches allow scientists to compare different evolutionary possibilities and estimate how strongly the available evidence supports each one.
The researchers combined anatomical information from living and extinct apes with genetic evidence from living species. They also incorporated the geological ages of fossil specimens, helping them estimate when different evolutionary branches separated.
By bringing these sources of evidence together, the scientists reconstructed relationships among ancient and modern apes and explored where their shared ancestors may have lived.
The results challenge the long-standing assumption that the evolutionary roots of all living apes were centered in or around East Africa.
Could North Africa Be the Birthplace of Modern Apes?
Additional analyses of ancient animal distributions pointed toward northern Africa and the Middle East as the most likely geographic home of the common ancestor of all living apes.
That ancestor is estimated to have lived during the Early Miocene, an interval spanning roughly 23 million to 16 million years ago. This was an important period in primate evolution, when early ape lineages were diversifying, and environments were undergoing substantial changes.
Geography may help explain why this region was so important.
Millions of years ago, Africa, Arabia, and Asia were moving toward a new geological arrangement. As the African and Arabian tectonic plates traveled northward and approached the final stages of their collision with Asia, the connections between these landmasses began to change.
Sea levels also rose and fell, periodically reducing the stretches of water that separated different regions. At certain times, these changes made it easier for animals to move between Africa and Eurasia.
Northern Africa and the Middle East therefore occupied a potentially crucial position in the movement and evolution of ancient mammals, including apes.
The discovery of Masripithecus helps connect previously separated fossil records from Africa and Eurasia. Its presence suggests that apes were already evolving into distinct forms in this region before new land connections made it possible for them to expand into Europe and Asia.
Rather than being a peripheral location in ape evolution, the region may have been an important center of evolutionary diversification.
Scientists Rethink Where Our Ancient Ape Ancestors Lived
The findings have even prompted some of the researchers to reconsider ideas they held throughout their careers.
Erik Seiffert, a paleontologist at the University of Southern California and co-author of the study, explained how the evidence has changed his understanding of ape origins.
"For my entire career, I considered it probable that the common ancestor of all living apes lived in or around East Africa. But this new discovery, and our new and novel analyses of hominoid phylogeny and biogeography, now strongly challenge that idea. And, importantly, the likelihood of this scenario doesn't depend on Masripithecus -- but it is very much consistent with it."
Importantly, the researchers are not claiming that Masripithecus was a direct ancestor of humans or even necessarily the direct ancestor of living apes. Instead, its position on the evolutionary family tree provides evidence about where the broader ancestral lineage may have originated.
The distinction matters because humans emerged much later in evolutionary history. The Egyptian fossil offers clues to an earlier stage, when the distant ancestors shared by humans and other living apes were evolving.
The team's findings also suggest that the traditional emphasis on East African fossils may have provided an incomplete view of this much older evolutionary story.
More Evolutionary Secrets May Be Hidden in Egypt
Although the discovery offers compelling new evidence, scientists still have much to learn about Masripithecus and the early history of modern apes.
Only part of the animal's jaw has been recovered, leaving important questions about its overall appearance, body size, movement, and behavior unanswered. Additional fossils could provide a more complete picture of how this ancient species lived and how it relates to other early apes.
The researchers believe that further exploration of North Africa and the Middle East could reveal additional species and help clarify when and where the major branches of the modern ape family tree began to emerge.
For now, Masripithecus moghraensis offers a striking reminder that even fundamental ideas about our distant evolutionary past can change when scientists uncover evidence in places that have received relatively little attention.
A fossil jaw preserved for nearly 18 million years may be helping scientists piece together a chapter of evolutionary history that was missing all along.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center (MUVP). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Shorouq F. Al-Ashqar, Erik R. Seiffert, Sanaa El-Sayed, Belal S. Salem, Abdullah S. Gohar, Hossam El-Saka, Mohamed Amin, Hesham M. Sallam. An Early Miocene ape from the biogeographic crossroads of African and Eurasian Hominoidea. Science, 2026; 391 (6792): 1383 DOI: 10.1126/science.adz4102

articles.title: Planetary defense: How military and civil satellites are watching fireballs to help keep Earth safe from space rocks
articles.text:
Planetary defense: How military and civil satellites are watching fireballs to help keep Earth safe from space rocks
"Planetary defense is not only about finding an object before it reaches Earth. It is also about understanding what happens during atmospheric entry."
It came from outer space, exploding high above the South Atlantic off the coast of Argentina.
That April 1 event — an incoming meteor, also termed a bolide — was observed by both U.S. space-based military and civil sensors.
Hush-hush U.S. government satellite sensors detected the speedy fireball cutting through our atmosphere. The object's brightness peaked at an altitude of nearly 60 miles (90.5 kilometers) over the South Atlantic.
That dazzling spectacle was also caught by the National Atmospheric and Oceanic Administration's GOES-E and Europe's Meteosat Third Generation (MTG) Imager-1 satellite. Those two independent spacecraft in geostationary orbit detected the bolide via onboard lightning imagers.
This skyfall show is among a number of recent episodes that spotlight the value of combining multi-sensor data to not only portray fireball dynamics but also to help appreciate human-caused space debris impacts, as well as strengthening planetary defense knowhow.
Catastrophic fragmentation
Take, for instance, another extraterrestrial incident.
In this case, an April 24, 2025 fireball over south-central Alaska yielded one of the most densely recorded "seismoacoustic" datasets ever obtained for a nature-made bolide en route to busting up.
A network of 37 seismic stations, 16 single infrasound sensors, and four infrasound arrays recorded 30 ballistic and multiple fragmentation arrivals. All this was complemented by Doppler weather radar detections of falling meteorites and independent optical video observations.
Now, toss in for good measure yet another encounter.
A roughly 12-foot-wide (3.7 meters) space rock plowed through Earth's atmosphere over northwest Queensland, Australia, on May 20, 2023, accompanied by a raucous round of sonic booms. And U.S. government space-based sensors caught the fall.
Researchers later determined that the object underwent catastrophic fragmentation, producing one of the 20 most energetic events reported by NASA's Center for Near-Earth Object Studies (CNEOS) since 1988 and the most energetic seen over Australia. It was equivalent to the explosion of a 7.1-kiloton bomb.
Location, time and estimated energy
"For many fireballs, U.S. Government detections reported through NASA's CNEOS database provide an important starting point by establishing that an event occurred and, in many cases, providing basic parameters such as location, time and estimated energy," explained Elizabeth Silber, a senior research and development physicist at the U.S. Department of Energy's Sandia National Laboratories in New Mexico.
"Civil and scientific observing systems can then add independent measurements that help refine and validate that initial characterization," said Silber.
CNEOS, which is based at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, is NASA's center for computing asteroid and comet orbits and their odds of striking Earth. CNEOS computes high-precision orbits for such objects in support of NASA's Planetary Defense Coordination Office.
Different and complementary information
"The Alaska event is an especially useful example, because it was not reported by U.S. Government sensors in the CNEOS database. In this case, the event was reconstructed almost entirely from civil and scientific observations," Silber told Space.com.
She said that the seismic and infrasound data constrained the trajectory and acoustic energy, the video provided independent optical information, and the weather radar detected material from the fireball falling to Earth.
"So, the real strength is that these systems provide different and complementary information," said Silber. "When a U.S. Government detection is available, civil data can independently validate it and add much more detail. When one is not available, as in this case [for Alaska], the civil networks can still provide a surprisingly complete reconstruction."
Independent view
The Alaska study shows how valuable it is to put together diverse types of observations once an event has occurred, said Silber. Each measurement responds to a different part of the event.
"Seismic and infrasound sensors record the atmospheric shock waves and can constrain the trajectory, fragmentation and energy," she added. "Optical observations provide an independent view of the luminous flight. Doppler weather radar can detect surviving material after it has slowed and entered dark flight."
Bottom line: no single sensor tells you everything.
"Combining independent observations lets us move from simply knowing that an event occurred to determining how the object traveled through the atmosphere, where it fragmented, how much energy it released, and whether material may have survived to the ground," said Silber.
'Hard rain' is gonna fall
Researchers got pretty lucky with the April 1, 2026 event over the South Atlantic, according to NASA's Rob Landis, a planetary defense specialist: Two civilian spacecraft located at different locations in geosynchronous orbit allowed them to conduct a rather unique investigation of this bolide.
"With two civilian resources, we can actually discuss things more openly," Landis, who's now a visiting vehicle integration manager for the International Space Station at NASA's Johnson Space Center, told Space.com.
Lightning-watching instruments not designed for detecting bolides, he said, "afford the science community to discuss these events and these sensors in a forthright, open manner. These lightning imagers give us opportunistic bonus science for those who study the 'hard rain.'"
Landis said that, in his personal view, there's a lot of smaller stuff getting through the atmosphere.
"To the casual observer, these certainly produce wonderful natural fireworks and are mostly harmless," Landis said. But, he stressed, it's important to be able to distinguish between natural events and human-made ones.
"It would be a horrific tragedy if any nation responded to a natural event — if they misinterpret it as a preemptive strike," cautioned Landis.
Real-world tests
So, in the big picture, having collaborative, multiple and independent ways to observe atmospheric entries is of benefit to planetary defense thinkers.
"Planetary defense is not only about finding an object before it reaches Earth," Silber said. "It is also about understanding what happens during atmospheric entry — that is, how the object fragments, where it deposits its energy, how accurately we can reconstruct its trajectory and whether material survives to the ground."
Incoming events provide "real-world tests" of the methods and models used to answer those questions, said Silber.
Harkening back to the recent Alaska fireball fall, Silber said, was particularly valuable because it was unpredicted, yet the dense ground-based network allowed the trajectory and energetics to be reconstructed in considerable detail.
"From a planetary-defense perspective, that kind of redundancy is extremely useful. Space-based observations, seismic and infrasound networks, optical cameras, and weather radar each provide different information, and each has its own limitations," Silber said.
When several observation techniques are available, researchers can cross-check one another and produce a much more complete characterization of an event.
"That improves post-event situational awareness, helps validate physical models and strengthens our ability to interpret future atmospheric entries, whether they involve natural objects or artificial reentries," Silber concluded.
Leonard David is an award-winning space journalist who has been reporting on space activities for more than 50 years. Currently writing as Space.com's Space Insider Columnist among his other projects, Leonard has authored numerous books on space exploration, Mars missions and more, with his latest being "Moon Rush: The New Space Race" published in 2019 by National Geographic. He also wrote "Mars: Our Future on the Red Planet" released in 2016 by National Geographic. Leonard has served as a correspondent for SpaceNews, Scientific American and Aerospace America for the AIAA. He has received many awards, including the first Ordway Award for Sustained Excellence in Spaceflight History in 2015 at the AAS Wernher von Braun Memorial Symposium. You can find out Leonard's latest project at his website and on Twitter.

articles.title: Loài cây kỳ lạ chỉ có duy nhất một chiếc lá ở Việt Nam
articles.text:
Loài cây này hiếm gặp tới mức nhiều người ví von việc tìm thấy nó khó như kiếm lá diêu bông.
Ở Việt Nam có một loài cây vô cùng độc đáo. Nó chỉ có duy nhất một chiếc lá hình trái tim. Vì vậy, loài cây này được gọi tên là cây một lá.
Cây một lá có tên khoa học là Nervilia fordii (Hance) Schultze, thuộc họ Orchidaceae (Lan) là một chi gồm các loài thực vật độc đáo thuộc họ Lan, có đặc điểm chung là chỉ có một chiếc lá duy nhất trong vòng đời của mình. Nó còn có tên gọi khác là thanh thiên quỳ, lan một lá, lan cờ, châu diệp, slam lài, bửa thoọc (Tày), bầu thoọc…
Đây là các loài cây thân thảo lâu năm, có củ hình tròn hoặc hình bầu dục, lá hình trái tim với các đường gân tỏa như rẻ quạt, mọc ra từ một chiếc cuống nối với củ rễ. Lan một lá có một hoặc hai hoa mọc ra từ một thân thẳng. Khi ra hoa, cây không có lá. Chỉ sau khi hoa nở hết, chiếc lá mới bắt đầu phát triển.
Tại Việt Nam, có 5 loài lan một lá đã được ghi nhận.
Hiện nay, khoảng 80 loài lan một lá đã được phát hiện, phân bố rộng rãi ở lục địa châu Phi, châu Á và các các đảo khác nhau của Thái Bình Dương và Ấn Độ Dương.
Cây một lá tái sinh tự nhiên bằng các tia củ, vì thế trong một nhóm cây trong tự nhiên thường có nhiều cây ở các lứa tuổi khác nhau.
Tại Việt Nam, có 5 loài lan một lá đã được ghi nhận, gồm Nervilia aragoana, Nervilia crispata, Nervilia fordii, Nervilia plicata và Nervilia prainiana. Loài cây này thường được tìm thấy ở các vùng núi đá vôi và nơi ẩm ướt ở các chân núi. Cây thường mọc ở Lào Cai, Hòa Bình, Ninh Bình, Lạng Sơn, Cao Bằng, Hà Giang, Tuyên Quang, Hà Tây, Sơn La, Lai Châu,…
Trong dân gian, từ lâu nay, lan một lá đã được coi là cây thuốc quý. Tất cả các bộ phận của cây một lá đều có thể làm thuốc, dùng tươi hoặc phơi khô.
Theo cuốn "Cây thuốc và động vật làm thuốc ở Việt Nam, tập 1, nhà xuất bản Khoa học và kĩ thuật, Hà Nội" thì lá và rễ củ cây một lá có vị ngọt nhạt, hơi đắng, tính bình, mát và có tác dụng thanh nhiệt, nhuận phế, giảm ho, tán ứ, giải độc, làm dịu đau. Lá và cây còn được dùng làm thuốc giải độc, nhất là ngộ độc nấm, làm mát phổi, chữa ho lao, ho lâu năm, viêm phế quản. Nhai rễ củ tươi làm giải khát, bồi dưỡng cơ thể.
Cận cảnh củ của cây một lá. (Ảnh: Ineternet).
Trên thế giới đã có một số công trình nghiên cứu về thành phần hóa học cũng như hoạt tính sinh học của các hợp chất chiết xuất từ cây một lá. Kết quả cho thấy, cây một lá chứa terpenoids, flavonoid, axit amin và một số loại dầu dễ bay hơi. Các hợp chất này có hoạt tính dược lý chống viêm, chống vi rút, giảm đau, giảm ho, hen suyễn và viêm phế quản mãn tính, viêm phổi cấp, bệnh phổi tắc nghẽn mãn tính... Hiện nay, cây một lá đang được nghiên cứu để điều trị các chứng ung thư phổi, ung thư vòm họng. Với giá trị kinh tế và dược lý cao, cây một lá được coi là một trong những loài cây cần được ưu tiên trong bảo tồn nguồn gen hiếm.
Theo khuyến cao của các chuyên gia, khi thu hoạch, để bảo vệ cây chỉ nên thu hái toàn cây, hoặc chỉ lấy lá, dành củ cho cây phát triển. Lá cây có thể thu hái quanh năm, dùng tươi hoặc khô đều được. Thu hái về để riêng lá to và lá nhỏ, sơ chế.
Theo báo An ninh thủ đô, cây một lá là loài cây có giá trị dược liệu quý nên chúng chủ yếu dùng để xuất khẩu, trong nước rất ít dùng. Vì lý do này, nhiều người dân ở khu vực có cây một lá sinh sống cũng hiếm có dịp được nhìn thấy nó. Nhiều người còn đánh giá rằng, việc tìm thấy cây một lá cũng khó như tìm lá diêu bông.
Tuy nhiên, cây một lá thường bị nhầm với cây bát giác liên (Dysosma chengii) vì đó cũng là loại cây củ và một lá. Tuy nhiên, lá của cây bát giác có 6 cạnh, còn cây một lá là hình tim. Thậm chí, có nhiều người còn nhầm lẫn cây một lá với lá cây mã đề.
Vì loài cây này có giá trị dược liệu quý nên chúng chủ yếu dùng để xuất khẩu, trong nước rất hiếm người dân bản địa có cơ hội thấy. (Ảnh: Internet).
Ngoài làm dược liệu, cây một lá còn được người chơi cây cảnh trên thế giới yêu thích, sưu tầm vì sự độc đáo và hiếm gặp.
Theo Tạp chí Khoa học và Công nghệ Việt Nam, trữ lượng cây một lá trong tự nhiên ở Việt Nam ngày càng suy giảm do bị khai thác nhiều. Lượng cây một lá trong tự nhiên không nhiều (ở Vườn quốc gia Pù Mát là 10 - 15 cây/100m2) khiến cho loài cây này trở nên quý hiếm và có nguy cơ bị đe dọa tuyệt chủng. Cây một lá được ghi vào danh sách các loài cây cần được bảo vệ trong "Sách đỏ Việt Nam".
Cũng theo Tạp chí Khoa học và Công nghệ Việt Nam, hiện các nhà nghiên cứu đang tiến hành nhân giống loài cây quý hiếm này tại Lạng Sơn. Lạng Sơn là tỉnh có điều kiện khí hậu, đất đai, địa hình thuận lợi cho sự sinh trưởng và phát triển của nhiều nguồn gen dược liệu quý hiếm, trong đó có cây một lá. Viện Nghiên cứu và Phát triển Vùng đã thực hiện nhiệm vụ "Nghiên cứu bảo tồn và phát triển nguồn gene cây một lá" trên địa bàn tỉnh Lạng Sơn nhằm thu thập bảo quản nguồn gene cây một lá, xây dựng phương pháp lưu trữ, bảo quản, phục tráng, nhân giống nguồn gene; xây dựng các mô hình bảo tồn, khai thác và phát triển nguồn gen quý này để phục vụ phát triển kinh tế - xã hội của địa phương.
Hiện các nhà nghiên cứu đang tiến hành nhân giống để bảo tồn loài cây quý hiếm này. (Ảnh: Internet).
Các nghiên cứu về kỹ thuật nhân giống cây một lá cho thấy, thời vụ trồng cây tốt nhất là tháng 3-4 hàng năm (tỷ lệ sống đạt từ 96,0-96,7%, tỷ lệ nảy mầm đạt 87,33-95,3%). Kích thước củ có ảnh hưởng lớn đến sinh trưởng của cây một lá. Củ giống có đường kính từ 1,0 đến lớn hơn 2,0 cm đều cho tỷ lệ nảy mầm cao (87,33-97,33%).
Do bị khai thác nhiều, trữ lượng lan một lá trong tự nhiên ở Việt Nam ngày càng suy giảm. Việc tiến hành nghiên cứu để nhân giống loài cây quý này đã được thực hiện ở nước ta những năm gần đây.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 1, 1962: The Soviet Union Launches Mars 1 spacecraft to Red Planet during the Space Race
articles.text:
On this day in space! Nov. 1, 1962: The Soviet Union Launches Mars 1 spacecraft to Red Planet during the Space Race
No one knew what it looked like until the day before Halloween, when the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico captured the first radar images.
On Nov. 1, 1962, the Soviet Union launched the Mars 1 spacecraft on a mission to fly by the Red Planet.
While it did end up flying by Mars, the mission was not exactly a success. After it separated from the rocket, it deployed its solar panels and started cruising toward Mars.
When mission controllers were checking out the telemetry it transmitted back to Earth, they found out that Mars 1 had sprung a leak in one of the gas valves that controls the spacecraft's orientation. And without a working orientation system, Mars 1 would have a hard time pointing its antennas in the right direction. It lost contact with Earth when it was about halfway to Mars.
Why it mattered
Ever since Galileo Galilei pointed his telescope to the red-tinted star and identified as a planet, Mars has captivated scientists' interests as to its nature. So it was of no surprise that as soon as we gained the ability to send missions into space, that the focus turned to the "fourth rock from the Sun."
As it turned out, though, reaching Mars, let alone entering its orbit or landing on its surface,, was and continues to be difficult.
Mars 1, despite its name, was actually the Soviet Union's fourth attempt at sending a probe to the planet. The first three ended in launch failures. Similar problems faced the United States, as well, but it was NASA's Mariner IV mission that became the first to successfully fly by Mars two years later.
Still, as humanity continues to push forward to the day people land on, explore and live on Mars, the 1962 Soviet mission stands as the first to get close to revealing the first details about the planet.
Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.
Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.
- Robert Z. Pearlman collectSPACE.com Editor, Space.com Contributor

articles.title: Tái xuất sau hơn 20 năm biến mất, loài thú lập tức gây sốt vì quý hiếm hơn cả gấu trúc
articles.text:
Sau khi được phát hiện vào năm 1983 và nhìn thấy một lần nữa vào năm 1990, loài vật này đã biến mất không để lại dấu vết trong hơn 20 năm.
Trong thế giới ngày nay, có rất nhiều loài vật mà chúng ta chưa khám phá ra hoặc chưa từng nghe nói đến. Và cũng có những loài vật mà con người mới chỉ nghe nhắc tới tên rồi chúng biến mất không để lại chút dấu vết nào. Thỏ Ili Pika cũng như vậy. Mãi tới sau hơn 2 thập kỷ, các nhà khoa học mới có cơ hội chụp hình loài vật này.
Thỏ Ili pika xuất hiện trở lại sau hơn 20 năm biến mất. (Ảnh: CNN)
Với số lượng chỉ còn chưa tới 1.000 cá thể, thỏ Ili pika là một trong những loài đang bị đe dọa tuyệt chủng cao nhất thế giới. Thậm chí chúng được đánh giá là quý hiếm hơn cả gấu trúc.
Thỏ Ili pika là một loài động vật có vú thuộc họ Ochotona của bộ thỏ, đặc hữu của vùng tây bắc Trung Quốc. Thỏ Ili Pika sống ở vùng núi Thiên Sơn thuộc Tân Cương, Trung Quốc. Ngoài ra, chúng còn được tìm thấy ở vùng tây bắc Hoa Kỳ và tây Canada.
Thỏ Ili pika sống ở độ cao từ 2.800 đến 4.000 mét. (Ảnh: CNN)
Ili pika chỉ được tìm thấy ở độ cao 2.800 - 4.000 mét. Thỏ Ili pika dài khoảng 20cm, nặng khoảng 180 gram và có đôi tai lớn. Chúng có bộ lông màu xám pha nâu, chân tay ngắn với đôi tai tròn trông rất dễ thương, khuôn mặt lại giống gấu. Thoạt nhìn, thỏ Ili pika có vẻ ngoài đáng yêu như những chú gấu bông. Thức ăn của chúng chủ yếu là cây cỏ mọc quanh đó. Kẻ thù của thỏ Ili Pika là cáo, chồn, chim ăn thịt,...
Thỏ Ili pika thường tranh thủ kiếm ăn vào mùa hè. Chúng sẽ dùng toàn bộ thời gian trong giai đoạn ấm áp này để dự trữ thức ăn cho mùa đông buốt giá. Theo thống kê của các nhà khoa học, một chú thỏ Ili pika sẽ thực hiện 10.000 chuyến đi trong mùa hè để tích được 25 kg lương thực.
Chúng thường tranh thủ kiếm ăn vào mùa hè để tích trữ cho mùa đông giá rét. (Ảnh: CNN)
Thế nhưng có rất nhiều chú thỏ Ili pika "làm biếng" bằng cách "ăn trộm" thức ăn của những con thỏ khác. Vì thói quen kỳ quặc này nên chúng có biệt danh khác là "kẻ trộm đáng yêu".
Người phát hiện ra thỏ Ili pika là ông Lý Duy Đông vào năm 1983. Sau đó ông đã quyết định đặt tên nó theo tên của quê hương mình là Ili. Ông Lý nhớ lại lần đầu mình bắt gặp 1 con Ili pika "Tôi leo lên một ngọn núi trong suốt 4 tiếng. Lúc đó tôi đang dừng lại để thở, thì bỗng nhiên tôi trông thấy bóng của một sinh vật nhỏ xíu chạy ngang qua. Tôi ngồi xuống chỗ mấy tảng đá, rồi một đôi tai thỏ thò lên từ khe hở của tảng đá quanh đó. Con vật nhỏ bé đang nhìn tôi và chớp mắt. Tôi đã nghĩ rằng đây là loài vật xinh đẹp và lạ lùng nhất mà tôi từng thấy. Tôi không thể tin vào mắt mình".
Tuy nhiên, có nhiều con thỏ Ili pika "lười biếng" lấy trộm đồ ăn của con khác để làm của mình. (Ảnh: CNN)
Các nhà khoa học đã thực hiện thống kê về Ili pika, và họ ước tính số lượng thỏ Ili pika đã giảm từ 2.900 con vào những năm 90 xuống còn 2.000 con trong năm 2005. Hiện tại có lẽ chúng chỉ còn khoảng 1.000 con. Theo các nhà khoa học, kể từ sau khi được tìm thấy, số lượng của loài này đã giảm 70%.
"Những con vật nhỏ bé có thể tuyệt chủng bất kỳ lúc nào. Chúng sẽ không còn tồn tại ở những nơi từng sống trước đây nữa", ông Lý chia sẻ cùng CNN.
Ili pika vốn sống ở độ cao khoảng 3.200-3.400 m, nhưng giờ đây chúng đã leo lên những nơi cao 4.100 m. Năm 2008, Liên minh Bảo tồn Thiên nhiên Quốc tế (IUCN) xếp chúng vào nhóm động vật gặp nguy hiểm, nhưng chưa có tổ chức hoặc nhóm chuyên gia nào có ý định nghiên cứu hoặc bảo vệ chúng.
Thỏ Ili pika đứng trước nguy cơ tuyệt chủng vì sự thay đổi khí hậu và do con người. (Ảnh: CNN)
Ô nhiễm không khí toàn cầu, sự biến đổi khí hậu và sự gia tăng áp lực chăn thả động vật được cho là những mối đe dọa chính đối với loài động vật này. Một nguyên nhân khác là do sự xuất hiện quá nhiều của loài người ở các khu vực dưới chân núi đã khiến diện tích sinh sống của chúng bị thu hẹp dần.

articles.title: Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists
articles.text:
Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists
- Date:
- November 1, 2026
- Source:
- University of Southampton
- Summary:
- A mysterious particle overlooked for decades may hold the key to why matter survived the Big Bang, allowing stars, planets, and life to exist. Scientists believe this forgotten neutrino reshaped the early universe and may have left detectable gravitational wave signals that could help unlock the cosmos’s deepest mysteries.
- Share:
Scientists have proposed a surprising new explanation for why the universe exists, and it centers on a mysterious particle that physicists have largely overlooked for decades. Their theory suggests this forgotten particle may have played a crucial role in shaping the early cosmos and allowing matter to survive after the Big Bang.
The research addresses one of the most fundamental mysteries in physics: why does the universe contain matter instead of nothing at all? Scientists believe matter and antimatter were produced in nearly equal amounts in the early universe. When these opposites encounter one another, they annihilate and release energy. If they had existed in perfectly equal quantities, virtually all matter could have disappeared, leaving no material to form stars, planets, or life.
Now, researchers from the University of Southampton and the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur believe they may have found an important piece of the puzzle. Their explanation involves a little-understood relative of the neutrino, an extremely lightweight particle that rarely interacts with ordinary matter.
A Forgotten Particle With a Powerful Role in the Early Universe
The team focused on a type of particle known as a 'decoupled' heavy neutrino. Unlike ordinary neutrinos, this hypothetical heavier relative has generally been considered too weakly connected to other particles to significantly influence the universe.
However, the researchers found that its unusually long lifetime could have made it far more important than previously thought. According to their calculations, the particle may have survived long enough to temporarily dominate the universe's energy density as the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang.
That brief period of dominance could have altered how the early universe evolved, influencing the conditions that ultimately allowed matter to outnumber antimatter.
Dr. Rishav Roshan of the University of Southampton, an author of the study, explained:
"This decoupled heavy neutrino has long been dismissed as an irrelevant background detail in particle physics.
"However, it decays incredibly slowly. As the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang, the particle lived long enough that it temporarily took over the energy density of the universe and triggered a matter-dominated period."
The findings were published in Physical Review Letters, a scientific journal of the American Physical Society.
How a Heavy Neutrino Could Explain Why Matter Survived
Previous attempts to explain why matter prevailed over antimatter generally left out the decoupled heavy neutrino. Because it interacts so weakly with other particles, scientists assumed it would have little influence on the processes responsible for creating the imbalance.
The new research challenges that assumption. The team found that even a particle with extremely weak interactions could indirectly affect the conditions under which matter gained its crucial advantage.
This imbalance, known as matter and antimatter asymmetry, is essential to understanding our existence. For reasons physicists are still trying to explain, the early universe ended up with slightly more matter than antimatter. That small difference allowed some matter to remain after most particles and their antiparticles annihilated one another.
"The fact that we are here at all proves that an asymmetry between matter and antimatter occurred," added Dr. Roshan.
"The decoupled neutrino shifted the temperature in the early universe at which fundamental particles - like electrons and other leptons - interacted with their anti-particles with the help of Standard Model Higgs boson.
"This temperature acts like a switch that shapes how the matter-antimatter imbalance was built up."
The Higgs boson is a fundamental particle associated with the mechanism that gives many elementary particles their mass. In the researchers' proposed scenario, the heavy neutrino changed the temperature conditions governing important particle interactions involving the Higgs boson.
By shifting when these interactions occurred, the particle could have influenced how the imbalance between matter and antimatter developed. In other words, something long considered insignificant may have helped determine why the universe contains matter at all.
Ancient Gravitational Waves Could Reveal the Answer
The theory could also have important implications for understanding how the universe expanded in its earliest stages.
Study co-author Dr. Sudipta Show of the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur said the findings suggest that the forgotten particle may have dramatically altered the expansion history of the young cosmos.
He added: "It offers us a new explanation for how matter won.
"The dramatic shift in the early expansion of the cosmos leaves distinct but detectable imprints of changes, for example on primordial gravitational waves.
"These gravitational wave signatures open up new avenues for us to unravel the evolution of the early universe after the Big Bang."
Gravitational waves are ripples in the fabric of space and time. Scientists believe processes in the extremely early universe may have generated primordial gravitational waves that carry information about conditions from that distant era.
According to the new theory, the temporary dominance of the heavy neutrino could have left recognizable signatures in those ancient signals. Detecting such patterns could eventually provide a way to investigate whether the proposed particle really influenced the universe's earliest evolution.
For now, the explanation remains theoretical. But it offers physicists a new possibility for solving one of cosmology's deepest mysteries: how matter survived when its encounter with antimatter could have left the universe almost entirely empty.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Southampton. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Rishav Roshan, Sudipta Show. Delayed Charged Lepton Yukawa Equilibration in Minimal Seesaw. Physical Review Letters, 2026; 137 (11) DOI: 10.1103/nfkx-q6z7
