articles.title: Tesla is ditching its solar roof tiles for a good reason - Engadget
articles.text:
Tesla is ditching its solar roof tiles for a good reason
Tesla had to cut losses after significant mistakes and overspending
Tesla's Solar Roof panels were designed to look like regular shingles while delivering 98 percent of a normal solar panel's efficiency. It did so by reflecting light to make the tiles appear like normal ones from street level despite being transparent when viewed from above. Unfortunately, the novel concept didn't live up to expectations. In August 2026, Electrek reported that Tesla was discontinuing the product and that its third-party installer network would only be supplied with conventional solar panels going forward.
First revealed in 2026, the Solar Roof hit mass production in 2020. In a first-quarter earnings call in 2021, Tesla CEO Elon Musk admitted that "significant mistakes" were made that led to overspending and significant delays. Two years later, a Wood Mackenzie report found that only 3,000 U.S. homes had installed the product. Despite multiple redesigns, the Solar Roof tiles sold under Tesla's expectations of 1,000 installations per week. Here's how it all went down.
What was the Tesla Solar Roof?
The Solar Roof's claim to fame was that it didn't look as unsightly as a traditional solar panel. Tesla's patent application notes that "The louvers are designed to provide viewing obstruction to the photovoltaic cells... when viewed from a side angle but to minimally impede solar energy passed to the photovoltaic cells."
Nearly 10 years after its glitzy reveal at homes that appeared on the Desperate Housewives TV show, Tesla appears to be sunsetting the Solar Roof tiles. Shortly after the launch event, the company acquired SolarCity, America's then-largest solar energy provider founded by Musk's cousins, for $2.6 billion. Years later, shareholder litigation over the acquisition revealed that the tiles shown at the event weren't operational, according to Electrek.
Tesla's Solar Roof page, tesla.com/solarroof, has been redirected to its solar panels. The product is also nowhere to be found in its Energy navigation menu. The company's online configurator for a Solar Roof quote now redirects to its conventional panels, indicating a pivot away from its poorly selling products. TechCrunch learned that solar installers are still offering Tesla's Solar Roof depending on the timeline of the project.
Why was Tesla's Solar Roof discontinued?
High prices and missed sales targets led to the downfall of Tesla's Solar Roof. In 2021, Electrek found that customers were hit with a drastic spike in costs. The publication used a 3,947 square-foot roof with a 12.3 kW solar roof tile system as a frame of reference. Pricing went from $54,966 before incentives to a rate between $79,938 and $100,621 within a year. This wild swing in prices made Solar Roofs a luxury to own. Tesla bet on its product's aesthetic value while traditional solar panels went down in cost every year thanks to efficient modules and mass production.
Tesla installed between 21 and 32 Solar Roofs a week at its peak in 2022, Wood Mackenzie data found. Those numbers are a far cry from Musk's 1,000 per week target. User reports of these roofs underproducing electricity and cases of their roof underlayment melting didn't help Tesla's odds. Flexible panels from rivals like Merlin Solar are still being sold, which means integrated solar panels haven't gone extinct yet. But Tesla abandoning the idea risks an industry-wide seismic shift away from the concept despite its aesthetic merits.

articles.title: HomePod Mini 2 first look: Three things I love and one disappointment
articles.text:
When I first heard about the new $149 HomePod Mini 2 at Apple’s Welcome Home event last month, I was disappointed. It’s been six years since Apple launched its entry-level smart speaker, and all it got in the second gen was a chip bump, some color glowy stuff, and better AirPlay? For $50 more than the original, which launched at $99, Apple didn’t even upgrade the sound system. It felt like the company phoned this one in.
HomePod Mini 2 first look: Three things I love and one disappointment
The new Mini is faster, quieter, and gorgeous in green, but its upgraded Mac speaker feature didn’t work for me.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Now that I’ve got my hands on a couple and set them up in my home office, I’m more enthused. The Mini 2 is so much faster than the first-gen Mini, playing music in a few seconds and responding to smart home commands just as quickly. If you’re fed up with standing over your HomePod waiting for it to finally do what you asked, then that alone is worth the upgrade.
Here are my three favorite features of the new Mini 2 after spending a couple days with it, and my one big disappointment.
Siri is much snappier and much less chatty
The biggest upgrade for the Mini 2 is Siri AI, but that isn’t available yet. Apple says it’s coming “later” in a software update. However, the basic smart voice assistant has definitely improved. Siri on the Mini 2 is much snappier than on the first-gen Mini, regularly responding in under three seconds. This is thanks to a newer, faster processor (the S10, up from the S5) and Wi-Fi 6E support (up from Wi-Fi 4).
When I asked Siri to play Taylor Swift, a song started in a couple of seconds. It correctly told me who won this year’s World Series in under two seconds, and turned off the light or opened the shades in under three seconds.
That’s a huge improvement over the up to 10 seconds I often have to wait for Siri to get things done on the first-gen Mini. However, asking something harder, like who will win the US midterm elections, still brings up the familiar offer to look at some web results on my iPhone. As I said, Siri AI isn’t here yet.
The other new behavior I am really enjoying is that when I ask Siri to perform a smart home action, such as open the shades or turn on the lights, instead of “OK, Jen,” or “One sec,” followed by a wordy confirmation of the action that I often get on the first-gen Mini, the Mini 2 just does it and doesn’t talk back. It’s not silent for every action, but it’s quiet enough to be a noticeable improvement.
This Mini is gorgeous in green and sounds great
The green color is divine. This is the prettiest small smart speaker I’ve seen — and I’ve tried them all.
Yes, Amazon’s Echo Dot Max’s purple is fun, the Google Home Speaker’s pale green is elegant, but Apple’s deep green is seriously sophisticated. It’s a color that fits in really well in various places around my home, and I’m so glad the company finally released a green option. It’s a big improvement over the slightly garish yellow and orange of the prior-gen Minis and the best of the new colors.
I saw all the colors in person at Apple’s Welcome Home event, and while the pink is pretty, it’s very pale, and the blue is functionally identical to the first-gen blue, maybe a shade lighter. While a lot of folks will be happy with black (don’t get white unless you plan to dust it regularly), the green is my new go-to.
Two green HomePod Mini 2s look so good on the walnut Nanoleaf monitor stand I’m testing; it’s like my office got an instant upgrade. And while Apple didn’t update the speakers in the Mini 2, it’s still a very good speaker for its size, doing a fine job with Bad Bunny’s bass and delivering clear mids and vocals. While $300 is steep for computer speakers, two as a stereo pair in my office definitely delivered on room-filling sound.
You can finally disable touch
A few weeks ago I fumbled for my phone on my nightstand and accidentally hit the top of my HomePod Mini, blaring music in the bedroom at 3AM. My husband was not happy.
A new setting in the Home app now lets you lock the Mini’s top controls. This goes for all HomePods, old and new, and it’s a major quality-of-life upgrade. How often do you intentionally touch the top of your HomePod? I bet far less often than accidentally!
The other new trick for the top of the HomePod is Sound Glow. This makes the LEDs display colors that match the album art of the song you’re playing (it’s also backward compatible with the first-gen Mini and the second-gen HomePod). It’s neat, but only works with Apple Music and Podcasts and is so subtle that I don’t feel it adds much to my music-listening experience.
Signature feature fail
Beyond the speed improvement, the other new feature I was excited about is the HomePod Mini 2’s ability to be the default speaker for your Mac using what Apple calls “a responsive and persistent AirPlay connection.” This creates a wireless point-to-point connection between the computer and the HomePod.
You can pair a single speaker or a stereo pair to your Mac, and the feature also works with the second-gen HomePod. (Two or four HomePod Mini 2s can also now be part of a surround sound setup using the new Apple TV 4K.)
Disappointingly, I couldn’t get the Mac speaker set up to work. I have the required hardware: a Mac that supports Wi-Fi 6E, running the public release of macOS 27.2 (a Mac Mini M4), and HomePods on HomePod Software 27.2. But the Sound pane in my Mac’s settings didn’t offer an option to set a HomePod via AirPlay as the default sound output.
The Mini showed up and connected like any other AirPlay speaker, with the same flaws as regular AirPlay — occasional artifacting, drop-offs, and some lag with notification sounds — along with the Mac defaulting to its built-in speakers when the computer restarts, or anytime I activate Siri on the HomePod. I also tried with a stereo pair of Minis, but they also played over regular AirPlay.
The chip bump and speed improvements make this a bigger upgrade than it initially seemed
According to a 9to5Mac’s hands-on, when the persistent AirPlay is enabled, the HomePod Mini should show up as a default system output device in the System Information, and there should be an option to enable it under “Play sound effects through” in the Sound pane in System Settings, but neither was there for me. I have seen other reports of the same issue.
I tried resetting both HomePods completely after they updated to 27.2 out of the box (I was on the HomePod Software betas, but 27.2 is now in general release), and the feature still isn’t working. I reached out to Apple, but the company hasn’t responded to my requests yet; I’ll update this article if I hear back or find a solution.
There’s more to come
I’ve only been testing the Mini 2 for two days, and while the real test will come when it gets its Siri AI upgrade, the chip bump and speed improvements make this a bigger upgrade than it initially seemed. Apple does need to work on the Mac pairing feature; it has a lot of potential, but based on my struggles here, it feels unfinished.
I plan to do a full review once Siri AI launches, and of course compare it to Apple’s big new smart home release: the upcoming $299 Apple HomeView smart display. It is also a Home hub, but the screen gives it more functionality. At $149, though, the Mini 2 is now the cheapest way to get an Apple Home hub with Thread and Matter support.

articles.title: Claude Ultra drops the five-hour limit for verified $200 subscribers
articles.text:
Anthropic has renamed its two Claude Max plans and dropped the five-hour usage limit on the more expensive one. It now calls the $100-a-month Max 5x plan Max, and the $200 Max 20x plan Ultra. Prices stay the same, the company said on X on Friday.
Verified Ultra accounts no longer have a limit that resets every five hours. Most existing subscribers got the change on Friday. Newer accounts keep a temporary limit until Anthropic verifies them, which it said helps prevent fraud and abuse. Those users will get an email when it is lifted. Weekly limits stay the same.
“If you’re a subscriber, there’s nothing you need to do.” Claude, Anthropic’s official account, on X
What each plan now includes
Anthropic’s pricing page now lists Max as five times Pro usage, every five hours and every week. It comes with $100 a month in API credits.
The page lists Ultra at ten times Pro usage every week, with no five-hour limit for verified accounts. It comes with $200 a month in API credits, up from $100 on Max. Both plans include Fable, Anthropic’s top model, for up to half of the weekly limit. In Europe the two plans cost €90 and €180 a month.
Earlier changes to Claude’s plans
The old Max 20x name pointed to 20 times Pro usage. The pricing page now lists ten times Pro usage a week for Ultra, and Anthropic’s post did not mention the change.
A lawsuit filed in June claimed Anthropic oversold the usage on both Max plans. In May, Anthropic doubled five-hour limits for Claude Code, citing new computing capacity from SpaceX. In April, it blocked OpenClaw and other third-party agent tools from using Claude subscriptions.

articles.title: Giá xăng dầu hôm nay 1/11: Thế giới tăng, xăng trong nước giảm sâu
articles.text:
Giá dầu thế giới hôm nay
Giá dầu quốc tế trong tuần này trải qua một tuần biến động mạnh với 2 phiên tăng và 3 phiên giảm.
Cụ thể, trong phiên giao dịch đầu tuần này (26/10), giá dầu thế giới quay đầu giảm nhẹ sau khi tăng mạnh vào phiên cuối tuần trước. Chốt phiên giao dịch 26/10, giá dầu Brent giảm 0,78%, còn giá dầu WTI của Mỹ hạ 1,46%, trong bối cảnh kỳ vọng căng thẳng giữa Mỹ và Iran hạ nhiệt.
Giá dầu quốc tế tiếp tục đi xuống ở phiên giao dịch 27/10 khi đàm phán tại Trung Đông xoa dịu lo ngại nguồn cung. Chốt phiên này, giá dầu Brent giảm 1,67%, trong khi giá dầu WTI hạ 1,83%.
Tuy nhiên, đến phiên giao dịch 28/10, giá dầu thế giới đảo chiều tăng do vụ tấn công nhằm vào nhà máy lọc dầu tại Saudi Arabia và giao tranh tại Yemen, làm gia tăng lo ngại về nguy cơ gián đoạn nguồn cung năng lượng ở Trung Đông. Kết phiên giao dịch 28/10, giá dầu Brent tăng 1,26%, còn giá dầu WTI tăng 3%.
Tới phiên giao dịch 29/10, giá dầu quốc tế lại quay đầu giảm nhẹ, khi kỳ vọng Mỹ và Iran nối lại đàm phán hòa bình phần nào làm dịu lo ngại về nguy cơ gián đoạn nguồn cung do xung đột leo thang tại Trung Đông.
Ở phiên giao dịch cuối cùng của tuần này (30/10), giá dầu thế giới tăng mạnh, chạm mốc cao nhất kể từ cuối tháng 4, khi giới đầu tư lo ngại xung đột Mỹ - Iran có thể leo thang sau cuộc bầu cử giữa nhiệm kỳ tại Mỹ. Chốt phiên giao dịch cuối tuần, giá dầu Brent tăng 2,37%, trong khi giá dầu WTI tăng 2,08%.
Giá dầu Brent đóng cửa tuần này ở mức 113,4 USD/thùng, còn giá dầu WTI kết tuần ở mức 104,1 USD/thùng.
Như vậy, trong tuần này, giá dầu Brent hạ 3,3 USD/thùng, trong khi giá dầu WTI tăng 0,8 USD/thùng so với mức kết của tuần trước.
Còn tính chung trong cả tháng 10, giá dầu Brent tăng 13,6%, giá dầu WTI tăng 15,2%. Đây là mức tăng cao nhất trong vòng 6 tháng qua của hai loại dầu tiêu chuẩn.
Giá xăng dầu trong nước hôm nay
Ở thị trường trong nước, giá bán của các mặt hàng xăng trong tuần này được điều chỉnh tới 2 lần.
Tại kỳ điều hành ngày 29/10, giá xăng dầu đồng loạt tăng mạnh. Theo đó, giá bán lẻ xăng E5RON92 không cao hơn 26.027 đồng/lít, tăng 666 đồng/lít.
Giá xăng E10RON95-III được điều chỉnh lên mức tối đa 25.734 đồng/lít, tăng 521 đồng/lít.
Tương tự, giá dầu diesel 0.05S tăng 696 đồng/lít, lên mức không cao hơn 30.246 đồng/lít; giá dầu mazut 180CST 3.5S tăng 223 đồng/kg, lên mức tối đa 23.596 đồng/kg.
Tuy nhiên, sau khi thuế tiêu thụ đặc biệt được hạ về 0, giá xăng đồng loạt được điều chỉnh giảm mạnh.
Theo quyết định điều chỉnh giá bán lẻ các mặt hàng xăng phổ biến trên thị trường từ 0h ngày 1/11 của liên bộ Công Thương - Tài chính, giá bán lẻ xăng E5RON92 hạ 1.804 đồng/lít, giá bán không cao hơn 24.223 đồng/lít; giá xăng E10RON95-III được điều chỉnh về 24.159 đồng/lít, giảm 1.575 đồng/lít.
Như vậy, trong tuần này, giá xăng E5RON92 giảm 1.138 đồng/lít, trong khi giá xăng E10RON95-III hạ 1.054 đồng/lít. Còn giá dầu diesel 0.05S tăng 696 đồng/lít, dầu mazut 180CST 3.5S tăng 223 đồng/kg.

articles.title: Claude Code now refuses to help build copies of existing games
articles.text:
Game developers have been hitting refusals from Claude Code since late October, some on projects they say they have a right to build. Bruno Ferreira reported the complaints for Tom’s Hardware on Saturday, citing a wave of issues on Claude Code’s public GitHub tracker. TNW read the issues.
Anthropic has not announced a change, and its Claude Code changelog does not mention one. Tom’s Hardware said there was no official statement.
What one developer reports
The owner of Conflict Simulations LLC builds personalised digital versions of board wargames for clients who own the games. Around 27 October, Claude Code began getting “a server-side instruction” to refuse game work, the developer wrote in a GitHub issue on 30 October. Sessions now refuse the work, citing an instruction against reproducing games.
“A blanket category rule against ‘games’ cannot tell the difference between piracy and commissioned professional work for a game’s owner.” The owner of Conflict Simulations LLC, on GitHub
In an update, the developer said the sessions kept doing the work after the rule reportedly arrived. The refusals began only after they asked Claude to check whether the rule affected their projects. They continued in new sessions on the same code. One commenter suggested the project’s memory or Git history now carried the refusal, and the developer said they would try to clear it.
Anthropic’s support bot told the developer the policy covers all customers, with no exception, the developer wrote. Both support tickets were later passed to staff, and the developer has filed an appeal. They asked Anthropic to aim the rule at real copyright infringement and to offer a verification path for professionals.
The wider context
Not everyone on the thread agreed. One commenter said that unless the work is for the rights holders, it is no different from any other reverse-engineered port.
Other developers reported a separate kind of block this month. Claude Code’s cyber safeguards flagged anti-cheat code for one developer’s game and a security review of another’s own game. Tom’s Hardware said the timing of the two kinds of restriction may be a coincidence.
Anthropic says its generally available models have conservative cyber safeguards that block most cyber work. On 6 October it expanded its Cyber Verification Program, which lifts some of those blocks for vetted security teams. Members of Project Glasswing, its earlier programme for its Mythos model, move into the top tier.
The company also faces copyright claims, including a suit over 274 Elvis Presley songs filed in October. Separately, a tampered Claude Code extension reached Cursor users on 29 October. Anthropic has not said whether the game rule exists or will get an exemption path.

articles.title: How to clear the cache on your Android device - Engadget
articles.text:
How to clear the cache on your Android device
Clear up space and speed up your phone.
Every time you use an app or browse sites online, your Android phone builds up a collection of small files in the background called a cache. That's how apps and websites load images, scripts and page elements faster the next time you open them, instead of downloading the same data over and over again.
It's a lot more convenient for the apps and browsers to pull data from storage, of course, but that convenience has a cost as the files start piling up, turning into a storage drain. Over time, this can lead to your phone feeling more sluggish or with you unable to install new apps because you're running out of space.
The immediate benefit of clearing your cache is the fact that you'll free up storage space and improve your device's performance. Let's be clear: clearing the cache won't fix every performance issue your phone has, but it's a safe and low-effort move that will make your Android phone a bit speedier.
What happens when you clear the cache and will you lose anything?
Clearing the cache on your device is one of the safer maintenance tasks you can perform on an Android device. Before getting into it, however, it helps to know exactly what changes and what stays the same. Clearing your cache is always a good idea if your phone is slower than it used to be or apps take longer than usual to open. It's also a good step to take if you want to clear up some storage space or if specific apps are crashing, freezing or behaving inconsistently.
Once you go through with it, you'll have quite a bit more storage space since cached images, scripts and temp files will be gone. You might also notice an immediate speed-up of your device or browser, particularly if the cache has grown large. Apps and websites will take slightly longer the first time they load since they have to rebuild the cache from scratch. Realistically, you probably won't notice that much of a difference.
The most common concern about clearing cache is whether this move will make you lose any data, but thankfully, the answer is no. Not in any way that actually matters, anyway. Clearing cache doesn't delete your saved passwords, logins, pictures, documents or your game progress because all of these are tied to different type of data, such as cookies or app data. Now, if you also clear cookies alongside the cache, that's a different situation. Doing so will sign you out of sites that relied on those cookies to keep you logged in. If you leave the cookies untouched, your login sessions on sites stay intact.
How to clear cache on your Android phone
There are two main ways to clear cache on your Android device. The first one is through the Chrome browser for web-related data, while the second is through the Settings app for individual apps.
Clearing your cache in Chrome for browser-related slowdowns:
- Open the Chrome app on your Android device.
- Tap the three dots to the right of the address bar and select Delete browsing data.
- Choose a time range. The system sets the default to 15 minutes, but you can pick a longer time window such as the last 24 hours, the last seven days, four weeks, or all time. Selecting All time will clear your entire browsing cache while shorter ranges are useful if you only want to clear recent activity.
- In order to select specific data types, go to More options and make sure the box next to Cached images and files is checked, while the others are clear.
- Tap Delete data to confirm.
Depending on when the specific issue you're troubleshooting started, it's important to select the right time range. Picking to delete the cache from the past 24 hours for a problem that started two weeks ago won't cut it. If you're going for a full cleanup, picking All time ensures nothing cached gets left behind.
Clearing app caches through Settings for targeting problematic apps:
- Go to Settings > Apps and pick the app that's giving you trouble.
- Scroll down and tap on Storage and you'll see exactly how much space the cache takes up.
- Tap Clear cache.
If you're looking for the fastest way to clear your cache on Android overall, the Chrome method handles browser-related issues in under a minute. The Settings route, however, is quicker when you already know which app is causing issues.
Users who don't want to manually manage this process out of the fear that they'll "break" something can rely on built-in cleanup tools. Samsung, for instance, offers Device Care, which can spot and clear unnecessary cached files, while Google's own Files app includes cleanup suggestions flagging junk files and unused cache for removal.

articles.title: These Travel Mugs Have Never Met a Lukewarm Latte
articles.text:
If there’s one thing WIRED staffers love almost as much as tech gear, it’s caffeine. We take our coffee so seriously that we don't suffer fools when it comes to travel mugs. Through painstaking testing that's yielded spilled lattes, lukewarm brews, and dented thermoses, WIRED testers have pinpointed the very best travel mugs available. Whether you need a sturdy option that can survive the chaos of an NYC morning commute or a self-heating tumbler for all-day sipping, consider yourself covered.
Want more help leveling up your morning brew? Be sure to check out our guides to the Best Coffee Subscriptions, Best Coffee Grinders, Best Espresso Machines, Best French Presses, Best Portable Coffee Makers, Best AeroPress Coffee Makers, and How to Make Better Coffee at Home.
Updated November 2026: We've added the BrüMate Strova and Ember Tumbler 2, and information on what to look for in a travel mug. We've also updated links and prices throughout.
The Best Travel Coffee Mug
The Hydro Flask Coffee with Flex Sip Lid is my go-to travel mug. It’s low-maintenance and built like a tank, making it a forgiving choice for the clumsiest of sippers. The brand's powder coating can handle clammy hands, and the 16-ounce tumbler fits into most car cup holders.
It's also a multipurpose mug that isn't limited to housing just your steaming morning brew. Because Hydro Flask wide-mouth lids are conveniently interchangeable, you can swap in a straw lid for cold beverages (or anything else you'd like to drink). And if you purchase the travel mug directly from Hydro Flask, you can get it engraved with text or a graphic, in addition to picking from the 10-plus available color options.
A Mug That Can Handle Your Mornings
Imagine sitting by a campfire under the stars, sipping hot cocoa, then waking up at sunrise to a cup of coffee by the lake. A handleless mug just doesn't do that scene justice. Hydro Flask's travel coffee mug brings that camp aesthetic to life. It also just feels great to hold in any setting—including for morning dog walks or while you get yourself ready for your day at home. The slider lid keeps out curious bugs and helps to slow the release of heat, but it’s not leakproof.
I also appreciate the mug's stainless steel rim that's smooth to sip from sans lid. Just note that it’s not TPU powder-coated like most Hydro Flask bottles, so it's a bit less grippy and you’ll have to hand wash it.
Best Value
If you’re a fan of the Owala FreeSip’s spout, then the lightweight SmoothSip Slider will not disappoint. Its triple-layer insulation helps to keep drinks hot for around six hours or cold for 24. The slider lid works fine for everyday use and didn't leak when I flipped it upside down. But I still wouldn’t toss it into a bag because of how easy it is to unlock. Alongside being available in fun colors, Owala also releases limited-edition designs you can shop. Also notable is that Owala bottles are lead-, BPA-, and phthalate-free.
Best Flippable
After an unfortunate entanglement with a coffee mug and my computer, there was a period of time when the only bar where everybody knew my name was the Genius Bar. Now, lid security is my top priority for any liquid I tote around. For that singular concern, BrüMate's cupholder-friendly Strova gets a W from me. The brand claims its patented BevLock lid is fully leakproof, and after putting the mug through its paces—flipping, shaking, and dropping it—before I even considered placing it in my purse to intermingle with my water-sensitive electronics, I came to trust the promise: I couldn't make a single drop of coffee slip through the closed-mouthpiece edges or perimeter of the lid. Further, the mug's ceramic-lined interior both protects the temperature and taste of whatever you're drinking, and it comes in more than a dozen colors and designs any aesthete would be happy to show off.
The compromise you'll have to make is that the Strova is a bit awkward to sip. The mouth opening is quite small, running in a thin, tight line, like an expressionless face, as opposed to larger, easier-to-sip options that might conjure more of an open-mouthed cackle. The construction means you have to tip the mug up past your nose to sip when it's half full or less. This may look a bit aggro while you're drinking, but it’s frankly a small price to pay for confidently avoiding spillage. —Alexis Berger
| Specs | 
|---|
| Materials: Insulated stainless steel body, ceramic-lined interior | 
| Dishwasher safe: Most are top-rack dishwasher safe (some special-edition styles have finishes that are not). Check the bottom of your mug for washing instructions for your specific model. | 
| Size options (in ounces): 18 | 
Best Self-Heating
A long morning commute can be a slog. Add in successive underwhelming sips of tepid coffee, and you're less and less likely to walk into work bright-eyed and bushy-tailed. For owners of the Ember Tumbler 2, that vignette is mere fiction. This travel tumbler, from the brand that normalized spendy warming mugs, holds a generous 16 ounces, fits into a car cupholder, and—most importantly—keeps your beverage hot. It claims to have a battery life of three-plus hours, but I noticed my brew losing its steam after about two. You can control the temperature on the tumbler itself by pressing a button on the bottom that toggles between five heat levels, or you can choose a precise temp via the Bluetooth-connected app. But if you're driving, you'll probably just want to default to the hottest temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit before you depart.
The Tumbler 2's slim profile is easy to pick up with one hand while you keep the other firmly on the steering wheel. Do keep the tumbler upright in that cupholder when you're not sipping, though. It dripped when I flipped it upside down, even with the sipping lid's slider closed, so I certainly wouldn't throw it into a purse or computer bag. (The tumbler also comes with a screw-off, top-handle lid, which is less leaky, but also less useful.) Drips aside, the drinking experience is nice, with the lid's smooth texture and curved lip allowing for easy, natural sips.
If cupholder compatibility isn't your priority, you might consider the new 16-ounce Ember Mug 3 ($160), the first edition of the brand's classic line that's available in this larger capacity. It's not formally a travel mug, but it does come with a sipping lid that helps your drink stay warm longer, making it a nice option for the work-from-home crowd. Both the Mug 3 and Tumbler 2 are conveniently top-rack dishwasher safe. —Alexis Berger
| Specs | 
|---|
| Materials: Stainless steel, plastic | 
| Dishwasher safe: Top-rack dishwasher safe | 
| Size options (in ounces): 16 | 
Best for Iced Coffee and Matcha Lattes
Fellow nailed it with the Carter Move. This sleek mug has a ceramic-coated interior that doesn't hold scent or taste, meaning your matcha today won’t taste like yesterday’s coffee. A 270-degree twist locks the lid effectively; I’ve tossed it in my bag without a second thought and have never experienced annoying leaks or regrettable spills. The included splash guard keeps ice cubes from smacking your teeth and protects against drips and splatters while you walk and drive. Fellow also drops limited-edition colors and sometimes releases design collaborations with artists. The mug fits into most car cup holders and is conveniently compatible with the Cold Lid + Straw ($12) and the Carry Lid ($12), allowing flexibility in how you drink and tote it.
The Carter Move fits most standard drippers but isn’t compatible with the AeroPress Coffee Maker or Prismo AeroPress Attachment. If that's a deal-breaker, you might consider the Carter Wide ($30), a great alternative to the Move that works with most manual coffee brewers. In that case, you'll have to compromise on a splash guard, which I really like in the Move.
Best Budget Mug With a Handle
For less than $25, the Ello Campy delivers a nostalgic charm, harking back to the enameled camp cups that ooze 20th-century Americana. The Campy isn’t enameled—just painted to look like it—but it pulls off the effect well. The cork-lined handle stays cool even when piping-hot brew fills the mug, while the vacuum insulation retains your drink’s heat. The screw-on plastic lid is designed to avoid heat conduction, and the mug also features a sliding lever for sipping. It’s not spill-proof, but if you hold it upright, it should keep its contents contained. However, it doesn't fit into cupholders, which may be a deal-breaker for drivers, and the paint is likely to chip off with wear.
| Specs | 
|---|
| Materials: Stainless steel, BPA-free plastic | 
| Dishwasher safe: The lid is top-rack dishwasher safe. Hand-washing the vessel is recommended. | 
| Size options (in ounces): 18 | 
Honorable Mentions
Some travel mugs are perfectly good enough—just not as great as the top picks above.
KeepCup 12-ounce Coffee Cup for $31: This double-walled, insulated mug aims to replicate (and replace) paper cups from coffee shops. It's a solid option if you're looking for a glass cup (the rubber grip is plastic, though). That said, it’s not the best at preserving the temperature of your drink, and the lid is a tad wobbly.
Oxo Good Grips Thermal Mug for $29: WIRED reviewed this bottle in 2022, and it earned high marks for its sturdy build and dishwasher-friendliness. But since it's older, it now fluctuates in and out of stock.
REI Co-op Camp Mug for $23+: REI's stainless steel cup is decent enough, but it doesn't particularly stand out in the wider category of travel mugs. Our tester says the exterior coating was tough enough to show no scratches, even after knocking it over a few times outside.
Zojirushi Stainless Steel Mug for $40: In addition to having a lid lock that's effective for avoiding accidental spillage, the mug is also a great option for temperature control: A reviewer once left tea in it for 18 hours (unintentionally) and discovered the drink was still hot when she finally opened the lid. The downside is that the cover has three separate parts—a mouthpiece, a gasket, and a lid—that are deeply ridged and annoying to clean.
Avoid These Mugs
They can't all be winners. These two cups fell short compared to our favorites.
Greens Steel Beast 20-Ounce Insulated Tumbler for $23: The Beast Tumbler has more than 81,000 positive reviews on Amazon, but the rubber seal around the lid easily comes out of place. That meant it leaked like a sieve.
Toaks Titanium Double Wall 450-Milliliter Cup for $40: More often than not, we at WIRED champion Toaks gear as an affordable source of titanium camp cookware. But this mug costs $12 more than the Hydro Flask pick above, and has a rougher finish.
Frequently Asked Questions
What to Know About Lead Soldering
Since WIRED editors began testing reusable water bottles and travel mugs, we've discovered that some brands use lead soldering to seal their insulated bottles. While exposure is unlikely (you'd have to drop or damage the bottle or mug to detach the lead pellet), we still believe it's an unnecessary risk, especially since many of our top choices use safer sealing methods. We've removed mugs from brands that have admitted to using lead in their products.
What to Look for in a Travel Mug
There's no shortage of travel mugs available to buy. Narrowing down the best options for you depends on your priorities and how a given mug can satisfy them. Here are key considerations for selecting a great travel mug:
- Leakproof design: When you're buying a mug with the express purpose of toting it around with you, I'd argue that its most important quality should be holding the beverage without leaks or spills. Some travel mugs feature patented locking technology that promises no drips at all, while other models are less intensely engineered—and sometimes the latter works perfectly well. For example, if you're using your mug to sip a coffee during your morning walk or while taking in the sunrise during a camping trip, you might not need the same promise of leakproofing as someone who tosses their mug into their laptop bag.
- Material: Travel mugs are often made from stainless steel, ceramic, or BPA-free plastic—and often a combination of all three. Glass mugs are also available, though less common.
- Stainless steel is a common material in travel mugs. It's effective for retaining heat, especially options that are double-wall–insulated, which basically means the mug will keep your drink hot from the inside without burning your hand from the outside. Stainless steel mugs are often dishwasher-safe, but not microwave-safe, and can sometimes give off a bit of a metallic taste into beverages.
- Some mugs have a smooth, ceramic lining on the inside, which helps to preserve the taste of the beverage—i.e., your afternoon tea won't have a hint of yesterday's coffee—and protect against that metallic hint of a stainless-steel option.
- Plastic appears often in travel-mug lids. Prioritize options that are free of bisphenol A (BPA), a known endocrine disruptor.
- Glass, like ceramic, provides a neutral taste, but it can be heavy and is typically less durable than other materials, opening you to the messy risk of a shattered mug.
- Shape: If you're commuting in a car with your travel mug, you'll want to ensure it fits into your cupholder, and if you're carrying it with you on walks, you'll likely want it to have a handle.
- Price: Our top-pick travel mugs currently span in price from less than $20 to nearly $200. If having precise temperature control of your coffee at any given moment matters to you, a spendy mug may be worth the investment. Most of the picks, though, hover around $30. —Alexis Berger
How I Tested
I’ve been running on caffeine since I was 12 (sorry, Mom and Dad) because I took middle school way too seriously. Fifteen years later, caffeine is basically part of my personality, and I’ve been unofficially testing travel mugs for most of my life.
To officially test the mugs in this guide, I, along with other editors, drank both coffee and tea at piping-hot and ice-cold extremes, rating heat retention and taste, ensuring no picks have any hint of metallic notes. Shape and design matter, too: How comfortable is it to hold a given mug? Does it fit into a car cup holder? Does it offer additional features worth considering? I aggressively shook the mugs that promised to be leakproof and dropped those that claimed to be durable from about 4 feet high onto both wood and concrete surfaces to evaluate how well they held up. Finally, travel mugs can be a pain to scrub, so I factored in ease of cleaning.
Simply put, I need a travel mug that pulls its weight. If it didn't keep my coffee warm, my bag dry, and make my life a little easier, it didn’t make the list.

articles.title: New Zelda and GTA represent a games industry that no longer exists
articles.text:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the biggest game releases of the year, follow Andrew Webster. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepbackhere.
New Zelda and GTA represent a games industry that no longer exists
The two biggest games of the year launch in November, offering some reprieve from a terrible year.
New Zelda and GTA represent a games industry that no longer exists
The two biggest games of the year launch in November, offering some reprieve from a terrible year.
How it started
The two biggest games of 2026 are set to launch just a few weeks apart in November.
On the one side you have the behemoth that is Grand Theft Auto VI, an experience 13 years in the making, and the sequel to one of the best-selling games in history. Its predecessor, GTA V, has sold a staggering 230 million copies since it launched in 2013, and was re-released across three generations of consoles. Developer Rockstar is a pioneer in the realm of open-world games, dating back to GTA III, and the scale and ambitions of those worlds have steadily grown since then. With GTA V and later Red Dead Redemption 2, the studio’s ideas reached a new level of realism. And the sixth GTA looks poised to eclipse them both, which has created an unprecedented level of demand.
Analyst firm Circana estimates that 29 percent of gamers in the US intend to buy the game, with demand so large it could boost flagging console sales. “Many consumers who have yet to upgrade to a current-generation console may choose to purchase a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series specifically to play the title,” analyst Mat Piscatella says in a statement. GTA VI’s reach is so vast that almost every other major game launched early to avoid it.
The one exception is Nintendo. The company’s tentpole release for the holidays, and its next major exclusive for the Switch 2, is a lavish remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.
The release is notable for a few reasons. For one thing, it’s an attempt from Nintendo to modernize one of the most influential and beloved games in its long history. The original Ocarina of Time was the world’s first introduction to a 3D iteration of Hyrule, which, in turn, made it an early glimpse at what was possible in three-dimensional spaces, laying a blueprint for countless games that came afterward. Nintendo has since expanded on that, turning Switch-era adventures Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom into wide-open adventures designed for player creativity. They went on to become some of the best-selling games for Nintendo’s most successful console.
Ocarina of Time’s launch also comes just ahead of a live-action Zelda movie in 2027, which could catapult the franchise to a new level of prominence. That’s why Nintendo is seemingly the only company unafraid of competing with GTA.
These aren’t just two blockbuster games – they’re two series with the pull to make this a real cultural moment, akin to “Barbenheimer” but for video games. They’re the kind of launches that make it onto Saturday Night Live and have NBA players worried.
It’s just too bad about the rest of the industry.
How it’s going
These major November releases are something of a mirage, two outliers that stand out amid the wreckage that is the rest of the video game industry. While there have been plenty of major releases and great games this year, the main theme of 2026 has been just how dire things have become. Layoffs, studio closures, unpopular business models, the ever-looming threat of AI, and massive increases in hardware costs have combined to create an ominous cloud over the medium.
Here is just a snapshot of what the year has been like: Xbox is in the middle of a “reset” that involves laying off thousands of developers, shutting down some studios, and gutting others; Fortnite developer Epic cut more than 1,000 jobs due to a sharp downturn in the live-service games space, and it’s currently going all-in on vibe coding; Sony is also struggling, slashing jobs at Destiny developer Bungie, watching console sales plummet as costs skyrocket, and raising the ire of gamers by moving on from physical media; and meanwhile, major publishers like EA and Ubisoft are in their own dramatic states of upheaval.
And the bad news hasn’t really let up. Just last week, EA shut down beloved studio BioWare and canceled the next Mass Effect game, and this week Sony studio Sucker Punch cut staff despite the success of last year’s Ghost of Yōtei. Every day, it seems, brings some new unwelcome development.
What happens next
Clearly, things are changing for the video game industry; they have to change. What that future looks like, though, remains unclear. The next generation of game consoles is being threatened by exorbitant prices, and all the while the rise of AI-powered tools is sending ripples across the industry, threatening the established order between players and creators as games are ported to every platform imaginable. “These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models,” Xbox CEO Asha Sharma said in a recent memo. But how that plays out remains to be seen.
It’s not all doom and gloom. There have been rare success stories, where studios like FromSoftware and Remedy have managed to carve out a sustainable existence in a turbulent field. But for the most part, the established norms that have been part of the blockbuster games industry for years are going away. Big games are too expensive to make, hardware is too expensive to buy (and the cost is only going up), and somewhere, something has to give.
It’s tempting to look at Zelda and GTA as answers to these problems. After all, if Nintendo and Rockstar are doing so well, there must be a solution out there. But they’re also two very specific cases that are essentially impossible to replicate. Nintendo maintains ownership over all aspects of its platform, from the hardware to the games, and it has taken a careful and largely risk-averse approach that has allowed it to weather the current storm and create a growing entertainment empire. Rockstar, meanwhile, is the rare example of being too big to fail. GTA V was so massive for so long — Circana says it was among the top 20 best-selling games in the US for 13 straight years — that it allowed the studio to build up both an unprecedented amount of anticipation and, it seems, a game big enough to match it.
In that way, Zelda and GTA are throwbacks to a time when major games were sure bets. Their duelling releases are fascinating both because these games are so impactful, but also because, with all of the impending upheaval, the industry might never see a moment like this again.
By the way
- The Ocarina of Time remake makes some smart modern tweaks to the formula, which you can learn about in our hands-on with the game.
- While the wait has been long for GTA VI, it seems there’s a good chance its inevitable sequel won’t spend so many years in development.
- There’s one other notable game that was unafraid to launch in November: Moomin: Midsummer Madness.
Read this
- Rockstar is very secretive, but you can get a sense of what went into GTA VI’s protracted development from these cover stories in Edge magazine and Businessweek.
- Ocarina of Time is an especially interesting game in 2026 because of how much Zelda has changed since it first debuted. For more on that, here’s our interview from 2023 with Tears of the Kingdom director Hidemaro Fujibayashi.

articles.title: Chatbots Are Leading Hikers Astray, With Dangerous Consequences
articles.text:
This story originally appeared on High Country News and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
By the time the three hikers called for help from a rocky face on Mount Shasta in Northern California, they’d made a series of bad decisions. They didn’t bring enough food, and they’d overestimated their fitness. Instead of turning back in late afternoon when they hadn’t yet reached the top, they summited at 7:30 pm and had to descend in the dark. Their lack of preparation and poor planning, as they admitted later, came partly from relying on Google’s artificial intelligence chatbot Gemini. By morning, they were lost on a gnarly part of the mountain, and one hiker had banged up his knee.
“We get plenty of people who come unprepared or don’t do any research at all. To these guys’ credit, they did try,” said Nick Meyers, US Forest Service program manager of the Mount Shasta Wilderness Climbing and Avalanche Center, which responded to the call. “But I think they kind of turned their brains off.”
The three 20-year-olds aren’t the only ones making missteps in wild spaces with the help of artificial intelligence. Another Mount Shasta visitor pitched her tent near a “No Camping” sign, insisting she had a right to do so because AI told her she could, Meyers said. His team also encountered a man wandering around at a trailhead with an AI-generated map that showed prominent features on the wrong side of a nearby mountain. In British Columbia, a helicopter crew rescued a 16-year-old hiker from a ledge in the Widowmaker Arete on the back of Crown Mountain. The teen had used Anthropic’s chatbot Claude to help him plan his trip. News stories focused on that fact went viral across Canada and the US, though the hiker said later that he also consulted Google Maps and the popular hiking app, AllTrails.
Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming has also seen a marked uptick over the past year in the percentage of visitors who report using AI for travel information, said Park Superintendent Chip Jenkins. “It went from zero to 26 percent. And I’m guessing that curve is not going to flatten.”
It remains to be seen whether increasing AI use will lead to an increase in backcountry accidents and search and rescues, Meyers said. His office, which oversees a massive wilderness area in Northern California, averages a dozen rescues each year, and 2026 is shaping up to be an average year. Calls to search and rescue in Wyoming have actually gone down compared to 2025, with only 312 calls so far in 2026 compared to a total of 466 in 2025 and 377 in 2024.
Some search and rescue veterans say that AI chatbots are just the latest tools giving people new ways to get into trouble. Roughly a decade ago, when hikers, backpackers, climbers and other outdoor enthusiasts began to source their destinations, inspiration, and information from Instagram and other social media sites, they faced sometimes deadly consequences. Before that, hikers and other recreationists were led astray by their reliance on Google Maps or smartphone connectivity.
“Over the last two decades, there’s been a phenomenal push in the media to get more people outdoors, and consequently we have more people outdoors and recreating,” said Jim Moss, a Colorado-based recreation attorney and search and rescue volunteer. It’s still unclear how questionable advice from a robot will influence all those people, he added.
Turning to an AI chatbot for guidance does come with unique risks. Chatbots can “hallucinate” persuasively presenting misinformation as real, and their use can lead to a phenomenon called “cognitive surrender,” said Chris Flathmann, a human-centered computing professor at Clemson University in South Carolina who has studied AI and search and rescue.
“When humans work with AI systems, they can get so deep into it they give up thinking critically for themselves,” he explained. When AI pretends to be an expert on an unfamiliar topic, “you can’t call BS on that because you don’t have the expertise.” And once you stop thinking critically, it can be hard to start again, especially in a stressful backcountry situation.
Chatbots also tend to tell users what they want to hear and to do so with authority regardless of whether the sources they’re consulting are reliable, Flathmann and others said. Claude or ChatGPT might answer a query with extensive directions and advice that sound credible but are actually scraped from Reddit threads and out-of-date YouTube videos—and might even be entirely fabricated.
TikTok and Instagram may offer a viewer inspiration, but AI tends to offer instructions—right or wrong—as well as encouragement, Flathmann said. “AI isn’t trying to trick people into going up mountains, but I think it’s the natural evolution of what happens when you get a tool like this.”
Regardless of the resources recreators use, experts have the same advice: When you’re headed to a new place, make sure you double-check your information against reliable, authoritative sources like up-to-date public-land agency maps and websites, trail association websites, or guidebooks. Even better, talk to a real-live guide, a national forest official, or a park ranger.
“If you’re going to go into places that will kill you,” Meyers said, “you should take your planning seriously.”

articles.title: Salesforce to buy military AI startup Rune for a reported $375m
articles.text:
Salesforce has agreed to buy Rune Technologies. The US startup’s AI software helps the military plan supplies near the front line. Salesforce announced the deal on Thursday. Rune will join Missionforce, the defence business Salesforce launched a year ago.
Salesforce did not disclose the price. It is paying $375m in cash and shares, Margaux MacColl reported for Resilience Media. She cited two sources familiar with the matter. TNW has not independently verified the figure.
“Salesforce is doubling down on national security with our most significant acquisition in this space.” Kendall Collins, chief executive of Missionforce and Government Cloud, in Salesforce’s announcement
What Rune makes
David Tuttle and Peter Goldsborough founded Rune in 2024, after leadership roles at Anduril. Its software, TyrOS, forecasts what frontline units will need and suggests how to share out resources and route transport. It keeps working with little or no network connection and syncs when the network returns.
The US Army and Marine Corps already use it, Salesforce said. In June, the Army awarded Rune a $99m contract for TyrOS, according to the Pentagon’s contract notice. The Army received only one bid.
Rune has raised $30m. Its investors include Andreessen Horowitz, Point72 Ventures and IQT, formerly called In-Q-Tel, according to Resilience Media. One of its sources put Rune’s last valuation at $134m.
“With Salesforce, we can take what we’ve built further, connecting operational logistics from the frontline to the enterprise.” David Tuttle, Rune’s chief executive
Salesforce’s defence push
Salesforce said its defence business is growing 80% a year, with customers in all six branches of the US military. It also cited a 10-year Army contract with a $5.6bn ceiling. Salesforce describes Missionforce as the system of record at headquarters, and says Rune adds the frontline layer.
The company frames Rune’s tools as “super intelligence”, the label behind its recent SIForce rebrand. On 20 October, Salesforce agreed to buy marketing platform Braze for about $5.7bn. It also completed its Fin acquisition in September.
Salesforce expects the deal to close in the fourth quarter of its 2027 fiscal year.

articles.title: Amazon made the AUX input on older Alexa devices less useful - Engadget
articles.text:
Amazon made the AUX input on older Alexa devices less useful
The AUX jack survives on older Echo speakers. The voice commands that made it convenient don't.
Amazon has disabled Alexa voice controls for the AUX input on several older Echo speakers. An Amazon email shared by a customer and reported by Ars Technica says that commands such as "Alexa, play from line in" and "Alexa, set AUX input" have stopped working. The change may seem minor, but it is frustrating for anyone who used those commands to switch to a wired audio source.
The affected devices are the second-generation Echo Plus (2018), third-generation Echo (2019), original Echo Studio (2019) and fourth-generation Echo (2020). Amazon confirmed the removal, and a spokesperson told The Verge that it had notified "the very small number of customers" who use voice requests for AUX playback. The company did not say why it removed the feature, though.
Fortunately, the physical AUX connection continues to work in more ways than one. Owners can still play audio through a cable and use the Alexa app to enable or disable AUX input on supported models.
What is the AUX port on older Echo speakers for?
That small 3.5mm AUX jack on supported Echo speakers can serve two purposes, depending on the model. When used as an input, it allows the speaker to play audio from an external source, such as a phone or computer. As an output, it routes Alexa's audio to another speaker or amplifier. It's the same physical connection, simply operating in the opposite direction.
The third-generation Echo, fourth-generation Echo and second-generation Echo Plus support both input and output, while the original Echo Studio supports input only. Older Echo Dots, including the third- and fourth-generation models, have jacks that support output only. By contrast, the fifth-generation Dot removed a 3.5mm connection altogether.
There is still a solid reason to hold on to that older hardware. For example, an early-2000s Sony CD changer can send audio to an original Echo Studio through an RCA-to-3.5mm cable. You can continue playing those CDs through the Echo without purchasing a Bluetooth transmitter or replacing the player. The connection is unchanged, even if Alexa is now less cooperative about using it.
You can still use AUX, just with fewer conveniences
If you have a compatible Echo that's connected to hardware using a 3.5mm audio cable, open the Alexa app, select the speaker under Devices, and find AUX Audio in its settings, then choose Line In to play audio from an external source through the Echo. On models that support both directions, Line Out instead sends the Echo's audio to a wired speaker or receiver. Depending on the app version, the setting may be listed under General.
After connecting the devices, use the source device's own controls to start playback or skip tracks. Alexa's discontinued voice commands managed the Echo's AUX input, not the connected equipment's playback functions.
Ultimately, you don't need to replace your Echo simply to keep using its AUX port, if one is present. Just keep in mind that upgrading Echo devices with a 3.5mm input will likely mean losing the feature. An example of this loss would be upgrading from a first-generation Echo Studio to the redesigned 2025 Echo Studio.

articles.title: Prop 45 in California could be hiding a loophole for data centers
articles.text:
A high-stakes California ballot measure pitched as a fast track for “essential” infrastructure could wind up giving data center developers a loophole to evade public scrutiny, environmental advocates warn.
Prop 45 in California could be hiding a loophole for data centers
Proposition 45 makes it easier for developers to speed through environmental reviews.
Proposition 45 would shorten timelines for state-mandated environmental assessments for eligible projects and make it more difficult for residents to challenge those projects in court. Proponents say passing the measure would help alleviate the state’s housing shortage and meet rising electricity demand with new renewable energy projects. Environmental groups and some legal experts, however, warn that data center developers backing the proposition could escape scrutiny if Prop 45 becomes law.
“The concern here is that data center developers will find a way to shoehorn their projects into the definition of an essential project and then get to take advantage of … the fast-track review that it’ll create,” says Fernando Gaytan, a senior attorney at the nonprofit environmental law organization Earthjustice, which opposes Prop 45. “Communities get cut out of the conversation.”
“Communities get cut out of the conversation.”
Prop 45 would loosen standards for certain projects subject to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). CEQA requires state agencies to perform environmental reviews and work with project developers to find ways to limit any harmful impacts to the environment and public health. Crucially, CEQA also mandates that state agencies gather community input and consider public comment before issuing any approvals.
Specifically, Prop 45 would create a 365-day deadline for agencies to complete the environmental impact report for a project. It also stipulates that any legal challenges would need to be settled within 270 days. It would only allow for 45 days of public comment, and it would only require state agencies and developers to consult with Native American tribes that have been federally recognized. CEQA as it’s currently written sets a minimum rather than a maximum number of days for public review, and mandates consultation with tribes that might be impacted by a project even if they’re not formally recognized by the federal government as having “government-to-government” relations with the US.
During the CEQA review process, state agencies develop alternatives that developers can take to mitigate environmental and health risks. Prop 45 would turn that on its head, making developers responsible for coming up with a single alternative project plan for regulators to consider. The proposition would also strip away an agency’s authority to repeatedly ask a developer for more information about a proposed project; state regulators would need to specify all the information a company is required to provide at the start of the application process.
On top of all that, Prop 45 would bar courts from halting a project altogether even if it finds that the regulatory agency failed to correctly comply with CEQA. The judge would only have the ability to pause specific parts of a project that are problematic, rather than forcing a full stop to construction. That’s the piece that’s most egregious for Gaytan. “It’s hard to undo harms once you’ve already started a project,” he says.
Data centers are a hot-button election issue for midterms across the US and have become a point of contention for Prop 45 as well. The proposition lists nine types of “essential” projects that would be eligible for streamlined review, including housing, clean energy, and “broadband Internet access.”
Gaytan and some other legal experts contend that the latter designation — broadband internet access — could include data centers. The language includes any project that would “provide mass-market retail service by wire service, wireless service, or radio to customers in this state that provides the capability to transmit data to, and receive data from, all or substantially all internet endpoints, including, but not limited to, any capabilities that are incidental to and enable the operation of the communications service.”
Proposed data centers that include any broadband transmission infrastructure might be able to squeeze into that definition, UC Davis School of Law professor emeritus Richard Frank and attorney Matthew McKerley write in a recent column in the Daily Journal. They also point out that companies currently developing data centers have poured hundreds of thousands of dollars into a campaign to support Prop 45. And while Prop 45 excludes certain types of projects, like nuclear energy and dial-up internet access service, it doesn’t explicitly bar data centers.
Proponents, meanwhile, argue that Prop 45 would not apply to data centers. “The fact that data centers may play a role in supporting the Internet does not make them ‘essential broadband Internet access projects’ under Prop 45,” attorney and lobbyist Kurt Oneto writes in The National Law Review. The Yes on Prop 45 campaign didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Prop 45 has managed to garner support from the California and Hawaii chapter of the NAACP, which has been among one of the most vocal civil rights organizations to oppose data center developments across the US. The NAACP filed suit against xAI over air pollution from gas turbines at its Colossus 2 data center, and the Texas chapter has called for a statewide moratorium on data center development.
“Working families and communities of color pay the highest price when essential projects like housing, clean energy, water, health care facilities, and transportation take years longer and cost millions more than they should,” Rick Callender, president of NAACP California/Hawaii State Conference, said in a September 9th press release. “Prop. 45 is about accountability, not shortcuts, creating a smarter process that gets these projects built sooner while protecting civil rights and environmental safeguards.”
Regardless of whether Prop 45 influences data center development in California, its opponents worry that it could disempower the same communities that the new projects it covers are supposed to benefit. “It’s about public participation and democracy,” Gaytan says. “It’s about neighbors being able to say, ‘I want you to be transparent with me about what’s going behind that wall.’”

articles.title: Google is in talks to protect data for Trump’s $185bn Golden Dome
articles.text:
Alphabet’s Google is in talks with the US Defense Department to help protect the data behind Golden Dome, Bloomberg reported on Friday. Sana Pashankar and Kiel Porter cited people familiar with the matter, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the talks are not public. TNW has not independently verified the report.
Golden Dome is President Donald Trump’s plan to shield the US from foreign attack with layers of defences, from the ground to space. In March, Gen. Michael Guetlein, who runs the programme, said the Pentagon had added $10bn to its cost, as Courtney Albon reported for Air & Space Forces Magazine. That took the estimate to $185bn.
What the new group would do
The Pentagon is setting up a new industry group to secure the data that feeds Golden Dome’s military software, according to Bloomberg’s sources. Several companies are likely to join it.
Their task would be to keep data flowing into the programme’s new command-and-control software even under attack. Bloomberg’s examples include attempts to cut off landlines, cell towers and other communications links.
The talks with Google have focused on its data storage, networking and cybersecurity work, one of the people said. They are at an early stage, and plans could change. Aalyria, a networking company spun out of Google, is part of the group, the people added.
A Pentagon official told Bloomberg that the office may explore early concepts. No final decision has been made on a new group or on which companies would join it, the official said. Google and Aalyria declined to comment to Bloomberg.
Google and the Pentagon
A separate group that includes Anduril, Palantir and SpaceX is building the command-and-control software itself. SpaceX also won a $2.29bn Space Force contract in May for the Golden Dome backbone.
A role would be Google’s first publicly known work on Golden Dome, Bloomberg reported. In 2018, thousands of Google employees protested against Project Maven, a Pentagon AI contract, and Google did not renew it.
In April, Google signed a classified AI deal with the Pentagon. Google DeepMind’s UK staff then voted to unionise, with 98% in favour.

articles.title: France’s gigabyte tax would charge Netflix and Google €0.055 per GB
articles.text:
France’s National Assembly has voted to tax companies for every gigabyte of data they send to French internet users. The measure, an amendment to the 2027 budget, would charge content providers €0.055 per gigabyte. Its Socialist authors estimate it would raise €10bn a year. It passed by 11 votes to 10 on Friday, with 14 abstentions, according to the official record of the session.
The government and the finance committee both opposed it. The vote is only a first step. The tax must survive the rest of the budget process to become law.
How the gigabyte tax would work
Internet providers would measure the data flowing to their customers and note which company sent it, under the text of the amendment. They would report the totals to the tax authorities every quarter, under the supervision of telecoms regulator Arcep. The text bars any record of what the data contains or where it goes.
Some data travels through content delivery networks, which store copies close to users. That data would count as it leaves the network. The text caps the tax at 15% of a company’s French revenue or 2% of its global revenue.
The amendment’s explanatory note cites an Arcep estimate that 200bn gigabytes reach French internet subscribers each year. It says Google, Meta, Amazon, Netflix and Akamai account for about half of that traffic.
“I fail to see how a tax can be passed on to users of Facebook, Instagram or TikTok, since these services are free.” Laurent Lhardit, the amendment’s author, in the Assembly (TNW translation)
Who else would pay
Public accounts minister David Amiel told MPs the scheme would need sensors on the networks, or measurement on users’ own devices. Half of the tax would fall on smaller content providers, many of them French, he said. On the authors’ own estimate, that is about €5bn. Philippe Juvin, the finance committee’s general rapporteur, warned that the big platforms could pass the cost on to advertisers.
VideoLAN, the French nonprofit behind the VLC media player, said the tax would cost it more than €1m a year. VLC has passed 6 billion downloads.
“So, the French socialists, and Parliament members just voted a tax, that they don’t understand, which would cost VideoLAN more than 1 million euro per year.” VideoLAN, on X
What happens next
The Senate, where the conservative Les Républicains hold a majority, is unlikely to back it, Martin Clavey reported for Next. The government could also force the budget through without a final vote. In that case, it can leave the amendment out of the text, Next noted.
In June, President Trump threatened 100% tariffs over digital services taxes. Amiel told MPs France already has tools to tax big tech, such as its digital services tax. He also pointed to EU competition fines, which France says should cut EU contributions.

articles.title: A Newly Discovered Trail of Cosmic Debris Illustrates How the End of the Solar System Could Look
articles.text:
Astronomers at the European Southern Observatory (ESO) have discovered a debris disk around a white dwarf, consisting of the remnants of the solar system that once orbited it. For researchers, these structures could offer a clue as to what the end of our solar system will look like once the sun runs out of fuel.
The white dwarf J1328−1450 is located about 1,600 light-years from Earth. Astronomers were already aware of it thanks to star-mapping catalogs, but new observations taken with ESO’s Very Large Telescope (yes, that’s its real name) revealed that it is surrounded by a disk of debris with an unusual structure: Two distinct rings of gas separated by a gap.
According to the observatory, this disk of material is likely the remnant of the planetary system that once orbited J1328−1450. As it passed through a red giant phase and subsequently became a white dwarf, the star may have destroyed some of its planets and left other rocky bodies exposed to an extreme environment. Some of the released material ended up forming a disk of gas and dust around the dead star.
The process that shaped this system could repeat itself in our own. In about 5 billion years, the sun will exhaust its fuel and expand into a red giant. During this phase, it could engulf nearby bodies, like the closest planets. It will then shed its outer layers, leaving behind a white dwarf. Any rocky bodies that survive this transformation could break apart and form a debris disk around the dead star, like the one astronomers are now observing in J1328−1450.
But the white dwarf’s two debris rings hint at another possibility. Their structure appears to be shaped by bodies that astronomers have not yet been able to identify directly. The data suggest that, following the star’s transformation, at least two planetary objects may have survived among the remnants of that system.
Researchers believe these two bodies could be very different in size. The one closest to the white dwarf would measure just a few kilometers in diameter, while the more distant one could be as large as Pluto or even the moon. Their interaction with the surrounding material would explain the formation of the two rings, although it has not yet been confirmed that they exist as separate objects. An alternative possibility is that the structure originates from different parts of a single planet-like body, such as its crust and core.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.
