articles.title: Binance sees $3.64 billion in net outflows as withdrawals resume after massive hack
articles.text:
Binance said it recorded $3.64 billion in net outflows after reopening withdrawals on Sunday following a $6.3 billion hack, as customers rushed to move funds off the platform.
The exchange processed $4.65 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits between 6 a.m. and 3:30 p.m. UTC on Nov. 1, Binance said in a post on X.
The resulting net outflows represented 2.1% of Binance's $171 billion in total assets, based on its latest available proof-of-reserves data as of Oct. 28.
Binance said withdrawal volumes had declined and were stabilizing following an initial spike, while deposit volumes remained substantial.
The exchange began restoring withdrawals in phases at 6 a.m. UTC on Sunday, with services resuming across all 15 networks and assets included in the initial phase by 12:36 p.m. UTC. It said testing was continuing for the remaining networks and assets.
Binance founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao sought to reassure users following the breach, writing on X that "98% choose to stay!" He said most of the net outflows occurred within the first couple of hours after withdrawals resumed. "Trust isn't earned by what you say in good times. It's earned by what you do in hard times," Zhao added.
The withdrawals followed a record $6.3 billion hack of Binance last week. The FBI attributed the attack to North Korean hackers, identifying the operation as TraderTraitor.
The exchange has said it would absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds rather than pass the losses on to users.
Binance said it had covered around 95% of the impacted amount, up from 90% in its previous update. The exchange said the remaining 5% consisted of less liquid tokens that would take longer to source in the quantities required.

articles.title: Stock futures tick higher ahead of busy week of earnings, jobs data and the midterm elections: Live updates
articles.text:
Stock futures moved higher on Sunday after a losing week on Wall Street as investors braced for a packed week of earnings results, jobs reports and the upcoming midterm elections.
S&P 500 futures traded up 0.3%, while Nasdaq-100 futures gained 0.4%. Futures linked to the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 116 points, or 0.2%.
The moves come after the three major averages suffered a losing week, bogged down by selling pressure in tech as investors continued to scrutinize names related to the artificial intelligence buildout. The S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average each fell less than 1% on the week, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2%.
In Asia, Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 0.54% while the Topix declined 0.74%. The Kospi dropped 1.39% at open, while the small-cap Kosdaq slipped 0.81%. Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 was 0.24% lower.
The week got off to a good start after Anthropic publicly filed for an IPO, which boosted AI-linked stocks. However, selling pressure resumed later in the week amid signs that capex spending could be abating after both Alphabet and Microsoft posted lower-than-expected capex forecasts. Amazon also left its full-year capex guidance unchanged.
Still, 3Fourteen Research's Warren Pies isn't too concerned, pointing to a ramp-up in forward earnings estimates and adding that "there's a lot to like" about Anthropic's S-1 filing.
"I just don't see anything broken with the AI trade fundamentally," he said on CNBC's "Closing Bell Overtime" on Friday. "Technicals are another story."
The tech-heavy Nasdaq and the S&P 500 logged a losing October amid AI spending concerns, with the Nasdaq suffering its worst losses since March 2025. The Dow, however, rose almost 2% as investors rotated into defensive areas like healthcare.
"Rather than running for the hills amid heightened AI risks, investors are seeing plenty of return potential in other types of stocks," Mike Dickson, Horizon's head of research and quantitative strategies, said in a note last week.
Dickson added that while this week's midterm elections "have some investors worried that changes in Washington, D.C., could impact the markets, it's important to remember that stocks tend to stay steady regardless of which party gains control of Congress."
The elections will be held on Tuesday, when Democrats are expected to take control of the House of Representatives, while Senate control remains uncertain.
Investors are also awaiting October's nonfarm payrolls reading, which is scheduled for release on Friday and is expected to show an increase of 55,000 jobs on the month, according to economists polled by Dow Jones.
In addition to the closely watched monthly jobs report, a fresh round of earnings releases is also due this week. "Magnificent Seven" member Apple is scheduled to report after the bell on Monday. McDonald's and Qualcomm are slated to report later in the week.

articles.title: The AI trade has broken down. How we got here and what investors should expect next
articles.text: We don't want to get caught too deep in the weeds. Don't overcomplicate things. It will only lead to suboptimal thinking. I start with that simple precept because when you're facing the biggest challenge yet to The Greatest Story Ever Told — the rise of the data center — you just need to follow the money, as the reporters did in the Watergate investigation. You'll find that the investment story has broken down, and the money has moved on — perhaps not for good, but until the dust settles around the data center buildout. Let's revisit the brutal tableau of last week. We had a debilitating sell-off, a real "give up" that was unlike anything we have seen. That includes the collapse in late July of Situational Awareness , that ridiculously hyped hedge fund led by Leopold Aschenbrenner that blew up because it had no risk controls. I have contempt for that kind of recklessness. Throughout my career, I've prioritized risk control over stock picking, dating back to my time at Goldman Sachs in the 1980s. If you don't have risk controls, get the heck out of the business. But Situational didn't get blown out because of Aschenbrenner's thesis: that there may never be a better investment story than the data center buildout, which touches so many sectors. It got blown out by a momentary glitch, magnified by his lack of controls. This time, it was the thesis itself that blew up. At the exact same time, we finally got a countervailing thesis: the prospect of lower interest rates. Rates always trump any other concept in investing because they are the sum total of the forces shaping the market — the Federal Reserve, the economy, inflation, Treasury debt, money demand. Rates are too big to lie. Rates fell slightly last week, and all I heard about was a "flight to quality" among investors. But that's only partially true. We are beginning to see a slowdown in inflation. That quarter-point rate increase in September is proving very powerful when coupled with a determined Fed Chair in Kevin Warsh, who doesn't seem to be playing ball with the president. Warsh seems independent, and people didn't count on that. The shift is real, and so are the alternatives beyond the AI trade — food, drugs, and soft-goods stocks. Biotech may offer the best long-term opportunities. They have been transformed from fly-by-night fireflies to the next Merck or Eli Lilly . AstraZeneca , a perennial second-rater, gets rerated in real time. These alternatives to the AI trade might have staying power. Maybe the valuations of the winners keep growing? Can we pay $200 for Merck? Maybe. Seems excessive. But didn't we start paying incredibly high multiples for tech? Isn't that a reason to take some profits in Apple unless you are as storied about holding it through thick and thin as I am? (Obviously, I am signaling that if you want to step aside from the impossible situation of Apple at 40 times earnings and revisit it, that makes sense.) Do we just buy into the rotation? The answer to that depends on your investing strategy. If you share ours, it gives you an automatic buy-in, hence the endless references to Johnson & Johnson . Hence the Kimberly-Kenvue gambit. Hence the love of Coca-Cola . The AI buildout remains the elephant in the room. Lower rates may make alternatives more attractive, but they don't make The Greatest Story go away. What's really happening? With the midterm elections looming, the moment has become so fraught that even the diehards are struggling to bear the pressure. Let's go over the three big forces that are defeating the data center. First, the election is allegedly a referendum on the data center. We know they will still be built. But if the Democrats do well, we have to presume fewer will go ahead. For example, if we need 200, only 150 are put in motion. Isn't that why GE Vernova is down? The gas turbine maker reported zero cancellations and an order book that continues to grow, even though its quarter wasn't perfect . Investors bailed anyway, compounding a dreadful week capped off by the gang that couldn't shoot straight at Intel . The hyperscalers and the bitcoin managers turned data center builders could suffer if the Dems score a landslide. Lawsuits make it a disorderly election unlike any we have seen. We know data center builders didn't hire enough people to operate their facilities once they were finished. Initially, they despoiled the water supplies and raised electricity prices. That's no longer true. Data center builders subsidize where they build, not the other way around. However, the damage was already done, compounded by the endless discussion of jobs taken, led by none other than the financially suicidal Dario Amodei. The Anthropic CEO had the temerity to say so many self-destructive things about the coming dinosaur age of white-collar jobs. When you hear AI could displace half of all entry-level white-collar jobs in the next one to five years, as Amodei said, you can see the dinosaurs trudging to their deaths. He and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman are such quizzical figures: so dreadfully immature about the power of their words, so cavalier about the consequences. How do they know jobs will disappear? Why can't they see AI's positives — even recursive systems, where gremlins create more gremlins — could create new jobs and maybe more of them? Why be so downbeat that it gives ammo to AI's biggest haters? Can't they just say, "Some good, some bad?" Can't they at least relate their own work to previous industrial revolutions, giving a nod to the optimistic yet historical Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang? Why embrace the hysterical over the historical? So we are supposed to side with them? In the end, could the AI leaders' own hubris — all this much ado about nothing — kill Anthropic's IPO? That would be worse than the electorate rejecting the AI buildout itself. That wouldn't be a nail in the coffin; it would be cremation. What's the reality? There will be plenty of data centers built either way. But the big move from December, when we realized how gigantic the build-out could be, still seems destined to be continually reversed. Does it go back to December? The country's in a mood to turn negative on the AI players. So we have more bans and more siting issues, and we have to take numbers down no matter what. That was the proximate cause of last week's debacle. Second? Nvidia. As you know, Nvidia has been my favorite stock for ages. It makes the most money. It is the sun around which all the data center planets revolve. But Nvidia is starting to look like what Richard Nixon called the United States in 1970: a "pitiful, helpless giant." Nvidia is the pitiful, helpless giant, now revealed, according to the bears, to have just propped up an ecosystem for its own earnings, with a CEO now revealed to be a dubious character. Now your author, showing fealty to the man and his company, completely disagrees. According to a report in The New York Times last week, Huang formed a close relationship with a top executive at a Singapore-based data center company who was found to be a spy passing information to Beijing. Huang can't stop a customer that appears to need every chip it can get from transshipping some to China. That's been happening for decades. The implication is that President Donald Trump was informed of the situation but looked the other way because Huang flattered him — a view even people outside the stock world now hold, thanks to the Times' story. In truth, all executives, every one, play the same game with the president. Trump has identified the winners and he wants to help them. Jensen's just doing what Jensen has always done: selling chips to help his company make money and to ensure the U.S. dominates data center culture. He wanted to sell his chips to China again because he knew it was good for shareholders and for the U.S. if China didn't develop its own ecosystem and instead relied on Nvidia's. There isn't more to it. But I also know that my view was irrelevant. The writing on the wall says the reverse continues, and the pirouette rally-to-intraday crash was the top. It's not too late to sell, but to buy it back when it's right again is very hard. But I concede that the stock is untenable for almost all right now. Why is that? Why have the long knives just gotten sharper? Simple: the hatred for the data center hasn't just reached the electorate. Everyone who is a part of it wants out. We are sick of the neo-clouds and their inability to pull off what they said they could. We are dubious about their balance sheets. We know their bonds suck. We know their orders are suspect. Most important, Microsoft is the best stock in this godforsaken group because it trimmed capex just enough to stay within its means. It isn't issuing shares through at-the-market sales that could put a lid on the stock. Its core business isn't eroding, as at Google. And it isn't promising that returns are just around the corner, as Amazon is. Amazon's results echoed Gertrude Stein's line in "Sacred Emily": a miss is a miss is a miss. Microsoft is now praised for being reasonable with its spending. That's not what you want to hear if you own Micron , Iren or Nebius . The latter two are vulnerable and are only propped up by the ridiculous amount of short interest. Amazon, though, gets chastised for trying to meet its customers' demands. CEO Andy Jassy and CFO Brian Olsavsky are willing to spend beyond their means because they see a moment when they could win. They see that Alphabet's core business, aside from Google Cloud, has become a mess because it seems to be set up now for its advertisers, not its customers. And it's happening at the very moment when its AI assistant Gemini has dropped back below ChatGPT, Claude, and even Grok. Jassy seems to recognize that Google is hobbled — something that makes me want to sell our position. We've held on because of its lower valuation and my belief that its leaders aren't chowderheads, oblivious to how serious the threat is. Jassy knows that Microsoft is getting credit now, but won't two years from now when Amazon Web Services is still growing at 40%, and its retail business is closing in on a trillion dollars. He is in the driver's seat, even if the spending is momentarily punishing shareholders. Unlike Intel, which investors now despise, Amazon said there will be a huge return on its spending beginning in the second half of 2027, when its semiconductor business takes off for massive profitability. Believe Jassy at your own peril? Or let 'er ride? I am in the latter camp, which comes off right now as a death wish, but I am not a hedge fund manager, and I won't be judged by short-term thinking. And lastly, there are the stocks themselves. I'll tease you with a few thoughts now and save the in-depth analysis for Friday's Annual Meeting. Suffice it to say, nearly all of the quarterly results have been excellent, with one exception: Kioxia , the Japanese memory chipmaker, lowered its guidance. That doesn't just show that Kioxia is a mess, but also that the group is unreliable despite SK Hynix's extraordinary numbers. Sure, GE Vernova ruined the short term, and yes, Caterpillar became more of a truck company, and we didn't get the order spike from Lam , but earnings aren't reverting to pre-2025 levels. And the stocks shouldn't revert to December of 2025, before they levitated. Yet, should doesn't matter. At this very moment, we are looking at the denouement and trying to figure out whether it will come after the election and the president's move to send oil to the $150s. We are trying to figure out if Marvell Tech 's bid for Lumentum actually happens and whether it sends both stocks up or down, the latter being dreadful and giving us nowhere to run, nowhere to hide. So I leave you with the mindset of every long manager except the braindead or the brainwashed, and I at least have given you how people feel, with the best possibility being that the election is a clearing event and the neoclouds don't collapse and crumble regardless of the outcome. (See here for a full list of the stocks in Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust.) As a subscriber to the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer, you will receive a trade alert before Jim makes a trade. Jim waits 45 minutes after sending a trade alert before buying or selling a stock in his charitable trust's portfolio. If Jim has talked about a stock on CNBC TV, he waits 72 hours after issuing the trade alert before executing the trade. articles.title: Judge dismisses Alaska Senate election lawsuit; DOJ vows appeal
articles.text:
A federal judge on Sunday dismissed the Department of Justice's extraordinary lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the Alaska Senate election if incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan loses, citing possible voter confusion from another candidate with his name on the ballot.
The ruling came two days before Election Day and two days after the U.S. Attorney for Alaska said ongoing criminal and civil investigations into non-incumbent Dan J. Sullivan's decision to run for the Senate.
The campaign of Democratic nominee Mary Peltola, state election officials and outside advocacy groups had asked Judge Sharon Gleason to dismiss the DOJ's lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Anchorage.
The Department of Justice quickly filed a notice of its intention to appeal the decision to the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals.
Peltola is locked in a tight contest with Sen. Dan Sullivan, whose winner will be determined by a ranked-choice system.
The outcome of the race is one of several contests that determine which party has a Senate majority, where Republicans currently hold a narrow lead.
Neither the other Sullivan nor the fourth candidate on the ballot, Gerald Heikes, is considered a contender.
But voters who rank them as a first choice could swing the outcome by ranking Peltola or Sen. Sullivan second.
Peltola's campaign has been accused of encouraging retired schoolteacher Dan Sullivan to run for the Senate against the incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and Peltola.
Her campaign has denied those claims.
"No sham investigation or baseless lawsuit from a weaponized Department of Justice is going to stop Alaskans from electing Mary on November 3rd so she can lower costs for Alaska's working families," Peltola's campaign said in a statement after Sunday's ruling.
"Alaskans will choose their next U.S. Senator – not Dan Sullivan or his DC allies," the campaign said.
In her 20-page decision, Gleason did not resolve whether another Sullivan had been recruited to confuse voters.
Instead, she said the federal government had failed to establish that it had legal standing to file a civil complaint to postpone certification of the election if Sen. Sullivan lost.
In that event, the DOJ wanted an investigation into voter intent and possible confusion from having two Dan Sullivans on the ballot.
"The absence of any explanation from the United States as to how its requested relief could redress its alleged injury while simultaneously maintaining the secrecy of the ballot is telling," Gleason said in her ruling.
She noted that early voting in the state was already underway, and that ballots already cast have been commingled in a way that would prevent officials from linking individual ballots to voters.
"More fundamentally, the United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified 'investigation' of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy," Gleason wrote.
The judge also cited a Supreme Court decision that established the so-called Purcell principle, which "strongly cautions" against courts altering election rules on the eve of election.
She noted that DOJ claimed it was not seeking to alter the "time, place or manner of Alaska's election."
But at the same time, Gleason said, the DOJ was asking her for an order "preventing the State
from certifying the election if certain circumstances occur; a court order requiring the State to segregate and preserve certain ballots; and a court order permitting the United States to conduct an investigation into the intent of those voters who cast ballots for Daniel J. Sullivan."
"These requests certainly involve the time, place, and manner of Alaska's election, which are the responsibilities of the State, not the executive branch of the federal government," Gleason said.
The judge said she would not allow the DOJ to amend the lawsuit, which was revised last week to add a new legal claim under the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution to the first claim under the National Voter Registration Act. The amended complaint also added details of a New York Times article about the alleged recruitment of the second Sullivan.
"The Court finds that further amendment would be futile because this Court lacks the authority to order that certain ballots cast by Alaskans be segregated so that federal law enforcement officials can conduct an unspecified investigation of the voters who cast them," Gleason said.
A DOJ spokesperson said in a statement, "The court dismissed the case on procedural grounds but did not dispute the argument of the United States that Daniel J. Sullivan (a/k/a Decoy Dan) entered the race as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters."
"DOJ plans to file a notice of appeal," the spokesperson said. "Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes."
The White House, when asked for comment, referred CNBC to the DOJ's statement.
President Donald Trump has said he ordered the lawsuit, which was filed Oct. 22.
Trump argued that Peltola and other Democrats had recruited the former school teacher to run in hopes of confusing voters who wanted to cast their ballots for Sen. Sullivan.
Trump, in his first comments after the ruling, said: "So we have two Dan Sullivans. This is voter fraud at the highest level. But the Democrat candidate who is involved in the scheme, Mary Peltola, should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted."
The New York Times on Wednesday reported that Peltola campaign aides and DSCC aides had been involved in efforts to recruit the retiree for the race.
Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have denied having any involvement in his campaign.
DSCC Executive Director Devan Barber said in a statement, "Today's ruling is a victory for democracy and a clear message to Donald Trump and Senate Republicans: No one, no matter how powerful, can toss out free and fair elections just because they don't like the result."
"We will never stop fighting back against the shameful, brazen efforts from the Trump administration and their weaponized Department of Justice to subvert the U.S. Senate race in Alaska, or any other election as voters reject Republicans at ballot boxes across the country – and we are confident Alaska voters will elect Mary Peltola to the Senate," Barber said.
Sen. Sullivan, in an interview on CNN before Gleason issued her ruling, said he would accept the election results if he lost.
But he also blasted Peltola's campaign and the DSCC.
"Recognizing they couldn't run on their record, so they had to cheat," Sullivan said. "I think a lot of Alaskans, even Democrats, are thinking she is not fit for office; she's continually lying to the Alaskan people, and I guarantee you she's lying right now."
Alaska election officials have pointed to steps they took to avoid voter confusion on the ballots for the race.
The ballots list Sen. Sullivan as "Dan S. Sullivan," with the words "incumbent" and "registered Republican" next to his name.
The other Sullivan is listed as "Daniel J. Sullivan," with no other words next to his name.
Election officials originally had blocked the retired teacher from the primary ballot. But a state judge allowed him on the ballot. Alaska's Supreme Court upheld that ruling.

articles.title: Here are 3 big things we're watching in the stock market in the week ahead
articles.text: The busiest week of third-quarter earnings season ended on a sour note. The market could use a few victories in the days ahead, which will be filled with more quarterly reports and updates on the health of the U.S. labor market. Another big variable: the outcome of Tuesday's midterm elections, which will determine which party controls the House and Senate for the next two years. There are six Club stocks reporting earnings this week, and the jobs data will also influence expectations for future Federal Reserve policy. 1. Our focus here is stocks, not politics. But the elections across the country cannot be ignored , given the implications for the AI buildout trade if anti-data-center politicians rack up big victories. If the opposite happens, we're likely to get a relief rally. In addition, President Donald Trump has said he's waiting for the midterms to pass before ordering any new military action against Iran. If tensions are ratcheted up, that could spell bad news for oil prices, bond yields and future inflation — all potential headwinds for equities. Now, let's get into what to expect from our portfolio companies and the jobs report. 2. Earnings: Apple will kick things off Monday after the close. This will be John Ternus' first call as CEO, and he's got his work cut out for him. The iPhone 18 Pro, Duo, and new Mac and home-device offerings give him plenty to work with. However, the stakes have been raised after Intel's disastrous guidance for the current quarter was attributed to inflation-induced demand pressure in the PC market. Therefore, it's the outlook Apple management provides at the end of the prepared remarks that will determine the stock reaction. We're seeking answers to two big questions: Is demand for Apple's products holding up better than the overall market thanks to a more affluent customer base? And how are gross margins looking? Apple has already implemented a series of price hikes on some of its hardware offerings due to rising memory costs, but margins can still be squeezed if the full increase wasn't passed through. Management has to balance price hikes against the risk of demand destruction. Given the hardware memory situation, Apple's high-margin Services business becomes all the more important. As a revenue stream entirely separate from memory costs, we're interested in how much it can protect Apple's overall profitability. Revenue: $ 113.4 billion EPS: $1.99 The question for Eaton is less about big-picture demand for its data center products, as results from Alphabet's Google Cloud, Microsoft , and Amazon indicate the AI buildout is very much intact. Rather, it's about how much progress Eaton has made in increasing manufacturing capacity, and if that's led to further margin expansion. Pricing is another tailwind for Eaton, which reports Tuesday morning. We're also interested in hearing about the progress made in integrating Boyd Thermal , which added liquid cooling to Eaton's portfolio of power distribution units, switchgear, transformers, and other electrical equipment. Any updates on the planned divestiture of its mobility unit , which has been a drag on overall growth, are also helpful. Aerospace missed the mark last quarter, though it was up roughly 13% year over year, so we'll be looking for improvement there. Overall, keep in mind that order growth is a key metric beyond reported sales. The reason? Orders reflect current demand, while sales represent past demand that's been fulfilled — and investors are always looking toward the future. Revenue: $8.5 billion EPS: $3.54 DuPont , which specializes in materials used across a ton of end markets, including healthcare, water safety, construction, automotive, and aerospace, also reports Tuesday. Generally, organic sales growth is a key metric to watch. By end market, healthcare, which includes medical packaging, and water are the ones that excite us most over the long term. The Middle East is an important region for DuPont's water business because countries there rely on advanced purification technologies to provide clean drinking water. It has faced some disruption due to the war in Iran (delayed shipments, project timeline shifts), though it's all been manageable, and strength in the industrial water and semiconductor markets has provided an offset. Will that continue to be the case? Another war-related note: the market will be sensitive to how oil and gas inflation is affecting EBITDA margins (the full-year guide includes a 30-basis-point headwind). Lastly, can growth in non-residential construction minimize the impact of sluggish home construction in the U.S.? Revenue: $1.84 billion EPS: $1.87 Qnity Electronics reports Wednesday, and shares of the semiconductor materials supplier are down almost 20% since the company's blowout earnings report in early August . Is the decline warranted, or will it prove to be a massive opportunity? Considering Intel's guidance on the worsening PC slowdown, commentary on current-quarter demand will carry more weight than the September-quarter results. Can possible weakness in consumer electronics be fully offset by strength in AI chip manufacturing? Intel also flagged a shortage of advanced organic substrates that is limiting chip output. We'll be listening for whether those bottlenecks are disrupting customers' production plans and, by extension, orders for Qnity's materials. Any early commentary on 2027 will be notable, as investors consider the potential for upside amid the AI buildout. Revenue: $1.49 billion EPS: $1.20 This is a market interested in defensive names, and Cardinal Health , which reports Thursday morning, fits the bill. But with shares less than 2% from their all-time highs, there's little room for error. Investors have come to love Cardinal for its ability to deliver double-digit earnings growth, so exceeding EPS estimates is the place to start. On Oct. 1 , Cardinal said it renewed its distribution deal with CVS Health through 2032. Expect analysts to seek color on the economics of that agreement, which lifted an overhang on shares. Other topics to watch for: How are shipments of generic medicines trending? This is a key profit driver for Cardinal, reported within its Pharmaceutical and Specialty Solutions segment. We'll also look for updates on the performance of higher-margin growth areas such as nuclear pharmaceuticals, direct-to-home delivery, and its OptiFreight healthcare logistics platform. These businesses are reported within Cardinal's Other segment. Finally, the impact of high oil prices on its Global Medical Products and Distribution segment — which delivers medical, surgical, and laboratory products to hospitals and ambulatory surgery centers — is worth monitoring. Revenue: $66.6 billion EPS: $2.94 Kimberly-Clark joins Cardinal before the bell Thursday, though the maker of Huggies and Scotts toilet paper already preannounced better-than-feared results on Oct. 15, taking away some of the intrigue. The release of preliminary financial results was likely tied to Kimberly-Clark's efforts to close its blockbuster acquisition of Tylenol maker Kenvue , which is supposed to close by year-end. Could we hear something this coming week? For its part, Kenvue reported better-than-expected sales Friday. Away from Kenvue, we hope to get updates on how Kimberly-Clark is managing cost inflation (including on logistics); sales trends in China now that regulators have pushed back on social-media claims that its diapers contained a toxic chemical; and the outlook for its professional business in the wake of customers working down existing inventory at a faster rate than they placed new orders. Revenue: $4.13 billion EPS: $1.64 3. Jobs, jobs, jobs: This week's slate of economic data is all about the labor market. The main event is Friday's October nonfarm payrolls report, with economists expecting 75,000 payroll additions and the unemployment rate remaining at 4.2% . The jobs report arrives with inflation running well above the Fed's 2% target, potentially forcing central bankers to raise rates in the coming months after making no change at last week's policy meeting. For this reason, it's crucial that unemployment remain at bay so that the Fed has the breathing room it needs to curtail inflation. As of Friday, the CME FedWatch Tool puts the odds of a quarter-point hike at just under 75% at the December meeting. Leading up to Friday, we'll get the September JOLTS (jobs openings and labor turnover survey) report on Tuesday and ADP's October employment survey. The JOLTS report provides insight into labor market tightness by tracking job openings, hires, quits, layoffs/discharges, and other causes of separation. However, the data is a month old, and we already know the net number of jobs added to the economy in September, so it's the least consequential of the three labor-market updates. The ADP data, on the other hand, is often used by investors to game the nonfarm payrolls report, though it only covers private-sector hiring. Other economic reports to keep an eye on include the Institute for Supply Management's monthly manufacturing report, out Monday, and the Census Bureau's factory orders report, out Tuesday, both of which provide insight into the state of manufacturing. The ISM's look at services activity will be released Wednesday. articles.title: Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy has stroke and is in the hospital, office says
articles.text:
Sen. Chris Murphy, a Connecticut Democrat, was hospitalized Saturday after suffering a stroke at his son's hockey game, his office announced on Sunday.
Murphy is "awake and alert," according to a statement from his chief of staff, Allison Herwitt.
"Yesterday afternoon, Senator Murphy started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son's hockey game. He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke. He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment," Herwitt said.
Johns Hopkins Hospital's main campus is in Baltimore, though it has other locations in and around Washington.
"The doctors are encouraged by his progress," Herwitt said. "We are optimistic he will make a full recovery."
Murphy, who came to the Senate in 2013, is not up for reelection on Tuesday, but he's been crisscrossing the country campaigning for Democratic candidates, with recent stops in Michigan, Minnesota and Florida. He was due in New Hampshire on Sunday to campaign with Democratic Senate candidate Rep. Chris Pappas.
He's seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate and is a prolific Democratic fundraiser.
Murphy, 53, spent six years in the House before running for the Senate. He rose to national prominence as an advocate for stricter gun control laws in the wake of the Sandy Hook shooting, which occurred in his home state. He's been a vocal critic of President Donald Trump and has opposed the war in Iran and the White House's deportation policies.
He's one of multiple sitting senators to suffer a stroke in recent years.
Democratic Sens. Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland each had a stroke in 2022. And Sen. John Fetterman, D-Penn., who was then running for office, suffered a stroke just days before his state's Senate Democratic primary.
"Thinking of my great friend & colleague, Chris Murphy. I know how fiercely he fights & I'm certain I'll be welcoming him back to the Senate soon," Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a fellow Connecticut Democrat, posted to X on Sunday.
This story is developing. Please refresh for updates.

articles.title: Democratic Rep. Stevens endorses Republican Rogers over rival El-Sayed in Michigan Senate election
articles.text:
Michigan Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, in a stunning move, endorsed Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers over Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday.
Stevens lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed earlier this year, but since then had backed his candidacy.
Her endorsement of Rogers came after days of rising tension with El-Sayed and his campaign over an inflammatory ad by a political action committee, Rebellion PAC, which depicted a couple debating whether they could afford groceries due to U.S. support for Israel.
El-Sayed's campaign has said it was not involved or affiliated with the ad.
The stunning endorsement was announced two days before Election Day, when voters will decide which party will control Congress for President Donald Trump's final two years in the White House. The outcome of the Michigan Senate race could determine which party holds a majority in the Senate, where Republicans currently hold a slim majority.
"Hey Michigan, as you may have seen, our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul, said I'm no longer welcome in his campaign, and I should stay away, and he's right," Stevens said in a video statement on X.
"And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today," she said.
"I don't belong in Abdul's campaign. I do not stand with Hasan Piker, who gets trafficked on our college campuses," said Stevens.
Piker is a controversial political commentator who has campaigned with El-Sayed.
El-Sayed, standing with Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., and Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md., outside a church on Sunday, dismissed Stevens endorsement of his opponent.
"I actually don't think about Haley Stevens," El-Sayed said. "There are families that are preparing to send their kids to schools tomorrow that look like they did 50 years ago. They're worried about what they're going to feed their kids for lunch. They're worried that if one of their kids gets sick, they're not going to be able to pay the bills. Those are the things that matter."
Rogers and El-Sayed are vying for a seat set to become vacant after Democratic Sen. Gary Peters decided not to seek re-election.
In recent weeks, a deepening rift has worsened between El-Sayed and Stevens. At the center of it is U.S. support for Israel, which was a major issue in the primary contest.
Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel; El-Sayed has called the country's conduct in Gaza after the Oct. 7, 2023, terror attacks by the radical group Hamas a genocide.
Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, endorsed Rogers before Stevens' flip-flop, citing what he said was rising antisemitism.
"I'm sorry people are upset," Stevens told reporters at a press conference in Detroit, standing with Rogers, whom she had attended church with Sunday morning.
"I understand that," she said.
Staffers in Stevens congressional office quit following her endorsement.
"As of this morning, many members of our team have resigned, including myself," Justin German, Stevens' chief of staff for eight years, said in a statement obtained by MS NOW.
"We are shocked and heartbroken by Congresswoman Stevens' decision to support Mike Rogers," German said, adding that he was speaking on behalf of the team "in wholeheartedly supporting Abdul El-Sayed for Senate," German said.
Stevens had the endorsement of much of the Democratic establishment during the bruising primary, making her endorsement of Rogers even more stunning.
She was the preferred candidate of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York, who on Sunday reiterated his support for El-Sayed and accused Republicans of Islamophobia.
"Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors," Schumer said. "We Democrats [are] equally united in our total revulsion at the racist, Islamophobic, and over-the-top false attacks on Abdul by Republicans."
In a later post to X, Schumer called her endorsement of Rogers "a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens."
Peters and Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin both disavowed Stevens for her endorsement.
"[A]nyone who makes an election this important about themselves, and not Michiganders and our democracy, should think hard about whether they are serving the greater good," Slotkin said in a post to X.
Curtis Hertel, the chair of the Michigan Democratic Party, appeared to suggest that Stevens had been kicked out of the party.
"Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future," he said in an X post.
In a Truth Social post, Trump praised Stevens' endorsement.
"Congresswoman Haley Stevens, a Highly Respected Democrat, who narrowly lost in the Primary to Abdul Mohamed El-Sayed, and who has been breathlessly wined and dined by the Dumocrats to help in their Michigan Campaign for the United States Senate against Mike Rogers, has just ENDORSED Mike Rogers for Senate!" the president said.
"Her following is huge, and the level of respect from the People of Michigan, especially our African American and Jewish populations, is virtually unparalleled," he said.

articles.title: Alaska Sen. Sullivan says he'll accept election results, slams Peltola campaign’s reported recruitment of 2nd Sullivan
articles.text:
Alaska Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan said Sunday he would accept the results of Tuesday's midterm elections, while slamming Democratic candidate Mary Peltola's campaign for reportedly recruiting Dan J. Sullivan to run as a spoiler.
"No, I'm going to accept the election results," Sullivan said on CNN's "State of the Union" when asked whether he would accept the results only if he wins. President Donald Trump's Department of Justice has sued Alaska, demanding the state not certify the election if the incumbent Republican loses.
The lawsuit cites theoretical voter confusion over the appearance of the second Sullivan on the ballot, which DOJ says could siphon votes away from the incumbent Republican Sullivan and benefit Peltola. Alaska's Senate race is rated as a "toss-up" by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, and Peltola holds a slight edge in the polling average compiled by FiftyPlusOne.
Peltola has repeatedly denied any involvement with the second Sullivan. However, The New York Times reported last week that her campaign was directly involved with recruiting Dan J. Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher, to run as a spoiler.
Ballot-stacking is typically not illegal, and both parties have used it in past elections. Still, Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered a criminal investigation into the alleged scheme. Alaska's Supreme Court upheld Dan J. Sullivan's place on the ballot during an earlier legal challenge.
Sullivan on CNN said that the Times report shows Peltola's campaign, along with the Democratic Senate campaign arm, "recognizing they couldn't run on their record, so they had to cheat."
"I think a lot of Alaskans, even Democrats, are thinking she is not fit for office; she's continually lying to the Alaskan people, and I guarantee you she's lying right now," Sullivan said.
Peltola denied any knowledge of the alleged scheme to draft a second Sullivan in an interview with KTUU on Friday.
"I honestly have no idea," Peltola said. "This is offensive to me on a number of different levels; first of all, this is Alaska, we're not in the business of tricking each other up here."
"I've won statewide before, on my own merits, without any tricks involved; I know I can win again," she said.
The stakes of the Alaska race are high. Democrats need to flip four seats while holding all currently Democratic seats to win a Senate majority. Alaska has emerged as a top opportunity for one of those flips.
The midterms will determine which party controls Congress for the remainder of Trump's term in the White House.

articles.title: Everything changed for the oil, AI and bond trades over the past month
articles.text:
If there was one safe bet over the course of 2026, it was that treasury yields would rise alongside a move up in oil futures contracts. Over the past month, that ended, and according to Jeffrey Rosenberg, senior portfolio manager of the Systematic Alternatives ETF (IALT) at BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, the breakdown in that trade has big implications for the market.
"Oil and treasury yields had this amazing correlation and in October it just stopped," Rosenberg said on the most recent CNBC "ETF Edge."
The relationship between oil and bond yields was featured in Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's FOMC press conference on Wednesday, with Warsh noting how oil futures have continued to rise, a factor the central bank must consider in its fight against inflation. But Rosenberg said what Warsh didn't talk about was "the most important takeaway."
"Treasuries and oil had an 80% correlation this year," Rosenberg said, which is "outsize" relative to normal correlations. "We've basically been trading off oil for good reason." "
What happened? Rosenberg says you can sum it up by looking to the deflated AI trade. As the market moved away from that oil-treasuries trading correlation in October, "It told us something important," he said. "In the market's mind, the geopolitical risk is secondary to AI risk," he said.
Over the past month — which became most painfully clear in Friday's Nasdaq market wipeout and, earlier the week, Google's biggest single-day decline in its history, wiping out half a trillion dollars in value — the AI trade experienced a retracement. Bond yields went lower, Rosenberg says, because the market is equating weakness in the AI trade as a broader weakness in the U.S. economy. And he said, last week's GDP report backed up that thinking. "AI is everything, everywhere, all the time," he said. Both the growth for the economy on the investment side and the wealth effect on the consumption side are all AI, he said.
"Q3 GDP was a blowout [number] and all AI-related," Rosenberg said on the "ETF Edge" podcast extended conversation. He pointed to equipment investment increases and consumption well above expectations and both fueled by the AI wealth effect, which with the latter is even more notable given that real incomes have been coming down in the U.S.
Business investment of 12.7% in Q3 was the biggest increase outside the pandemic since 2011, led by a 37% rise in information processing equipment. Industrial equipment investment rose nearly 25%, which while not a straight AI trade, does partially reflect spending on data centers.
Warsh did not agree in his assessment of the economy at the FOMC press conference. "It is convenient to say that the strength of the economy is all about this new technology wave. In fact, if we look at the data, really including data from the last meeting until this, the capex story is not just robust, not just strong, but it is broadening. And so if you wanted to tell the story somehow that this is strength we're seeing only in narrow pockets, that's a much harder story to tell now than it would have been several quarters ago," he said.
It is true that market breadth, a measure of how many stocks within the S&P 500 were showing positive trading momentum, improved significantly in October after having reached a 2026 low by late September, and as defensive sectors of the stock market like healthcare and staples rallied. But Rosenberg says the conclusion that the broader October market came to is that any "wobble" in the AI trade is going to be seen as a wobble in the growth outlook for the U.S., and as disinflationary. And in a disinflationary environment, there is "only one thing that hedges," he said, and that is "the thing everyone wants to hate. ... the long end of the treasury curve."
"That's the really important lesson from last month of market performance," he said.
Despite this view, Rosenberg is cautious about suggesting that this dynamic makes bonds a safe bet. "The simple answer is it's not a return to normal, where normal was bonds hedging stocks," he said.
That is because of the conflicting forces on bonds. Oil price increases and the persistent level of inflation above target are not going away as challenges to fixed-income assets and the "efficacy," Rosenberg said, of fixed income as a hedge.
"There's too much inflation and that limits the ability of the Fed to provide accommodation, and we haven't gotten away from that," he said. "But what we've learned in the last month is if it's big enough, if the AI trend turns against the macroeconomy and inflationary trends, it can bring about a wholesale change in that direction that's disinflationary and bonds may react like they did in October," he said.
Still, he says investors should not bet the trade will be one-directional or come without a potential cost. Investors need to weigh the potential diversification benefit from bonds based on the October action versus a scenario in which AI does not unravel the economy. And the longer the AI boom persists, coupled with the broader fiscal challenges in the U.S., "bonds will be challenged," he said.
How to trade the AI hyperscaler debt boom
The AI trade itself is a very big piece of the bond market, and that showed up over the past week in a major way between both the Google earnings decline and Microsoft coming back into the public bond market. "It was a surprise to the markets. It hadn't been back in close to a decade," Rosenberg said.
As the capex needs of the tech giants begin to overwhelm their free cash flow more regularly, the public bond markets are coming to terms with an expected flood of issuance. "When the bonds markets, the public bond markets, look at where it is all coming from ... it's a huge marginal issuer, and its increasingly all coming again and again," he said.
The hyperscalers are reaching the limits of the financing that bank loan and private credit markets can offer and while Rosenberg stressed that a $40 trillion to $60 trillion global bond market can absorb an expected $4 trillion in AI debt over the next four years, "the market is not unlimited in capacity."
That demand will lead to lower prices and higher spreads, though Microsoft's deal attracted huge investor interest and was oversubscribed.
Rosenberg said it's a good thing that more of the hyperscale debt is being pushed into the public bond market because it means there will be more transparency in the form of bond prices and CDS spreads. While spreads on Microsoft credit default swaps are currently trading near a five-year high, roughly 55, they are still a world away from Oracle CDS spreads, by comparison, which are closer to 300. That presents another trading opportunity for investors who may not want to buy bonds outright given the inflationary environment and fiscal challenges in the U.S., but may still be looking for ways to hedge bets on the AI boom.
"That old tool from the Great Financial Crisis," he said. "Short it. You can trade two ways in [public] credit markets and you can't do that in bank loans and private credit. But once they start going in public markets, you can do that."
Rosenberg said a 12% down day in Google is "not even on the chart" historically. "So it's moving into a different zip code, if you will, of market pricing and market volatility and market indigestion. It's not the end of the world, it's just a different world of the AI buildout," he said, with the greater transparency in the public bond market giving investors more ability to trade "the emotional swings between fear and greed," he said.
What the CDS market is telling investors with the large-cap hyperscaler names, according to Rosenberg, is not that the prospect of default is high, but that as all the companies try to access more debt financing, the capacity of the banks and financial intermediaries to find counter-parties for the risk is becoming more limited.
"Think about financial markets and these big investment booms. They don't move in one direction. They ratchet up, reset." But with the AI boom, it's only been "the positive part," Rosenberg said. "It's still an incredibly positive story, but you get a little of the balance with the AI pessimism."

articles.title: I'm a psychologist who studies couples: People in the happiest relationships do 1 thing differently after time apart—whether it's hours, days or weeks
articles.text:
There's a two-minute window every evening when couples can either strengthen their bond with each other or unknowingly weaken it.
In my experience as a psychologist who studies couples, what separates the happy couples from the unhappy ones isn't necessarily how often they argue or how much time they have together. It's whether the two people are genuinely in contact with each other's lives.
Partners in happy relationships know what the other one is really going through, week after week. The unhappy ones have often slipped into a kind of parallel coexistence, where they share a home and a calendar and not much else.
That difference can be built or lost in moments that may feel too small to matter. I call them "reentry moments."
What 'reentry moments' look like
"Reentry moments" are the first minute or two when a couple comes back together after time apart. These reunions follow any period of temporary physical separation, whether that's a workday, a weekend away with friends or a four-day work trip.
They serve three key functions:
- Coaxing your partner out of their head and into the present moment
- Gauging where your partner is emotionally
- Getting an update on your partner's day (or weekend or week)
Let's say your wife mentioned in the morning that she had a presentation that day. You get home and see her, as usual, with her laptop on the couch. You ask her, "How was your presentation?"
She stops typing, sets the laptop on the coffee table and tells you that no one really responded to it, and just thanked her and moved on. She spent the rest of her afternoon turning the presentation over in her head, trying to figure out what went wrong.
Connecting as soon as you reunite keeps you from misreading each other. If your wife is still thinking about the presentation and you ask whether she booked the rental car for your trip next week, the annoyance in her response can sound like annoyance with you. You might snap back, and now you're arguing about the rental car when neither of you cares about it.
There's a longer-term benefit, too. When your partner knows the first few minutes at home will be met with interest rather than judgment or indifference, they don't have to decide what's worth telling you and what to keep to themselves. They can just walk in knowing they're entering their safe landing space.
Why skipping a 'reentry moment' matters
Early in a relationship, nobody has to work hard to harness this moment. You simply want the details of your partner's day, and if you get the three-word version, you ask again. Years in, you may stop following up.
You might slip into a routine where you share a greeting, ask a question about dinner or tomorrow's schedule and go about your evening. Nothing overtly unkind happens in that exchange, and both partners might describe it as "fine." But you know slightly less about your partner with each flubbed reentry.
After a few hundred repetitions, you start working from an out-of-date picture of your partner. You don't know their new manager has suddenly started checking in on them three times a day. Or that they got into it with their sister on the phone an hour ago. So when they're unusually quiet at dinner, you might assume that something is wrong between the two of you.
Skipping this small but crucial moment makes it harder to understand and anticipate your partner's needs, whether that means taking over a chore, canceling a plan or leaving them alone for an hour. Being well-meaning but uninformed might look the same to your partner as not caring.
Eventually, you can lose more than just information; you start losing the close connection you share with your partner.
How to reconnect with your partner after time apart
Getting it right means deliberately stepping out of the "How was your day?" routine and trying something different:
- Be specific. "How was your day?" asks your partner to sum up eight hours on the spot, a daunting task, which is why it usually gets a one-word answer. Ask about something you already knew was happening that day. "Did your manager say anything?" shows you remembered what was on their mind yesterday. It's also much easier to answer honestly, and can lead to a more meaningful exchange.
- Follow up. Once they've told you something, keep going with it rather than moving to another subject. In my experience, a single follow-up question tends to get you further than several new ones.
- Tell your partner if you're depleted. If you have nothing left to give right at that crucial moment, say so rather than going quiet, because "I want to hear about it, I just need 20 minutes" lands very differently than silence.
- Make sure it runs both ways. Couples tend to fall into roles here without realizing it, where one person does most of the telling and the other does most of the listening. Usually, that's just a matter of who has more energy in the evening. But it means the listener's own day gradually stops getting shared.
- Act on it. All of this only counts if something comes of it. If you learn your partner had a difficult week and then carry on exactly as you were, the conversation hasn't done much for either of you. What makes a good "reentry moment" worth the effort is that it gives you something to act on, whether that's letting them sleep in the next day or planning a special date.
Over time, taking these steps can be part of what keeps two people attuned and responsive to each other rather than simply living side by side.
Mark Travers, Ph.D., is a psychologist who specializes in relationships. He holds degrees from Cornell University and the University of Colorado Boulder. He is the lead psychologist at Awake Therapy, a telehealth company that provides online psychotherapy, counseling and coaching. He is also the curator of the popular mental health and wellness website Therapytips.org.

articles.title: These Senate races may help determine the fate of Social Security
articles.text:
Senators elected this November must answer a crucial question before their six-year term ends: What will they do to fix Social Security?
The program's trustees project that the trust fund Social Security relies on to help pay retirement benefits may be depleted in the fourth quarter of 2032. Without action from Congress before then, those benefits could be cut by 22%.
Lawmakers may enact reforms to prevent those automatic cuts. Or they may kick the can down the road.
Most voters — 81% — say they are more likely to support a candidate who has a plan to avoid automatic benefit cuts to Social Security over a candidate who promises not to touch the program, according to a recent survey of voters in states with competitive Senate races by the Peter G. Peterson Foundation, a nonpartisan organization.
Even so, many Senate candidates' campaign platforms lack specifics on plans for the program's future.
While 35 Senate seats are up for grabs in November, including in special elections in Florida and Ohio, CNBC identified nine races where the candidates have mentioned their plans for the program's future. MS NOW says all nine races are closely contested battlegrounds, and it rates the possible outcomes.
Here is a closer look at those nine contests and what the candidates in those races have said about Social Security reform.
ALASKA
Alaska voters will choose between incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola, who served in the House from 2022 to 2025.
During his latest term, Sullivan voted yes on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which provided a new temporary senior tax deduction of up to $6,000 per eligible individual. Sullivan also voted for the Social Security Fairness Act, which ended reductions to certain government pensioners' Social Security checks. While both laws helped beneficiaries, they increased the program's costs.
Most older Alaska voters — 90% — say they are more likely to support a candidate who will ensure they receive the Social Security benefits they've earned, according to a September AARP survey.
During the 2014 Alaska Senate campaign, Sullivan said he would consider options to cut Social Security costs, such as raising the retirement age or means-testing benefits — a point his opponent raised during the 2026 race.
Sullivan's campaign did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment. During an Oct. 15 debate, he said benefits for retirees and near-retirees should be protected and that program reforms must be bipartisan.
Peltola's platform calls for eliminating taxes on Social Security benefits, according to her campaign website. Peltola also co-sponsored the Social Security Fairness Act.
"Mary will stand up to anyone to fight for Alaska seniors and protect the benefits Alaskans have earned," a spokesperson for Peltola's campaign said in an email statement to CNBC.
MS NOW rates the Alaska Senate race a toss-up.
IOWA
In the Hawkeye State, sitting Republican Sen. Joni Ernst is retiring, and the open seat's winner will be decided in a contest between Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek and U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, a Republican.
"One of the best ways to keep Social Security solvent is we have to remove the cap," Turek said at a Sept. 9 Des Moines town hall, referencing the maximum annual earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes.
Raising or eliminating the cap would mean high earners pay more into the program. In 2027, that threshold, adjusted annually, will rise to $192,300 from $184,500 in 2026. Proposals to raise the cap would generally leave that first threshold in place, and then reapply Social Security payroll taxes at a proposed earnings level, such as $250,000 or $400,000.
In a recent AARP interview, Hinson said, "Anyone who's going to propose cuts to Social Security is going to get a 'hell, no' from me." In 2024, Hinson voted on the House Appropriations Committee to cut Social Security Administration funding by up to $452 million.
In 2020, Hinson noted she was "open" to raising the Social Security retirement age but has since said she opposes that change. In the House, she voted for OBBBA and the Social Security Fairness Act.
When the candidates were asked during an Oct. 13 debate about Social Security fixes, both said they would support a bipartisan commission.
A Social Security field office in Hinson's district in Decorah, Iowa, recently closed for six months. Some reports indicated low staffing, and political opponents and advocacy groups blamed Hinson's support for staffing cuts backed by DOGE, President Donald Trump's so-called Department of Government Efficiency. In a June 10 statement, Hinson called the six-month closure "unacceptable" and said she advocated for the office to reopen.
Turek "will protect Social Security by lifting the cap to make billionaires pay their fair share," a campaign spokesperson said in an email statement to CNBC.com.
Hinson's office did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment.
MS NOW rates the Iowa Senate race as "leans Republican."
MAINE
Maine's incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, will face Democrat and former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson on the ballot.
During an Oct. 8 debate, Collins said the payroll tax cap should be "adjusted," signaling support for a largely Democratic proposal that has recently gained bipartisan backing. She also said Congress should create a commission of independent financial experts to advise on how to address the program's funding shortfall.
A September AARP survey found 81% of Maine voters age 50-plus say Social Security is an important issue for deciding their vote. Moreover, 93% said they are more likely to support a candidate who will make sure workers receive the Social Security benefits they've earned.
At the debate, Jackson said the threshold should be raised.
In a recent Bangor Daily News op-ed, Jackson said he wants to increase retirees' Social Security benefits. He also said he opposes privatizing the program and other benefit cuts.
In the op-ed, Jackson also said he will "never support" raising the retirement age. Collins said in a 2023 News Center Maine interview, in response to potential reforms being discussed at that time, that she does not support raising the age to 70.
Collins co-authored the Social Security Fairness Act. She voted against OBBBA in its final vote, citing its Medicaid cuts. However, she did vote "yes" on an earlier motion to further the bill.
Collins' campaign did not respond to CNBC's request for comment.
"Troy will work to scrap the cap and require the wealthy to pay Social Security taxes on their whole income and expand benefits — not raise the retirement age," a Jackson campaign spokesperson said in an emailed statement.
MS NOW rates the Maine Senate race a toss-up.
MICHIGAN
Michigan voters face a choice between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers for Senate. El-Sayed most recently served as Wayne County public health director, and Rogers served as a U.S. representative for Michigan from 2001 to 2015.
El-Sayed said during an Oct. 8 television debate that the Social Security payroll tax cap should be eliminated. "It's only fair that the rich should pay their fair share," he said.
He also said during the debate that taxes on Social Security benefits should be eliminated.
Rogers said during the debate that he supports a "bipartisan solution" through a committee to address the program's funding issues. "Put them in a room, lock the doors and say, 'Don't come out until we have a real solution that can get bipartisan support,'" he said.
An August AARP poll found that 93% of Michigan voters ages 50 and older said they are more likely to support a candidate who will ensure workers receive the Social Security benefits they've earned.
Rogers has not proposed raising the retirement age or privatizing the program during this campaign. However, he has said in the past that he would support raising the retirement age, according to PolitiFact. As a congressman, Rogers previously supported proposals to allow some Social Security payroll taxes to go to private investment accounts, according to the fact-checking website.
A campaign spokesperson said via email that Rogers understands Social Security is "a lifeline for seniors who've spent their entire lives working hard and investing into this state ... Mike will ensure that we invest in them."
El-Sayed's campaign did not respond to CNBC.com's request for comment.
MS NOW rates the Michigan race as a "toss-up."
NEBRASKA
Nebraska voters may choose between Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts and independent candidate Dan Osborn, a labor union leader backed by state Democrats.
Ricketts has said Social Security benefits should be "completely tax-free."
As Nebraska governor, Ricketts signed a 2022 law to phase out state taxes on benefits. As senator, he introduced a similar federal measure, which remains with the finance committee. He also voted for OBBBA. While eliminating taxes on benefits helps recipients, it reduces revenue for the program.
"Nebraskans reaching retirement age deserve to receive the benefits they have earned," Ricketts said in an emailed statement. "I am committed to protecting our seniors' benefits and working to improve the Social Security program for all Americans."
To extend Social Security's solvency, Osborn has called for raising or eliminating the payroll tax cap, according to his campaign website. "The solution is very simple — remove the Social Security cap, so everyone pays their fair share," he said in an email statement to CNBC.
Osborn is against Social Security benefit cuts, including raising the retirement age, and privatization of the program, according to his campaign website.
MS NOW rates the Nebraska Senate race "likely Republican."
NEW HAMPSHIRE
New Hampshire voters in November may choose between two veterans of Congress: Democrat Chris Pappas and Republican John Sununu. Incumbent Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen is not running for reelection.
Pappas, who has served as a U.S. representative since 2019, will "never vote to cut benefits," according to his campaign website. At an August event, he said high earners should pay their "fair share" into the program.
"I also think that seniors deserve a raise," Pappas said at an Oct. 14 AARP candidate forum. Social Security's cost-of-living adjustments have not kept up with the "true cost of living," he said.
Pappas voted for the Social Security Fairness Act. However, he voted against OBBBA, citing its cuts to social safety net programs, including Medicaid.
Sununu has served terms in the Senate and the House of Representatives. During his tenure, Sununu supported bills that would have diverted a portion of payroll taxes to individual investment accounts instead of the Social Security trust funds under a broader push by then-President George W. Bush.
Pappas has said during the campaign that Sununu led efforts to privatize the program — a statement that fact-checking organization PolitiFact said is "mostly true," noting that Sununu's proposals would have been voluntary, limited by age or both. Had the proposal passed, the program would be solvent today, Sununu said in an August WMUR interview.
"I never voted to change or reduce or cut benefits," Sununu said at AARP's candidate forum.
Sununu's campaign did not respond to CNBC's request for comment. Pappas' campaign referred CNBC to his comments on Social Security during the recent AARP forum.
MS NOW rates New Hampshire's Senate contest as "leans Democrat."
NORTH CAROLINA
North Carolina's Senate candidates — former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, and former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley — have raised the issue of Social Security during their campaigns.
Cooper told AARP in September that some members of Congress are "undermining" Social Security by giving the wealthy tax breaks. He told AARP that the program needs to be protected and strengthened: "In the U.S. Senate, I'll work with anyone I can to do just that."
A September AARP poll found 83% of North Carolina voters ages 50 and over say Social Security is an important issue for deciding their vote. Meanwhile, 93% say they are more likely to support a candidate who ensures workers get the benefits they've earned.
Whatley told AARP that his top priority will "always be to preserve and protect" Social Security and that he will not support any proposals that "take away anything from what is owed" to people who have paid into the program.
Whatley also said Congress must work in a "bipartisan way" to improve the program's solvency.
Whatley's campaign did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment.
In an emailed statement, a Cooper campaign spokesperson said: "Roy Cooper will work to protect and strengthen Social Security benefits for current and future generations."
MS NOW rates the North Carolina Senate race as "leans Democrat."
OHIO
Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio is pursuing a comeback bid, running against Republican Sen. Jon Husted. The special election will decide who will serve the remaining two years of the term formerly held by Vice President JD Vance.
As senator, Brown advocated for expanding and protecting Social Security benefits. He co-authored the Social Security Fairness Act.
A June AARP poll found that 83% of Ohio voters ages 50 and older said candidates' positions on Social Security will affect how they vote.
More recently, in an October AARP voter guide video, Brown said he opposes privatizing the program.
"We need to make sure that billionaires are paying their fair share by raising the tax cap so we can extend the life of the program," Brown told AARP.
In AARP's video, Husted said Social Security will require "genuine bipartisan solutions."
Husted voted for OBBBA. He also introduced a constitutional amendment to balance the federal budget, a move critics say may prompt large cuts to Social Security.
Asked about the candidates' plans for Social Security, neither Brown's nor Husted's campaigns gave CNBC more detail.
MS NOW rates the Ohio Senate race as a toss-up.
TEXAS
Voters in the Lone Star State may choose Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, the state's attorney general, or Democratic candidate James Talarico, a state representative and former middle school teacher.
Talarico said that to shore up Social Security he wants to eliminate the Social Security tax cap for individuals earning over $400,000. "I'll ensure the wealthiest Americans pay their fair share into Social Security," Talarico said in an AARP interview published Sept. 1.
A September AARP poll found 91% of Texas voters 50 and older said they would support a candidate who advocates for workers getting the full Social Security benefits they've earned.
Paxton told AARP that Washington "has no business cutting" Social Security benefits. Paxton also said in the interview that one of his goals is "rooting out" what he said is "waste, fraud and abuse" in the program.
Paxton said in a leaked audio recording that "there's no doubt we have to cut some of the mandatory spending," the Texas Tribune reported on Oct. 8. Social Security is among the federal programs funded through mandatory spending. Paxton told the newspaper in a statement that he would protect Social Security.
Paxton's campaign did not respond to CNBC's request for comment.
A spokesperson for Talarico said the candidate will "stand up" against attacks on Social Security and "fight to ensure all Americans can afford to retire."
MS NOW rates the Texas Senate race a toss-up.

articles.title: Mở rộng thị trường dịch vụ kinh doanh robot tại Trung Quốc
articles.text:
Mở rộng thị trường dịch vụ kinh doanh robot tại Trung Quốc
Thị trường robot tại Trung Quốc ngày càng đa dạng với các dịch vụ cho thuê, thiết kế và chế tạo theo yêu cầu, đưa công nghệ robot đến gần hơn với đời sống và sản xuất.
- 02-11-2026Rủi ro bảo mật và thiệt hại tài sản từ giao dịch “in-app purchase”
- 01-11-2026Tin cực vui cho người dùng Claude
- 01-11-2026Đại diện FPT đề xuất hợp tác với doanh nghiệp Nhật Bản phát triển AI cho khu vực công Việt Nam
Tại Trung Quốc, robot đang dần bước ra khỏi phòng thí nghiệm để trở thành những sản phẩm dịch vụ trong đời sống thường ngày. Từ chó robot đến robot hình người phục vụ sự kiện, thị trường này đang ngày càng đa dạng.
Tại thành phố Thâm Quyến, khách hàng không chỉ có thể thuê robot mà còn được đặt hàng, thiết kế sản phẩm theo nhu cầu riêng. Một thị trường dịch vụ mới đang mở ra, nơi công nghệ robot ngày càng đến gần hơn với người tiêu dùng.
Tại khu phố chuyên về AI của thành phố Thâm Quyến, một trong những dịch vụ được quan tâm nhất ở đây là dịch vụ cho thuê robot. Khách hàng có thể lựa chọn từ robot chó, robot hướng dẫn đến robot hình người có khả năng nhảy múa, chào đón khách.
"Chúng tôi có hơn 100 mẫu robot. Các robot chuyên dụng chủ yếu phục vụ những lĩnh vực như vệ sinh thông minh, chăm sóc sức khỏe và chăm sóc người cao tuổi. Chúng tôi cũng cung cấp các giải pháp tùy chỉnh cho từng nhóm nhu cầu", một nhân viên cửa hàng cho hay.
Có nhiều lựa chọn robot từ giải trí, vệ sinh đến vận chuyển và sản xuất. Ngoài thuê, khách hàng cũng có thể tìm kiếm các linh kiện cần thiết hoặc đặt hàng chế tạo robot theo yêu cầu riêng. Ngay trên tuyến phố, có thể dễ dàng mua các linh kiện robot như động cơ servo, bộ điều khiển, cảm biến và bộ giảm tốc, những bộ phận trước đây có thể mất nhiều tháng để tìm kiếm.
Bà Mao Fangping - Quản lý cửa hàng Robot 6S, TP. Thâm Quyến, Trung Quốc cho hay: "Năm nay, số lượng đơn đặt hàng của chúng tôi tăng khoảng 5 lần so với năm 2025. Trước đây, quá trình phát triển từ nghiên cứu đến chế tạo mẫu thử mất ít nhất 6-8 tháng. Hiện nay, một số sản phẩm đặt hàng chế tạo quy mô nhỏ có thể hoàn thành trong 3-4 tháng".
Từ thuê robot để trải nghiệm đến đặt chế tạo theo nhu cầu, những mô hình kinh doanh mới đang giúp công nghệ robot tiếp cận gần hơn với đời sống và hoạt động sản xuất. Robot được xem là đã ra khỏi phòng thí nghiệm và từng bước trở thành những sản phẩm và dịch vụ có thể sử dụng trong thực tế.
